Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why does my boyfriend make rude comments & talk at me like I’m a little girl when he’s mad? He’s older than me & will start saying he needs a woman around his age, calling me little girl and being condescending.
Answer: Rather than wondering “why?”, I think you should walk away and find somebody else. It’s really not worth the aggravation, and he’s not going to get better. Your response to him saying “I need a woman around my age” is, “OK. Bye!”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I've been talking to a married man, and he wants to meet, but I'm scared and don't want to ruin his family. How can I tell him no without hurting him?
Answer: That feeling you have of being scared and not wanting to ruin his family? LISTEN TO IT! You are absolutely right to be feeling that way. You need to run away from this guy as fast as possible, and don’t worry about hurting him.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why are scientists all such pathological liars? Is it because they really don't know anything at all, but have to pretend that they do?
Answer: I’d tell you, but considering I’m such a pathological liar, why would you believe my answer?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If you condemn Trump’s attempted assassination, then why not vote for Trump?
Answer: Simple. The glory of democracy is that I can express my disapproval of someone without wishing them dead or taking a shot at them. That’s the point! An assassin deprives me, and you, and everyone, from exercising their right to vote for whoever they want, and is therefore to be condemned in the strongest possible terms. I’m going to express my disapproval of Trump by voting against him. Assassination sets a country down a dangerous path, where violence is seen as the only way to send a message. This is what happened in Spain and Japan in the 1920s and 1930s, and the result was a disaster. Why would surviving an assassination attempt make you *more* likely to vote for someone?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are some reasons why scientists may conduct unethical experiments?
Answer: For the purposes of this answer I’m defining “unethical” as “mistreatment of human or animal test subjects, or irresponsible handling of hazardous materials”, though that’s not the be-all, end-all of ethics (you could, for instance, lie about your results. That’s unethical practice, but not necessarily an unethical experiment.) Here are some reasons someone might conduct unethical experiments. None of them are good reasons, and none of them justify bad behavior, but they are the temptations that can drive someone to do things they really shouldn’t: 1) Fame. If you conduct some unethical experiment that works out, and is revolutionary, the world tends to sit up and take notice. You can also shoot to fame more quickly. Say, for instance, that you are developing a new medical device. The right way, the ethical way, is to test it in animals first. When you are *very, very sure* (and you can PROVE) that it works in pigs, then maybe you test in monkeys. When you are *very very sure* (and you can PROVE) that it works in monkeys, then you test in humans. But that can take a long time. If you just stick the device into a human and see what happens, you can get a positive result much faster that will generate headlines. Similarly, in psychology, we remember the Stanford Prison Experiment, and Milgram’s Experiment. The ethics of each of them are….questionable. But 50 years later, we’re talking about them and not all the other experiments done at that time whose ethics were impeccable. 2) Impatience. Ethical experimentation requires review by review boards: experiments with animals and humans have to meet certain standards, and have to be peer-reviewed and approved before you can do anything. If you’re working with chemicals, there are safety requirements you have to meet, and you need to make sure you dispose of your waste carefully. So if you’re impatient, you might say “aah, who needs all this red tape anyway?” and cut ethical corners. And as the old saying goes, time is money, meaning another reason is…. 3) Being cheap. Some of the requirements that a review board is going to have will cost money. Safe handling of chemicals and chemical waste will cost money. Now, this can end up being a false economy: say, for instance, you don’t buy the right harness for your pressurized gas cylinders. You save maybe $500. That’s all well and good until a cylinder falls over, its stem breaks, the cylinder launches itself across a room, and totally wrecks any equipment, walls, or people who find themselves in the way, doing a lot more than $500 worth of damage. 4) Complacency and the slippery slope. There have been some truly evil people that never cared about pain or suffering inflicted by their experiments. But I suspect a lot more people who did something unethical started out with one tiny lie, or one omission, and they got away with it. They then did something a little bigger, and a little bigger, and a little bigger, and they justified it to themselves somehow: “well, my research is really important,” “if this works, it will save lives, and so who’s gonna care about ethics?” That’s part of the reason we have things like institutional review boards, to catch that kind of thinking and stop it. 5) The government lets you conduct unethical experiments: we’ve seen appalling cases throughout history of unethical experiments conducted with the knowledge, permission, and even endorsement of governments.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do professors view students who attend office hours as weak or needy? Does this perception vary depending on the professor's personality?
Answer: It depends on why the student is attending the office hours. The reason I hold office hours is to help my students understand concepts. Because that’s my job. Office hours are also an important barometer of how well I’m teaching: if I get the same question from multiple people in office hours, then I probably didn’t explain the concept well, and I should go over it again. If a student is using office hours to clarify their understanding of something, good on them. That takes time, effort, and some degree of courage. I would much, *much* rather have a student who uses office hours and is struggling, than a student whom I never see, it gets to the end of the semester, and now they complain that their grade is bad. The student in office hours at least cares enough to put in the effort to get a good grade. The complainer….not so much. However, if a student is constantly using office hours to complain about my grading, then yes, that gets on my nerves. This does not mean that they are pointing out a grading error I made (if I made a mistake, I need to correct it, and office hours are there for bringing this to my attention). But I’m not so patient with someone who is trying to convince me that their C-level work “deserves” an A.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it appropriate to refer to someone with a PhD as "Doctor" even if they have not legally changed their name to include the title?
Answer: How many people do you know whose legal name includes the title “Mister” or “Ms.”? How many members of the clergy have legally changed their name to “Reverend”, “Father” or “Rabbi” or “Imam”? And yet, I would presume the OP doesn’t have a problem referring to people by those honorifics.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do the French dislike American tourists?
Answer: I had a very nice time in France, even in Paris. This was after I had heard a lot of horror stories about rude French people. As an American who liked France a lot more than he thought he was going to, I think Americans make three big mistakes in France that result in eyerolls or worse:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it acceptable to present research at two different conferences with different topics and titles, even if the papers have no common content?
Answer: Yes. In fact, sometimes you will have the same author presenting two different papers *at the same conference* with different titles, topics, etc. People have diverse research interests.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: After a PhD, what is the best path to take?
Answer: It very much depends on you and your circumstances: I’ve known people who finished PhDs and are completely unattached. I’ve also known people who have a spouse and two kids. I’ve known daredevils and I’ve known people who are more cautious. There is no one “best” path that fits all of them. Here’s my view on each of the main routes you can take:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What was Hitler’s reaction to the nuke bomb in Hiroshima?
Answer: He didn’t have one. He was slightly dead at the time.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My former professor is 40 years older than me and told me that he loved me. He said, "A quarter of all faculty members in the U.S. overall are married to former students." Is this true?
Answer: Where did he get this number from? The burden of proof is on the person making the claim to prove it, not on someone else to disprove it. I would tend to doubt it. It’s also immaterial in this situation. Do *you* want a relationship with this guy? That’s the only thing that matters.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do some people resist accepting the truth when a conspiracy theory is proven false?
Answer: The problem is that, to those who believe them, a conspiracy theory can never be proved false. Any evidence that is presented against the conspiracy can be dismissed as a fabrication of the conspirators. Anybody who presents that evidence can be dismissed as an agent of the conspiracy. In fact, the more of that evidence there is to disprove the conspiracy theory, the more diabolical and the more widespread the conspiracy must be! So how do you argue against a conspiracy theory? The primary argument against any conspiracy theory is the old Ben Franklin quote: “three men can keep a secret, if two of them are dead.” Anything that requires the knowledge and cooperation of a large number of people will be impossible to keep secret for any great length of time.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are some signs that someone is a conspiracy theorist? Is it possible to respectfully challenge their beliefs without being condescending or rude?
Answer: The single biggest sign that someone is a conspiracy theorist is that they will not accept any arguments that their pet theory is untrue, and will dismiss any evidence that counters that pet theory as having been manufactured by….Them, The Conspiracy. In fact, the more convincing the evidence, the more that confirms just how dangerous The Conspiracy is. The other characteristics of a conspiracy theorist is that 1) they see everything as being explainable by The Conspiracy, 2) they are openly contemptuous of those who don’t believe as they do, and 3) the claims they are making are wild and world-changing. I haven’t seen a lot of conspiracy theories about, say, the shape of paperclips and ballpoint pens. It’s usually something having to do with mind control, serious crimes that are being covered up, elections, etc. Challenging someone’s beliefs in a conspiracy theory in a way that will convince them is difficult to impossible, because the better you are at presenting evidence, that’s just more evidence that They have got to you. I would quietly nod, and back away slowly from someone spouting conspiracy theories.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My boss told me that she expects my work to be flawless when she checks it and I responded “okay” with a smile. She told me to stop smiling. How should I have reacted?
Answer: I would react by very quietly starting to look for another job.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do Ph.D. students respond to people who question the value of a Ph.D. and make comments about potential financial struggles and the length of time spent in school?
Answer: An important lesson I’m glad I learned at about the time my PhD started is: no matter how you decide to live your life, somebody, somewhere, is going to disagree, or doubt your wisdom, or say that you should be doing something else. The thing is, they have got their own lives to lead. If you let them live theirs, they should let you live yours. Thank them for their concern, and do what you’re going to do.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How can someone be both fiscally conservative and socially liberal? Is it possible for someone to identify as both a conservative and a liberal?
Answer: I’ll put it this way: I want the Left to keep its hands off my wallet, and the Right to keep its nose out of my bedroom.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How are so many people fooled by con man evangelicals?
Answer: Kevin D. Williamson had a very astute observation in his excellent book “The Smallest Minority”: liberty, true liberty, where you have to make your own decisions and forge your own path, is terrifying. I mean, what if you make the wrong decision and have to live with the consequences of it?! Many people will join a movement or organization, be that a church, a political party, or the Army, because having somebody tell you what to do and how to do it, is comforting. And if everything goes belly-up, there’s always someone else you can blame except yourself. In a quote attributed to Maya Angelou, “people will forget what you did, people will forget what you said, but they won’t forget how you made them feel.” If you can make people feel that they are righteous, that they are chosen, that they have secret information that nobody else possesses…..you can often rob them blind and they will still love you.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the proper way to address someone with a PhD who does not want to be called "Doctor"? What is an appropriate alternative title for them?
Answer: Ask them what they want to be called. It's as simple as that. “Mark” or “Mr.” will do just fine for me. “Hey, you!” is a little too informal.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it ethical to lie about grades when applying to US universities if there is no way for them to verify the information?
Answer: One tenet of ethics is to behave the same way when nobody is watching, and when you have a policeman at your elbow. If you wouldn't do it when you could get caught, you shouldn't do it when odds are you won't be.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it necessary to apologize for asking a question that has already been answered? If so, what is the polite way to do so, especially if there are multiple people involved in the conversation?
Answer: You could just very simply say “I’m sorry if this has already been asked, but….” or “I’m sorry, I didn’t understand the answer to…..” Don’t overthink it. Now what can also sometimes happen is that the person who’s been asked the question didn’t really answer it, or didn’t answer to your satisfaction. What you can then say is “perhaps if I may rephrase the question….”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How can you determine if a professor has written a PhD thesis on a specific topic before beginning your own research?
Answer: You really shouldn’t be looking through other PhD theses in order to determine if your idea is novel….the thesis itself is kind of a formality. What you *should* be doing is looking through a huge stack of journal articles, and seeing if anyone has done your idea first. If you find something that looks a lot like your thesis idea in another article, ask yourself, “did they capture the whole story? Is there some follow-on work that needs to be done? Is this even a good paper?” Basically, Google Scholar and Web of Science (or another search engine) are your friends. Do a thorough literature search before you start your project!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are some last minute pieces of advice you would give to someone before a test (specifically the ACT)?
Answer: In terms of last-minute stuff for an important test, like 2–3 days out? Get a good night’s sleep. Really. At this point, you either know the material and you don’t. You won’t do yourself any favors by last-minute cramming, and you’re better off going into the test relaxed and well rested.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are there any female football (soccer) referees? How do they compare to male referees in terms of skill and ability?
Answer: There are definitely female referees at the very highest levels of soccer: there were three female referees and three female assistant referees at the 2022 FIFA World Cup (Men’s, not Women’s), and the Women’s World Cup and other high-level women’s competitions usually use female referees. They are just as capable as the male referees, because if they weren’t, you would have heard something about it. At the Grassroots level, where I work, the large majority of referees are men (about 85–90%), and it’s unusual for me to be assigned to a crew with a woman. I think female referees actually have an advantage over male ones in terms of game management: they tend to be a little calmer, and while some players get it into their heads that being macho requires you to argue with a male referee, that logic doesn’t extend to a female one.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do you think billionaire money worshiping sociopath investors like Warren Buffett or Donald Trump are really just con artists and crooks who feed off the fed and create the economy and inflation by cornering wealth as fast as it can be printed?
Answer: Warren Buffett made a lot of other people rich: if you invested $1000 in Berkshire Hathaway back in the 60s, and stuck with him, you would now be worth tens of millions of dollars. Buffet has turned around failing companies, and found companies that were well-run, but just undervalued. Who has Donald Trump made rich, other than Donald Trump?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is Donald Trump viewed as a bad person by so many people?
Answer: It’s really a puzzle, isn’t it? I mean, why would anyone think badly of someone who referred to members of his *own political party* as (amongst other things) Lyin’ Ted, Birdbrain, Little Marco, Tiny D, Meatball Ron DeSanctimonius, and Little Ben Sasse? Who in their right mind would dislike a sweetheart who has cheated on all three of his wives, and was caught on tape talking about how if you’re a big enough deal, you can grab women by the p*ssy with no consequences? And we aren’t even getting into his rather shady and unethical business record! He has a reputation for stiffing contractors, for bending the rules when developing his properties, for inflating the value of his properties when he’s looking for loans and for lowballing the value of his properties when it’s tax time. It’s rather telling that the closer someone is to Trump, the less they tend to like him.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the weirdest thing you've ever seen in America?
Answer: When we were driving out West on a family vacation once, we had to stop for a cattle drive: there was a herd that a few cowboys were herding down the middle of the road. They saw us, steered (pun only somewhat intended!) the herd to the side of the road, and waved us past. Maybe it’s just the reaction of a suburban kid, but that was really cool!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: To Americans, what is the weirdest or most blatantly wrong thing that anyone has said to you about your country?
Answer: When I was in Poland during the 2012 elections, somebody insisted that because Mitt Romney was a Mormon, that meant he didn’t believe in using technology and drove around in a horse and buggy. I explained that it was the Amish and Mennonites who don’t use certain technologies, and they are the ones you see the photos of, driving around with horse-drawn buggies. The Polish guy insisted I had no idea what I was talking about. Now, there is one specific type of technology Mitt Romney and Mormons won’t use: but other than that, I think Mormons are fine with using modern technology.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do you respond when people say “God bless you” after helping them?
Answer: You say, “thank you, I appreciate that. God Bless you too.” Then get on with your life. I would consider myself atheist/agnostic. BUT, if somebody is trying to be nice, in a way that is meaningful to *them*, why would I do anything but accept their well-wishes, and take the thanks in the spirit in which they are intended?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is San Diego the most desirable city in the US (warm, sunny, cool Navy stuff, Padres are a top notch baseball team, women never show skin, and everybody is Anglo Saxon…the way America should be since 1620!)?
Answer: This is one of the weirdest questions I have ever seen. “Everybody is Anglo-Saxon”….have you ever actually been to San Diego? And if you were ever there, did you bother to open your eyes and look at who actually lives there? Or have you ever gone to the beach, and had your cell phone tell you “Welcome to Mexico!”, because the nearest cell tower is on the other side of the border? Have you looked at the architecture, particularly in Balboa Park, named after the very Spanish Vazco Nunez de Balboa, and noticed that the buildings look very…Spanish? Or walked through the Japanese garden there? “Women never show skin”: again, what part of San Diego were *you* visiting? Incidentally, San Diego has a reputation as a hub of the p$rn industry. You mention the Padres. Who have historically been….OK, but only recently have they been very good. But neither the most famous Padre right now (Fernando Tatis, Jr.), or the most famous Padre ever (Tony Gwynn), were “Anglo-Saxon.” I am so utterly puzzled by this question.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Was the Battle of Britain a hoax?
Answer: Believe it or not, all of World War II was a hoax. The world was entirely at peace between 1936 and 1946, and the so-called “World War II” was in fact a conspiracy by the Gillette Company to get people to shave off their nose-wide moustaches and therefore increase razor-blade sales. Everything that the ignorant masses ascribe to being a part of World “War” “2” was the result of the coordinated actions of tens of millions of paid crisis actors, many of whom were so dedicated to their craft that they died in order to preserve the illusion that there was in fact a war on. Wake up, sheeple! This man is in fact Melanchthon “Honest Mel” Strange, a used-car salesman from Tulsa, OK. They posed him in a fancy suit and gave him the codename “Dwight D. Eisenhower.” The OSS objected, saying nobody would believe a guy named “Dwight” would be the Supreme Commander of the Western Allies, but they were overruled. The CIA had to pull off another operation some years later to fool the American people into thinking that “Eisenhower” was president. This is actually Al Capone. He got a reduced sentence from the Federal government in return for agreeing to impersonate a British Prime Minister. This picture proves, definitively, that all the so-called “tanks” in World “War” II were fake. (Before I get deluged with comments: this is satire. I am being deliberately ridiculous. Sadly, you never can tell on the internet these days)

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Liberals, I have absolutely no respect for you, your sick self-righteousness, or your woke cult of idiocy plaguing America. What do you think about that?
Answer: I don’t think about you. What do you think about that?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What were the reasons for the Union's defeat at Vicksburg during the American Civil War?
Answer: Historical revisionism would be the only reason for the Union’s defeat at Vicksburg. In real life, they won.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why did General Robert E. Lee ultimately decide to lay down his arms after learning about the events of Appomattox?
Answer: How bad was the situation for the Confederates at Appomattox? It was so bad, Phillip Sheridan was actually kind of disappointed that Lee surrendered, because Sheridan was rather looking forward to conducting a massacre. After he was ordered not to attack, because the Confederates had come into Union lines with a white flag, Sheridan was seen stamping around, saying “we’ve got ’em like THAT!” and striking his hand with his fist. “Smash ’em up! Smash ’em up!” was one of his favorite things to say.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: After becoming an older adult, do you find yourself to be more liberal or conservative?
Answer: I don’t think my politics have changed all that much from when I was a younger adult. What’s changed is, I have no idea if they are “liberal” or “conservative”, as increasingly those terms have no meaning. These are the things where my beliefs haven’t changed, but the world has changed around me:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do rural conservatives love and trust Trump so much when he is the exact opposite of them?
Answer: I had an important insight about this when hearing about the Alex Murdaugh trial. So, the Murdaughs are/were this really wealthy family in South Carolina (easily worth tens of millions of dollars). They’ve been the county prosecutors for over 100 years, big wheels in their community, etc., and the patriarch of the family (Alex) got convicted of shooting and killing his wife and son. The son, in his turn, had been involved in a boating accident where one of his friends drowned, though what exactly happened is disputed. Very William Faulkner-y stuff, in other words. What does that have to do with Trump? Well, what the Murdaughs did with their money was basically very hillbilly stuff: they bought *large* dog kennels for a large pack of hunting dogs, and *fancy* hunting rifles, and *expensive* bass boats and ATVs. Basically, the only difference between them and a guy a number of rungs down the socioeconomic ladder was how fancy the equipment was, not what they were buying. To bring this back to Trump: to many of his supporters, Trump’s style is what they would do if they found themselves with a lot of money. Trump is who they aspire to be. Add to that the fact that the people Trump attacks and makes fun of remind some people of the a**holes in their lives they can’t stand: the supercilious city folks, the “experts”, your boss, your ex-wife, whatever. You, the rural guy, can’t be mean to those people. But Trump can, and does. Basically, some people are fans of Trump for the same reason they’re fans of James Bond: because he can do things you really, *really* wish you could, but can’t.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why didn’t the Jews leave their home towns when they heard the Nazis came into power?
Answer: There are many excellent answers here, and I don’t want to repeat them. What I’d like to emphasize, however, is that if you had told somebody in 1900 “within the next 50 years, a country in Europe is going to try to exterminate every Jew, not just in their own country, but in all of Europe. Guess which one”, pretty much nobody would have guessed Germany. Russia, absolutely. Austria-Hungary, perhaps. Maybe France. But the Jews were largely assimilated in Germany. They served in the army, had businesses, had legal protections, and there hadn’t been any large-scale pogroms in a while. The Germans are famously law-abiding, and in 1900 it was spectacularly illegal to commit genocide. Because of this historical precedent, many German Jews hoped that the whole Hitler thing was just a phase, and it would pass. Many Jews, however, did see the writing on the wall and fled, where they ran into the problem of trying to find a country that would accept them, as detailed in many of the other answers here. Also, many of those who were murdered in the Holocaust lived in countries other than Germany. They weren’t expecting a World War to break out, leading to them losing their lives.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it considered harmful by some universities to pursue two different doctoral degrees simultaneously, such as a Ph.D. in organizational behavior and a Ph.D. in clinical psychology?
Answer: Why on earth would you want to do a thing like that? What are the benefits of getting two PhDs at the same time? A single PhD is time consuming and stressful, and I can’t fathom why you would want to do two of them. What would be far more logical would be to do a single PhD that in some way combines organizational behavior and clinical psychology. There’s usually pretty wide latitude on combining disciplines when doing a research project.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it legal for journals to publish articles that have been rejected by other publishers? How does this process work?
Answer: I mean, if it’s rejected it’s rejected. You can do whatever you want with an article that’s been rejected. Where you get into trouble is submitting the same article multiple places at the same time. You have to sign a bunch of disclaimers up and down stating that you are definitely submitting this article to just this one journal, this one time.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it considered ethical to mention our own research paper in conference presentations?
Answer: Yes, this is a very common practice. Some people do it a little too much (“according to MY genius work….”) In fact, one of the common types of talk are what I like to call a “greatest hits” talk, where a professor will talk about all of his or her papers of the last 15 years, but suspiciously never mentions anything their group has done in the last 5 years…..

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the consequences of using the title "doctor" without a medical doctorate but with other doctoral degrees?
Answer: The Doctor Police will kick down your door and drag you off to Medical Reeducation School. Or, you know, we’ll all just get on with our lives.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do you ask a professor if he/she is still taking undergraduate research assistants for the semester?
Answer: You can just ask them. Send an e-mail to them saying “Hi Prof. X, I’ve read some of your papers on [subjects] and I find them interesting. Would you consider having me as an undergraduate research assistant?” The other thing you can do is, find your department’s advisor for your major, and say “I’d like to get involved in undergraduate research. Who’s hiring?” They should be able to help you out if they are halfway competent as an advisor. Basically, the older I got, the less timid I became at simply asking people for things. The worst they can say is no, and you’re no worse off than when you started.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My daughter refuses to apply to Berkeley because Berkeley admits more applicants annually than Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Stanford, MIT, Caltech, CMU, UChicago, and Columbia combined, and she doesn't want to attend a safety school. What should I do?
Answer: This may be one of those moments where you have to grit your teeth and hope for the best. She might get a nasty shock when she doesn’t get into any of the schools you listed, then has to figure out what comes next. That will be a humbling experience, but I think my late teens and early twenties is when I learned some humility, which served me well. Or maybe she gets lucky, she gets into one of those schools, and it all works out great! I was a high-flying student in high school, and I applied to some prestigious colleges (MIT, Caltech, Princeton, Yale). I got into none of them. I ended up attending my safety school (Pitt), a school that wasn’t even on my radar and to which I applied simply because the application was free. And I ended up getting a darn good education! I went on to a prestigious graduate school, and I’ve got a job and career I’m happy with. College, and life, is very much about what you make it, not how prestigious it is. There’s far too much of this desire to get into certain schools just to say you’re “better” than other people.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How does one convert an evolutionist into a creationist?
Answer: OK, the first thing that would have to happen is that Jesus Christ himself would have to show up, and talk to me. I would need to see a few miracles coming from His hand to convince me He’s the real deal rather than somebody who is just claiming to be Jesus, which happens pretty often. It wouldn’t have to be too spectacular, I’d settle for him feeding 5000 people with a few loaves and fishes, and watching Him walk across a large body of water like Lake Michigan. I would then ask for answers to the following questions, and would want a good explanation for them: 1) If God created every single thing in its present form in six days, why are so many of His designs incredibly stupid? About 80% of humans will experience back problems at some time in their lives. Pregnancy for humans is dangerous and complicated: it is much less dangerous and complicated for other great apes like gorillas. Humans need midwives. Gorillas can deliver their own babies. Humans are exceptionally vulnerable to choking on food: in many animals, the tube for breathing and the tube for eating never meet (think dolphins). We are expected to go our whole lives with only two sets of teeth: sharks keep getting new sets all the time. The single most produced enzyme on earth, Rubisco, is actually pretty bad at its job. Heck, the way metabolism works doesn’t make sense when you think about it: to derive energy, we (and almost every organism on earth) do this weird thing where we pump protons across a membrane barrier, then when the protons diffuse back through that membrane we generate ATP. That’s a very silly and convoluted way to do it. A human engineer working from scratch would never design these systems this way, never mind an all-powerful, all-knowing being. 2) We know that viruses like COVID-19, that we had never detected before 2019, can come out of seemingly nowhere, and that new strains of this virus keep appearing and eventually becoming predominant. That’s also true for HIV, which *probably* didn’t exist before the 20th century. Does this mean that God is still creating new “life”? If He is constantly creating new life, why does that life seem to be inclined to kill us? (While I was at it I would ask if viruses constitute life or not. That’s a question that can cause flame wars in certain fora.) 3) The last question I would ask has been one that every scientist since Galileo, and probably since Thomas Aquinas, has asked: if humans were given a brain, an ability to reason analytically, an innate curiosity about how the world works, and a healthy skepticism, why then are we not supposed to use any of these things and unquestioningly accept, on faith, the explanations of the Bible or any other holy book? Given good answers to all three questions, I might revise my thoughts about creationism.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If mutations are damaging, why do evolutionists still insist genetic changes are beneficial?
Answer: Most mutations don’t do anything at all, some mutations are damaging, and a rare few are beneficial. The key idea behind evolution is that there is a SELECTION process. The (rare) beneficial mutations enable an organism to survive and prosper, and therefore they predominate. The (more common) bad mutations die out. The (most common) silent mutations that don’t do anything, just sort of hang out. It’s also important to note that evolution will leave you with a solution that is “good enough”, not perfect. Rubisco, the single most common protein on earth, is actually pretty bad at its job: it’s slow, for one thing. Why hasn’t it gotten any better? Well, because Rubisco is a key protein in the photosynthesis pathway. The difference between NO photosynthesis and inefficient photosynthesis is huge. It gives a big advantage to that organism. The difference between inefficient photosynthesis and slightly better photosynthesis is much smaller. There’s no pressure to improve photosynthesis. An interesting fact is that most proteins are actually not very stable. The forces that drive a protein to fold successfully are actually on the order of 5–10 kJ/mol, which is about the strength of a hydrogen bond or two. What’s the reason? Well, proteins are constantly being mutated in ways that, over time, lessens their stability, as most mutations are destabilizing. However, the mutations that are *so* destabilizing that they knock out the protein don’t propagate because the organism dies, and those proteins are removed by selection.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do people wish they could go back to the way life was in the 1950s or 60s?
Answer: I do find it funny that some of the same people who lament how much life has changed, and who wish for “simpler, gentler times” are some of the same people who will tell stories that start with “you kids these days, you don’t know how good you’ve got it. Why, back in my day we didn’t have bread. Why, we didn’t even have food. But we had discipline and, hey, where are you going? Kids these days don’t listen to their elders, that’s what’s wrong with them.”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My boss purposely makes all interview candidates wait 1 hour past the scheduled interview time. This is their "filtering" method, as they refuse to consider anyone who leaves during the 1+ hour wait. Is this legal?
Answer: How many people has your boss actually hired using this strategy? Were they actually any good at their jobs? Better question, why are *you* still working for them?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it mansplaining any time a man explains something to a woman?
Answer: Well, lemmie tell you all about it, little lady…. So, my expertise is in synthetic biology. One of my friends is a satellite engineer. If I explain something to her about synthetic biology that she wouldn’t reasonably be expected to know, that’s not mansplaining. If I start explaining rocket science to her….that is mansplaining, because she knows more about it than I do. Basically, mansplaining requires a patronizing attitude, or an assumption that somebody doesn’t know something they know a lot about.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the consequences of an adult student occasionally leaving halfway through a college lecture without notifying anyone beforehand (just quietly getting up and leaving)?
Answer: I mean, the student might fail the class because they aren’t listening to lecture and absorbing it. But other than that, as long as they are quiet and not disruptive about it, nobody’s going to care or even notice.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do you think there is a time to be funny or a time to be serious?
Answer: Ecclesiastes 3:1: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven. That goes for jokes as much as anything else.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How should I reply when someone says God bless you?
Answer: I just say “thank you” and move on. I might even say “Bless you too.” You should assume they are wishing you well and not be a jerk about it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it normal to not have a graduation party after grad school?
Answer: The research groups I worked in had cake and Champaign immediately after all of the thesis defenses, usually a sheet cake and decent but cheap Champaign. Some advisers would keep an empty Champaign bottle on a shelf in their office for each person that had successfully defended. One especially classy grad student had lunch catered after he defended successfully, but it wasn’t anything fancy. My parents came to my thesis defense and I think they might have taken me out to dinner or something, and I went out to lunch with my in-laws after my graduation. But that was about it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do undergraduate students refer to graduate students?
Answer: Frankly, if they are more formal than “Yo, Butthead”, that’s about the best you can expect. You’re on a first-name basis with the undergraduate students. Being called “Mister” would just be weird. Heck, at Caltech we called Nobel Laureates by their first names.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is there a labor shortage in the United States? Please no comments like "because of lazy people."
Answer: I am struck by how many corporations will talk about “free markets and capitalism! Yeah!” but then utterly ignore the fact that the labor market is also, ideally, a free market. Companies are trying to buy labor, but are not increasing the wages they offer. I remember doing a job search, and there was a company that wanted proficiency in at least three computer languages, 5 years experience, project management skills, etc., for which they were willing to pay $60k a year in Dallas, TX. Anybody who actually *had* those qualifications was going to be looking at a job at closer to $100k a year or more. The applicants they would have to that job would either be 1) suckers, or 2) lying about their qualifications and hoping nobody noticed. But I’m sure that once that job had been unfilled for a year to two, the company went to their congressman and whined about a shortage of qualified workers. Pay people more, and there won’t be a labor shortage.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If a PhD student's supervisor dies or leaves the institution midway through their studies, what happens to the student?
Answer: This very much depends on the institution, and when you say “left”, it depends where the supervisor is going. At least at my graduate institution, if you were working for an old professor who was likely to die, you had to be co-advised by somebody else. And generally the older professors hired mostly post-docs. If a young professor were to die suddenly (a Caltech professor tragically died at the age of 39 on American Airlines Flight 191 in 1979, the deadliest air accident in US history), the students would probably try to find other mentors at the same university. If the professor leaves the institution and goes to another academic institution, the expectation is that the students will follow him or her to that new institution. There can be an exception if the student is in their last year and finishing up, but if you’re a second year and your professor gets a job in Alaska, the expectation is that you follow them. If a professor doesn’t get tenure/ends up going into industry, the students generally end up joining other groups at the same university, and that now-ex professor is expected to still sit on the thesis committee.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is Italy dying?
Answer: I wouldn’t say Italy is dying, but I don’t know how much it’s really living either. I’ll answer this question by comparing Italy to Poland. Consider Poland. Here was a country that didn’t exist between 1795–1918, was thoroughly and completely destroyed in World War II to a degree that beggars belief (population of Poland in 1939: about 35 million. Population in 1945: about 25 million. 90% of Warsaw was destroyed, and the “Old City” of Warsaw was entirely rebuilt after 1945). It then had the “benefits” of almost 50 years of Communism (1945–1990). There’s that infamous Polish fatalism to contend with, and bureaucracy can be fierce. In some ways some of the handicaps placed on Italy were also placed on Poland. It’s not a perfect analogy (Poland hasn’t had as many problems with organized crime. Italy wasn’t a part of the Warsaw Pact, and doesn’t have to deal with weather that can absolutely suck between November and February), but the countries do have some similarities. But walk around a large city in Poland today (Warsaw or Krakow), and there’s a very real energy to the place. Young people are starting businesses. The country is benefiting from outsourcing from other countries. I’ve even heard Poles grudgingly saying “eh, things aren’t so bad”, which, from a nation that is characterized by Slavic fatalism, is high praise indeed. Go into the market square (Rynek) in Krakow on a weekend night in the summer, and the place just roars with activity (lots of tourists: I have mixed feelings, because on one hand, that means money, but on the other, the Old City feels too much like Disneyland nowadays). The country feels like it’s on the move. Contrast with Italy. Now I have to make some important caveats. First, I have only visited Italy four times, and never for more than two weeks (2010, twice in 2013, 2019). Beyond some rudimentary phrases, I don’t speak the language. Second, I need to specify that I really like Italy: the food, the art, the culture, the people, the history. For all its insanity, I like Naples. I think there are some aspects of Italian culture that Americans can learn from. However, every time I visit Italy I get the sense that the country is still coasting on the glories of the 15th and 16th centuries. There’s energy, sure, but it doesn’t feel like that energy is *going* anywhere. There seems to be this deep cynicism, that the best you can hope for is to scrape by and optimism is for suckers. I have met some phenomenally talented and ambitious young Italians, but they are usually working in Switzerland, the UK, or the US. There are some economic numbers to back up this sense I get from both countries. Economically, in GDP per capita Poland is approaching that of Italy’s poorer regions like Campania (where Naples is located), and GDP per capita in the wealthiest region of Poland (Warsaw) is about on a par with Italy as a whole. Also, Poland is growing economically at about 3.5% a year, in some years closer to 6%, whereas Italian growth is effectively zero. If current forecasts are correct, Poland may catch Italy by about 2030.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are people's opinions on George B. McClellan? Was he a good general? Did he deserve to be fired by Abraham Lincoln during the American Civil War?
Answer: I used to think that McClellan was a really lousy general, but I’ve done a little reassessing. He actually won or tied in all the battles he fought: while the Peninsular Campaign, broadly, was a Union strategic defeat, the Army of the Potomac actually won six out of the Seven Days Battles, with the seventh being a draw. The Union defeats in the East that were *really* embarrassing were Second Bull Run, Fredericksburg, and Chancellorsville, and in all of these somebody else was in command of the main Union army. However, McClellan didn’t turn any of those victories into anything especially meaningful, whereas Grant, during the Overland Campaign, would lose most of the battles he fought, but win the campaign anyway. Basically, McClellan knew how to organize, and he knew how not to lose a battle. But he was so afraid of losing a battle, and thereby losing the entire war, that he didn’t display any aggression, even when he should have. One thing I think we forget is just how young McClellan was: he turned 35 years old in December 1861. He was by this point an experienced engineer and Army officer, but he didn’t have experience managing an army of nearly 100,000 men: nobody in the United States had ever commanded a formation that large. The weight of expectation was very high: he was, at that age and with that lack of experience, expected to save the Union.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My friend got into MIT and he's like really stupid. Should I notify MIT admissions so they don't embarrass themselves?
Answer: Is he, like, really stupid? In the words of The Dude, yeah, well, that’s just like, your opinion, man.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I got 30% plagiarism in my thesis. Is it okay?
Answer: It is going to depend on the circumstances that caused the thesis to get that score. Are you quoting long passages verbatim, or excerpting paragraphs, but making it clear that’s what you’re doing? For instance, “According to Smith, ‘this is a highly objective and intellectual quote’, [1] which……” I could see that potentially being flagged as plagiarism, as your text matches another source verbatim, but it isn’t plagiarism because you are clearly quoting it and giving credit. Is the software flagging your citations and references, which take a specific format and therefore would be the same in other publications? Have you previously published a paper, and are now adapting that paper for one of your thesis chapters? If you’re stating that’s what you’re doing, you are going to get a high overlap with something previously published, but it’s likely OK. But absent those circumstances, *any* plagiarism is very bad news.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do scientists put Charles Darwin on such a high pedestal? Scientists are able to admit that even Isaac Newton got things wrong, but they don’t tolerate anyone to question a single word of Charles Darwin.
Answer: The reason scientists defend Darwin so very strongly is not because he was infallible, but because he is attacked so very strongly, and attacked for the things he *did* get right. I think if people were to attack Newton by saying that calculus is heretical and anybody who takes an integral is going to Hell, and therefore calculus should be *banned from schools* or at least disclaimed as “controversial,” you’d get some pretty passionate defenses of Newton too. There are a lot of answers saying pretty much the same thing (and they’re right!): that the biological community will openly tell you the things that Darwin was wrong about, and he didn’t get it all right. In fact, one of the early (and perhaps most legitimate) criticisms of evolution was that Darwin didn’t really have a mechanism by which it would occur. But boy oh boy have we solved that shortcoming since. Also, Darwin didn’t know about epigenetics, which is where changes in the environment of a parent can lead the parent to adapt to the environment, which results in heritable changes in that parent’s descendants in certain circumstances. For a long time this was considered quackery, but it’s now accepted that it does occur.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What do you think about Tulsi Gabbard stating, “This war and suffering could have easily been avoided if Biden Admin/NATO had simply acknowledged Russia’s legitimate security concerns regarding Ukraine’s becoming a member of NATO”?
Answer: Where do Russia’s “legitimate security concerns” end? Russia has at one point or another in its history owned Alaska and explored the Pacific Northwest, claimed the right to rule over about half of Germany, held part of northern China, desired to control Istanbul, and had their lunch handed to them in Afghanistan. You could argue that to satisfy Russia’s “legitimate security concerns”, Germany never should have re-unified, and Seattle should be Russian territory. But I don’t hear anybody in the appeasement crowd saying that the war in Ukraine should have been avoided by the expedient of stationing Russian troops in Berlin again. Everyone is in a hurry to give away things, like Ukrainian independence, which are not theirs to give. For all this talk about “legitimate security concerns,” nobody ever seems to talk about the legitimate security concerns of Ukraine and Georgia. Both countries were right to worry about a Russian invasion that intended either to separate portions of the country into Russian satellites, and/or change the regime ruling those countries by force. Why were they right to worry about such an invasion? Because one happened! This war wouldn’t have happened if we had simply acknowledged *Ukraine’s* legitimate security concerns in 2008, and *admitted* them to NATO. Finally, this argument assumes that because Russia is big and looked like it was strong and most Americans can find it on a map, it gets to have security concerns, but who gives a rap about the smaller countries? That’s a tenant of Realism, that some countries are basically pawns to be pushed around the chessboard of diplomacy by the great powers. But interestingly, nobody ever talks this way about Switzerland.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do some "pro gun" Americans think "when a criminal strikes I might not have time to wait for the police" is a reasonable argument against gun control and not just another issue that needs addressing drastically?
Answer: One thing I think a lot of people don’t grasp is just how BIG the United States is, and how sparsely it is populated in some places. I currently live on the East Coast, which is the most densely populated part of the country. One of the guys I work with lives in the country, about 30 miles (50 kilometers) from the nearest police station, and that’s along country roads. San Bernardino County, California (that’s one county, one state, population about 1.3 million), is slightly larger than Switzerland. Here is a list of the 100 largest counties in the United States by area. EVERY SINGLE ONE OF THEM is larger than Cyprus, and the top 50 are all larger than Montenegro: Also keep in mind that many of these counties are pretty sparsely populated and don’t have anything like the budget you would need to have police stations everywhere. The most sparsely populated counties in the US have 0.3 people per square kilometer or less than 1 person per square mile. You simply *cannot* patrol areas that large with a rapid response time. I would also point out that the way you could “address the issue drastically” in urban centers, to reduce police response times, is to hire more police. Well, that’s politically very difficult right now, when “Defund the Police!” is a slogan that has a lot of adherents.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is a PhD worth doing if you're not brilliant?
Answer: I maintain that a PhD is not a “smartness” degree. A PhD is a stubbornness degree. Basically, if you have a PhD, what that tells me is that you can fail for years, and years, and years, and not give up until you eventually succeed. I’ve seen brilliant people wash out of PhD programs, people a lot smarter than me, and I don’t think my thesis was especially inspired or revolutionary. But it was complete, I stuck it out for six years, and that’s what counts.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the consequences of taking time off between undergraduate and graduate school, or between graduate school and getting an assistant professor position?
Answer: I took a gap year between undergraduate and graduate school in order to do a Fulbright Fellowship, which is a US government program that sends students abroad for a year (and which also funds the studies of students from all over the world in the US). I did my Fulbright in Poland, so that’s what I can speak to. Your mileage may vary depending on where you go and what you do. Advantages: Disadvantages: On balance, I’m glad I took that gap year, because had I not taken it, on the one hand the transition to graduate school would have been smoother, but on the other, I might not have actually finished graduate school.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why does it seem that most of Europe has gotten over WW2 except the British?
Answer: Poland has most definitely NOT gotten over WW2. There are reminders and monuments to it everywhere, often of the “on this spot, April X, 1943, forty people were lined up and shot” variety. There are people in Lublin who, every time they look out their window, they are looking at the Majdanek concentration camp (residents of other cities may have similar experiences, I’m not sure, but I saw Majdanek and can personally attest that there are suburban houses just outside the wire, a number of high-rises looming over the site, and a city bus stop at the front gates). Every year, air raid sirens blare across the entire country at 5PM on August 1st. Buses stop and pull over, and nationwide there are two minutes of silence in commemoration of the start of the Warsaw Uprising, August 1st 1944. Some people (I’ve heard they tend to be nationalists, but I’m not sure), will stand with lit red road flares above their heads at this time. There are solemn church services at the same time, where they feature a few of the surviving participants in the rising: they were teenagers then, and are now in their 90’s. When I was there in 2012–2013, there were *still* some hulks of ruined buildings, and rubble, from the war, largely because it wasn’t clear who even owned what was left of that building: the original owners, and their families, were all dead except some fifth cousin in Cleveland who had no idea this building was even a thing. Poland was so thoroughly trashed in the war, and reminders are so prevalent even if you aren’t looking for them, I don’t think it’s anything they can “get over.” Others have said as much, and I tend to agree: I suspect you are an American who has visited Britain and nowhere else in Europe. The US view of World War II is very different from that in Europe. We (I’m an American, so I’ll say “we”) have the luxury of seeing it as something that happened Over There. We did lose a lot of troops, but very few civilians. None of our cities were destroyed, our people didn’t experience starvation or occupation, and for a lot of people nowadays, our connection with the war is not any deeper than Bob Hope and Bing Crosby. It fades in our memory because those who fought have mostly all died, and we don’t have visible reminders of it in our own country. This is not true in Europe.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is it all right in public schools to teach Darwinism but not creationism?
Answer: Why is it all right in public schools to teach that the world is round and not flat? Why is it all right in public schools to teach that vaccines are effective, but not homeopathy? Why is it all right to teach that objects in motion tend to remain in motion, not that objects eventually run out of “impetus” and fall down in a straight line? The evidence for evolution is overwhelming. For one thing, we can observe evolution *in real time* when we’re dealing with microorganisms. Try explaining COVID variants with creationism, I dare you.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If evolution wasn’t false, how do evolutionists explain that there are no non-carbon based living organisms? Is it possible that this is just a coincidence?
Answer: Let’s start with this: chemistry can broadly be divided into two disciplines: organic and inorganic. Organic is the study of carbon compounds, and inorganic is the study of *everything else.* Organic chemistry is a HUGE discipline, and carbon is a very special element. (Yes, yes, I know there’s physical, and analytical, and computational chemistry too, but I’m making a point here). Why no non-carbon-based lifeforms? Because carbon has an unusual ability to form long chains and complex molecules that other elements simply do not, and these complex molecules are necessary for life. You can’t do DNA or RNA in silicon or boron. While you can form crystals out of inorganic elements (which would be an example of long-range order), there are only seven different basic geometries of crystal known, and the reactions that form them are not fast.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do PhD students have enough time to date/start relationships?
Answer: I met my wife, had a relationship, and got married all while I was still a PhD student. So, yes. I would *strongly* recommend not neglecting the formation of relationships, including personal relationships, during graduate school. Graduate school can be emotionally very difficult, and you shouldn’t try to do it alone. If your boss doesn’t want you to date, find another boss, simple as that.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the reasons why a referee can give a player a yellow card for dissent?
Answer: The technical definition is “dissent by word or action.” So if somebody either verbally argues with a call, or they make a gesture that clearly shows they didn’t like the call, they can be cautioned. If they use foul or abusive language (or make a rude gesture), that’s a red. So: “Hey Ref, what was that call??!!” (yellow) vs. “Hey Ref, what the f#*k was that call you a#*hole?!” (red). But in theory it doesn’t have to be that big: “that was a bad call, ref” could technically warrant a yellow. But I wouldn’t give a yellow in that case, as it would seem excessive and you’d antagonize somebody who doesn’t need to be antagonized. You want to be an authority, not an authoritarian. It took me some time to figure that out. As with so much else in the craft of refereeing, the referee needs to set a bar, and that bar needs to change based on the needs of the game. We are trained to ask: is the dissent PUBLIC? Is the dissent PERSONAL? Is the dissent PROVOCATIVE? Somebody muttering “come on, man” at an offside call, loud enough that just the referee can hear it, is very different than a coach bellowing from 70 yards away “HOW IS THAT A FOUL!!”, is different from “HOW IS THAT A FOUL!! ARE YOU BLIND! WHERE DID YOU LEARN TO REFEREE! OK TEAM, GO AHEAD AND KILL ‘EM, WE WON’T GET A CALL ANYWAY!” The first case, I’d probably say to the player, loud enough that he can hear it, “yep, that’s what we got. Tough break, you’ll get it next time, aright?” The second case, I would stop the game and talk to the coach. Maybe a yellow, maybe not, depends on the overall temperature of the game. Is this happening in the 5th minute, or the 70th? Is it a dirty game, or a clean one? Is this his first outburst, or have I already talked to him and told him to stop? How are his players reacting: are they rolling their eyes and carrying on with the game, or are they echoing what their coach is saying, and/or starting to play more dangerously? Is what the coach said a reasonable reaction to what just happened, or is he putting me on? (I tend to be a lot less lenient about dissent about a ball out of play like a throw-in or corner than I am about dissent regarding a foul or non-foul: the foul call has an impact on player safety. The ball out of play call? No way.) The last situation I’ve illustrated is definitely yellow, any day of the week, with an additional reminder that he’s on thin ice for that second yellow. How do you handle dissent other than throwing cards? The referee needs to remember that he or she has tools other than the cards. You can glower at somebody who is dissenting. Sometimes just standing still and staring daggers can work wonders. You can talk to them, privately or publicly: there is a difference between the two, even if what you say is basically the same. The talk can be friendly, even kind of joking, or it can be stern. I remember one game where one player had been chipping away at a number of my calls, so I barked at him “#15 THAT’S ENOUGH!”, and had no problems with him the rest of the game. You shouldn’t *ignore* dissent or pretend it isn’t happening. I’ve seen a lot of referees try to do this, and it escalates, and that can end up with a game that is completely out of control.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are examples of “mansplaining” with context?
Answer: I’ve sometimes found this trickier than you would expect as I 1) work in a technical field, 2) try to be comprehensive with my answers, and 3) can’t always assume somebody has a background in my field, or in what specifically I work on. If I’m talking about what I do, and assume a knowledge base that isn’t there, the listener gets confused. So I think the concept of mansplaining can be over-applied: if I don’t know what you know, or if you are one member of a larger audience, perhaps I’m mansplaining to you, but the person next to you appreciates the extra background or context, and without it they would be lost. HOWEVER, that being said, mansplaining is a real thing. It happens when the speaker knows or reasonably should know their audience’s background or level of expertise, and ignores it. For instance, I have a friend who works for NASA as a satellite engineer. If I explain astrophysics or satellites to her, that’s mansplaining. If I explain synthetic biology to her, that’s not mansplaining, because she doesn’t know about it. If I’m talking to a woman who has a PhD in biology, I’m going to assume she already knows about the Lac operon. The most spectacular example of mansplaining I ever saw was at a dinner connecting high school teachers to young professionals in the sciences. A (male) high school teacher was talking to a recently-graduated (female) PhD who was working on the R&D side of one of the big antibody therapeutic development companies in the area. They had already had the whole “what do you do for a living” chat. The teacher proceeded to explain how antibodies work to the PhD who does this sort of stuff every day.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My essay got 1% similarity in Turnitin, but my professor still says it’s plagiarism. What should I do?
Answer: I would say, “OK, point to the exact passage that Turnitin says was copied.” A lot of these plagiarism detectors will flag specific instances of suspected plagiarism. If you lifted a sentence or two verbatim from another source, you might be in trouble, because lifting even a sentence or two is technically plagiarism. (Also depends how long this assignment is: is it a master’s thesis, or an essay? Also depends on what the sentence says. If it’s something like “Grass is green”, there really aren’t any ways to paraphrase that). I would go to the dean or the chair of your department, and insist on a formal hearing. You probably have a right to such a thing. The community college where I worked had a very elaborate system for dealing with allegations of cheating or other academic misconduct. I got to learn all about it, unfortunately, because I busted some of my students for copying off of each other in the early days of COVID where I was relying on the honor system. When I leveled the accusation, I had specific, compelling evidence (I lined up *several* suspect answers *across multiple tests*, and in several cases they were practically photocopies of each other). The students had the right to 1) know the specific accusation being made against them, 2) see the evidence being presented in support of that accusation, 3) retain legal counsel if they so desired and 4) to convene a formal hearing to determine whether or not sanctions should be imposed. I don’t remember whether the evidential standard was “preponderance of evidence” or “clear and compelling evidence”, because the students basically took a plea deal when they saw the evidence I had, but there was an evidential standard. I was very impressed that the college did this. If I were sitting on the board or tribunal that was deciding such a case, there would be four things I would want to know. 1) What is the *specific* passage in question? I’m not convinced by a 1% similarity: what *exactly* was copied? 2) What is the *length* of the passage in question? A sentence fragment? A sentence? A whole paragraph? 3) Is the passage cited? I would look much more sympathetically on a case where the passage was perhaps missing quotation marks, but the credit was clearly given. 4) How easily could the passage in question be paraphrased?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why would someone who has a very high IQ achieve nothing worthwhile in their life?
Answer: In many cases, a very high IQ correlates with some form of neurosis, or even serious mental illness. “Good Will Hunting” is in some ways very Hollywood, but in some ways accurate in that respect. Lack of work ethic can be a problem: somebody breezes through school, it’s all very easy, then all of a sudden it isn’t and the person hasn’t learned how to pound through the problem with hard work. A related problem is that when a person with a high IQ runs across a problem that isn’t easy for them, it can crush their spirits and make them doubt themselves. Those are the two big ones that come to mind.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: A professor I know deliberately does NOT hold office hours in the seven days leading up to an exam. His rationale is that he doesn't want to deal with so many students who wait until the last minute to get help. Is he allowed to do this?
Answer: You may want to talk to the department chair or the dean about this. In some universities there is an *obligation* to hold office hours. And in some departments, it might be an expectation as opposed to a formal requirement. You might not get anything from the chair or the dean about this, but you should at least bring it to their attention.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do you politely refuse to go to someone’s funeral when they invited you?
Answer: I think you should probably drop by the wake, sign the book, offer your condolences, and then leave. It really isn’t a huge commitment. Or at least send a card or something.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is the dropping of Dilbert by several newspapers an example of modern day woke cancel culture?
Answer: When it comes to woke cancel culture, I like to apply something I call the “2005 rule”: would this statement have been *broadly* considered racist in 2005? (that’s as good a year as any, social media was in its infancy, and we hadn’t been infested by whatever the hell brain virus hit all of us simultaneously when Trump started being a serious force in American politics in 2015–2016). Exhibit A: consider, just for a moment, Jon Gruden. He got fired for some very offensive e-mails he wrote….and absolutely nobody defended him, because those e-mails would have been offensive in 2005. I think Scott Adams’ statements would have been considered racist in 2005. So no, not modern woke cancel culture.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties?
Answer: Well, let’s see here, do you go to your employee’s weddings? Baby showers? Kids’ baseball games? Other things that are important to them? No? Is it possible that you just see your employee as a means to an end? And that’s fine. But consider, at some level, YOU are just a means to an end for that employee. And that end is paying the rent, buying groceries, etc. etc. Provided that the employee is doing their job at work, why do you have any right to demand that they do their job outside of work? One *possible* exception to this is if hobnobbing/networking is a part of the job. For instance, I go to scientific conferences as part of my job, and part of that job is schmoozing with the other attendees. But I know this already, and it was spelled out for me.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do people in the United Kingdom think the United Kingdom didn't exist in the 1100s?
Answer: Because it didn’t. The United Kingdom as a political unit was only formed in 1707 with the Act of Union. England and Scotland were separate countries until then, though they had been ruled in personal union (same monarch, different parliaments) since 1603. Heck, in 1100, Wales was an independent country, and England hadn’t really been a united country for very long. Now, the island of Great Britain has existed since about 7000 BC depending on who you ask, but it wasn’t governed by a single country until 1707.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is there a possibility that Russia pretends to be weak and to attack Ukraine slowly so that Russia hides its true military power or to achieve goals that Russia couldn't if Russia invaded Ukraine rapidly?
Answer: It’s also possible that Olga Kurylenko is just dying to go on a date with me, but I doubt it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: One point of view is that Russia is not so much fighting Ukraine as they are the presence of American weapons in Ukraine. Why is that position so hard for many to accept?
Answer: Because it’s a stupid point of view. How many American weapons were there in Ukraine prior to 2014? I’ll bet you pretty much anything that there are a lot more American weapons in Ukraine now than there were in 2014. So if Russia’s objective was to reduce the number of American weapons in Ukraine, they have failed spectacularly. Second problem with the premise of this question: why might Ukraine want those American weapons? It may have something to do with the fact that they are under attack. Why is it so important for Russia to remove American weapons from Ukraine, instead of, say, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and everywhere else they can be found? Third problem with the premise: it’s impossible to remove American weapons without removing the Ukrainians who are holding them. Wars are not fought against things. Wars are fought against people. Fourth problem with the premise: is Ukraine’s power grid an American weapon? Because Russia has prioritized targeting it. And I haven’t even gotten into the civilian casualties and horrible things Russia is doing in occupied Ukraine. Other posters have covered that already.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Can acknowledgements in a dissertation be humorous?
Answer: Depends what you mean by humorous. You can be warm and friendly, you can perhaps make some reference to an inside joke that you and the person you are acknowledging will understand, and I think you can (and perhaps should!) make fun of yourself a little bit. I also put a little post-script on the very last page of my thesis where I acknowledged my late grandparents and uncle, and wrote a few of their favorite sayings. However, you shouldn’t use your acknowledgements as an occasion to make fun of people, or to “acknowledge” someone by damning them with faint praise. Over your 4–6 years as a graduate student, a lot of people helped you. You need to sincerely recognize that. In short, you can be funny, but you also need to be sweet and sincere. It’s better to be sweet and sincere and not funny at all than funny, but nasty and insincere.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should this war be called, Ukraine/Russia war or Russia/America proxy war in Ukraine?
Answer: How about the War of Ukrainian Independence. That’s what it’s all about, isn’t it? If Russia wins, Ukraine will no longer be independent (and that was the Russian intent in the first place). If Ukraine wins, it will remain independent and choose whom to align with. It’s somewhat obnoxious how some commentators talk about Ukraine as though it doesn’t exist: they talk as though there’s Russia, then there’s Europe west of the Oder River, and all those guys in between the Oder and the Donets don’t really matter and can be disposed of as we please. But there *are* people there, who are as deserving of their own political independence as any others. So, War of Ukrainian Independence. That’s my vote.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I’m a 67-year-old cashier. My coworker is 19 and tries talking to me like an equal. How do I put him in his place and remind him that as an elder, I deserve unconditional respect and obedience?
Answer: You know, I’ve noticed that some people manage to become old without becoming wise. I think you are one of those people. “Unconditional respect and obedience”: if an 80 year old told you to go jump in a lake, you’d better do it and thank him for telling you to do so, by that logic.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the ethical implications of a graduate student taking classes from the same department she works at dating another grad student in said department (and vice versa)?
Answer: Umm, unless grad student A is taking classes for which grad student B is grading him or her (where there may be a question of grad student A “sleeping their way to the top of the class”), there’s absolutely no problem with grad student A dating grad student B. A lot of departments are enormous, and grad students might not even be in the same classes, never mind having one grad student grade the other. Who do you think grad students date?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do evolutionists deal with the lack of evidence for and the mathematical impossibility of their theory?
Answer: *Sigh* There is a mountain of evidence for evolution. And in terms of mathematical impossibility….says who? 1.8 billion years is a *lot* of time for the wonderful and wacky world that is biology to come about by random chance, but also *selection*. That’s the important thing: evolution is iterative. I’m sure other posters have talked about this at length. There are so many things that are very easily explained by evolution that simply are not explained, and cannot be explained, by creationism, and many of them have to do with the fact that, if life was designed, whoever the designer is was an idiot:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What happens to a professor's PhD students if the professor leaves the university before the students finish defending their thesis?
Answer: A few things can happen, and it depends on the professor, the circumstances under which they are leaving, how much the school really cares about its students, etc. If the professor leaves one university to go to another one, his or her PhD students usually pack up and go with the professor to that new institution, and finish their work there. If the professor dies, or leaves the university in disgrace, the students in the group will usually move to other groups in the same department depending on capacity. If the professor retires, and is being classy about it, he or she announces that they are retiring in 5–7 years, and stops accepting new students. That way, when the last student graduates, the professor quietly retires. I haven’t yet seen a situation where a professor leaves and the students are just SOL. Though it can be very rough on technicians, who end up pretty much getting bounced from the lab.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Would a professor be upset if a student missed his office hours?
Answer: Uhh….no. Most of the time during my office hours, nobody would show up and I’d be grading or playing Solitaire or something. The default condition was, nobody came to my office hours. And as far as I’m concerned, if you’re a college student, you’re an adult, and if you don’t want to use the resources available to you, that’s your choice. Now, where I *would* get upset is when a student would be struggling, wouldn’t come to office hours, and would complain at the end of the semester that they got a bad grade. I’m sorry, but I was available to you, you didn’t take advantage of it, and what do you want me to do about it right now? You made a choice. On the other side of the coin, I’ve had students who have been on the bubble grade-wise, who *did* come to office hours all the time, and were clearly putting in a lot of effort. When I see a student like that, I’m inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt and give them, say, a solid B rather than a B-minus.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Can you be a scientist if you're bad at math or science?
Answer: I think that a lot of people who get told (or who think) that they are “bad at science” in high school, aren’t really, because high school is measuring the wrong things. In high school, you’re given a set of facts to regurgitate, and your aptitude for science is measured based on how well you can memorize and repeat them. My organic chemistry professor once joked that if you asked a high schooler “what does a chemist do for a living?” they would tell you “a chemist is a person who sits in a room all day, and people come to him and say, ‘a balloon has 5.7 grams of helium in it at 25C at standard atmospheric pressure. What volume does it occupy?” What I think high school does a very bad job of teaching is how to actually think like a scientist: how do I come up with an interesting question to which nobody knows the answer, and how do I answer it? Being “good at science”, in the context of being a practicing scientist, doesn’t mean that you can memorize and regurgitate a lot of factoids. What it means is that you are able to ask the right questions, design the right experiments to test those questions, analyze the data you get out of those experiments, draw valid conclusions from those data, and do this process again and again and again. As to being “bad at math”, it depends on what field of science you are in. If you’re in physics, math is very, very important.
