If you’re in some branches of chemistry or biology, the math you use every day is pretty basic, though there are some very math-heavy sub-disciplines of each. For that matter, people in the sciences joke about what kinds of math they are actually good at: sometimes they are very good at theoretical math, but awful at arithmetic. I have personally seen a number of cases just like this comic strip (PhD comics by Jorge Cham): (This one’s titled “Your Math Skills.” Have a look at www.phdcomics.com, Dr. Cham has written some really funny ones over the years) So in short, people who have been told, or who have convinced themselves, that they are “bad at math” or “bad at science” might want to consider: are you bad at those subjects? Or are you bad at what you’ve been *told* those subjects are?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it possible to be expert in every field of science?
Answer: Uh, no. I once sat in a room at a “communicating science” workshop with other experts in different fields. We managed to confuse the hell out of each other when trying to explain our areas of expertise at a high level. And that wasn’t even “every field of science”, just a few of them. Just my field, chemistry, is extremely broad. It covers everything from what happens at the atomic level to what happens on the scale of galaxies. Even among other chemists there’s a lot of explaining that needs to go on between the different sub-disciplines.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why should I go to school when I am smarter than my teachers?
Answer: I haven’t read all the answers here, but I suspect a lot of them are going to say “how do you know you’re smarter?” And that’s something worth emphasizing: you don’t necessarily know that you’re smarter. OR, maybe you’re smarter, but they know something you don’t. The truly smart person looks for lessons from whoever is able to teach them. The person who thinks they are smart misses out on those lessons. But to take a slightly different tack, let’s say that you really are as smart as you think you are. I doubt it, but let’s grant that. Let me let you in on a little secret: school is partly designed as training wheels for life. And as you live your life, you’re going to have to deal with a lot of people who aren’t as smart as you are, but who you need to be on good terms with for one reason or another. Here, the stakes are low. In the working world, they are somewhat higher. There’s also a difference between intelligence and wisdom.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should I base my decision on when choosing a research group for my MSc thesis and future PhD (Chemistry)? Should I worry about the size of the group and the PI’s way of supervising?
Answer: I would advise you to base your decision more on personality of the group and less on what the group is actually doing. Part of that is me: I’ve been able to find the interesting parts of some very different fields of research, and others might have trouble making that adjustment, but my advice is find a pleasant group, and then find a way to make your work interesting within that group. The number one mistake you can make is to think that you’re special. It’s easy to think “oh, this professor is a jerk, but they’ll be nice to me” or “this group takes a long time to graduate, but I’ll make it out in five years because I’m me.” No. The problems of a group will apply to you as well. What do I mean on personality of the group? Well, 1) what are the expectations of work hours/work-life balance? And do you find such a schedule agreeable? If the boss has a reputation for insisting his group work 80-hour weeks, and you don’t want to, that’s setting the stage for unhappiness. 2) How hands-on is the professor? By that I mean, is he telling you what to do constantly, or do you never see him? There are some groups where the professor is in lab every day. There are other groups where you don’t see the professor for months at a time. There are advantages and disadvantages to each management style: some people need more guidance, some people find guidance annoying. Ask yourself, how closely do I want to be managed? 3) Does the professor play favorites? Does the professor pit his students against one another, working on the same project to see who “wins”, and is that healthy or toxic competition? 4) Do the people in the research group seem to like each other, or are they constantly at each other’s throats? 5) How long does it take to graduate, and why? Also have to ask yourself about what’s important to you: do you want to graduate in 4.5 years after working 80+ hour weeks, or do you want to graduate in 7 years after working 40–50 hour weeks? Be wary of groups where there’s only one grad student left, and he’s been there for 8 years. Those are the biggest things, I think.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the pros and cons of attending or teaching at Caltech?
Answer: Hoo boy, how long have you got? I can speak most accurately to graduate school, and have only some guesses as to undergrad based on what I heard and saw, but didn’t experience first hand. Pros: Cons: On balance, I loved Caltech. But my impression was that it might be better as a graduate student than as an undergrad.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is "toxic masculinity" just a way of saying men are toxic?
Answer: Here’s my catch-all answer to all this masculinity business: Any boy with a pack of matches can burn down a house. It takes a man to build a house. Sweating in the sun to build a house is masculinity. Burning a house down and talking about how much of a man that makes you is toxic masculinity. Being a man, as opposed to being a boy, is about controlling your strength and your urges, and using them for something productive.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What would happen if we gave the Ukrainians $45 million instead of $45 billion? Is the fact they need so much money evidence that they should surrender, as they don’t have the military power necessary to upkeep their sovereignty?
Answer: Do you think the United States defeated Great Britain in the War of Independence all by itself? Absolutely not! About half of the army that won the Battle of Yorktown was French. The Americans “borrowed” the French navy, was firing French muskets, using French ammunition, and using French money to pay for everything. If your standard for sovereignty is that a country should be able to stand on its own without foreign assistance, then not only should we not aid Ukraine, but to avoid charges of hypocrisy we should abandon our independence and pledge allegiance to our rightful lord and master, Charles III, by the Grace of God of the United Kingdom etc. King, Defender of the Faith “Hello there, you rebellious colonial ingrates!”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Can you be fired from your PhD program? If so, how can you tell if your supervisor is going to fire you?
Answer: Yes, and it very much depends on your supervisor. Some supervisors will fire their students at the drop of a hat. In the case of my adviser, you had to try pretty hard to get fired in order to get fired. I saw one guy get fired from our group, but he pretty much didn’t show up in lab at all for about six months, and his group meetings/technical updates were hilariously bad. It might also depend on the school: in some schools I think if your adviser drops you, you’ve got to leave the program, but in other schools, you can find another adviser. In terms of not getting fired (and I’ve written this answer elsewhere), try to avoid the “Three Nos” when you give research updates. That means 1) no results, 2) no plan, 3) no clue. If you have only two of these, you should be OK (“I have some results, I don’t know what they mean or where to go next” is OK. “I don’t have any results, but here’s why I think that’s the case and here’s what I’m going to do next” is OK. But “I don’t have results, and I don’t know what to do, and I don’t really know anything about anything”, you are in serious trouble).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are BSc students allowed to attend conferences?
Answer: Depends on the conference, but for the most part, if you can pony up the entrance fee, you can attend. I think for the American Chemical Society you have to nominally be a chemist or something, but that definition is so elastic that you could probably make an argument for being a chemist for most jobs in the scientific field.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What would happen if Trump simply declassified the documents he took before he left? Would that have been better? He forgot to declassify them. Why the "visit" from the FBI? Why the outrage?
Answer: Let me put it this way: *your Social Security number* (and everybody else’s SSN) is information held by the Government. However, the Government does not call it “classified information.” SSNs are considered “Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI)”, and are held at a lower level of security than the documents Trump had at Mar a Lago. So when we’re talking about classified information, we are talking about information that the Government believes is more sensitive, and would cause more damage to US interests if it were released, than every Social Security number in existence. Would you like your Social Security Number to be sitting around in a box at Mar a Lago? Would you like it to be published for the world to see?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Should soldiers who never fight in war be allowed to call themselves veterans?
Answer: In the words of George S. Patton: “An army is a team. It lives, eats, sleeps, and fights as a team. This individual hero stuff is bullshit. The bilious bastards who write that stuff for the Saturday Evening Post don't know any more about real battle than they do about fucking. And we have the best team—we have the finest food and equipment, the best spirit and the best men in the world. Why, by God, I actually pity these poor bastards we're going up against. One of the bravest men I saw in the African campaign was on a telegraph pole in the midst of furious fire while we were moving toward Tunis. I stopped and asked him what the hell he was doing up there. He answered, 'Fixing the wire, sir.' 'Isn't it a little unhealthy up there right now?' I asked. 'Yes sir, but this goddamn wire has got to be fixed.' I asked, 'Don't those planes strafing the road bother you?' And he answered, 'No sir, but you sure as hell do.' Now, there was a real soldier. A real man. A man who devoted all he had to his duty, no matter how great the odds, no matter how seemingly insignificant his duty appeared at the time. And you should have seen the trucks on the road to Gabès. Those drivers were magnificent. All day and all night they crawled along those son-of-a-bitch roads, never stopping, never deviating from their course with shells bursting all around them. Many of the men drove over 40 consecutive hours. We got through on good old American guts. These were not combat men. But they were soldiers with a job to do. They were part of a team. Without them the fight would have been lost.” As the Russians have amply demonstrated in Ukraine, you can have tanks and equipment and a lot of troops, but if your tanks don’t have gas and your men don’t have ammunition and food, you’re no good.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should you do if your PhD supervisor wants to take credit for your work?
Answer: This is a tricky question to answer, because it very much depends on what you mean by “take credit for your work.” If it means that your supervisor wants to have his/her name on your papers, and present your work at conferences, that’s completely normal and you’ve really not got a case/something to complain about. A classy supervisor will put the names of the students who actually did the work on a slide or a section of slides in a conference presentation, but that’s not obligatory and I’d say it’s about 50–50 as to who actually does that. But it’s broadly understood at conferences that professors are not actually in lab doing the work that goes on their slides. If your work is SO good that it ends up winning a Nobel Prize….it’s likely going to be your boss who actually wins said prize. That’s just the way it works. When looking at a scientific paper author’s list, I expect that the first author is the one who actually did most of the work, or led the execution of the project, and the last author or last two authors were the supervisors and other more senior folks, who conceived/planned/funded the work. Now, if your supervisor is *leaving your name off of papers you actually worked on*, that’s a different matter. I’d take it up with my supervisor, my thesis committee, the ombudsman if any, and the department chair. I would also start looking for a different supervisor. In short, if your supervisor wants his or her name on your papers, that’s normal and expected and you don’t have a leg to stand on. If your supervisor is excluding *your* name from your papers, that’s something to make a stink about.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the h-index, and why might a professor's h-index be low compared to their number of publications?
Answer: h-index is the number of publications by a particular author that have been cited at least n times. So if you have 5 publications, and all 5 of them have been cited at least 5 times, then your h-index is 5. If one of them has been cited 1000 times, one has been cited 300 times, and the other three have not been cited at all, your h-index is 2. If a professor has a lot of publications, but a low h-index, it means that he or she is publishing papers that are not being cited. There could be a few reasons for this. First, the field could be obscure, or it could be a field where you aren’t expected to rack up a lot of citations. Second, the work could simply be not all that good, or is only being accepted in obscure journals, which tend to not be read by many people.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I'm a direct descendant of the House of Bruce and House of Plantagenet. I have documentation and sources to prove lineage. How can I promote this for me and my children?
Answer: As we say in America, this fact, and five bucks, will buy you a cup of coffee.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the general reaction of professors when students confront them about grades or assignments?
Answer: My general reaction is to groan when a student asks me about a grade. Now, if I made a mistake (either I have the wrong answer in the answer key, or I penalized something incorrectly), please let me know, that does happen, and I’m happy to correct myself. I’m not perfect. I’m also fine when someone comes to me early in the semester and says “I need help, what do I need to do?” If someone is having problems at home that make it difficult for them to get things done, and they make me aware of it early, then I’m sympathetic. However, it is more usual for someone to come to me at the end of the semester with a bunch of excuses, or to say in essence, “sure I didn’t do the work, and I won’t do it now, but will you raise my grade anyway?” Uh, no. Because it’s not fair to your classmates: I don’t know what struggles or sacrifices they had to make to get the grades they did. But if I allow people to sweet-talk me into higher grades, it means if you worked for your grade, you’re a sucker. I’m not going to do that.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My PhD advisor is abusing me. I have published as many first author papers as they had initially asked. Many more co-author papers too. Yet my workload keeps increasing. I feel powerless being a foreign student in USA. What can I do?
Answer: There are a lot of good answers here about going up the chain of command, i.e. talking to your thesis committee, your department chair, an ombudsman office, and so forth. It’s also an excellent time for “quiet quitting.” I’ll throw in two suggestions that I’m not seeing in the other responses: If/when you go to your department chair, ask them, “may I finish my PhD work with another adviser?” Many schools will let you switch if things really aren’t working out. The other alternate is to quietly start looking for work elsewhere. As in, an industry or government position, either here or in your native country if returning there is a viable option. (And I just want to be very, VERY clear, I am *not* saying “foreigner go home.” I’m delighted to have you in our country. I’m only mentioning it because unfortunately, our immigration system sucks and adds a layer of complication to this whole question). Anyway, let the recruiters know what your situation is. Show them your papers, talk about your research, and say, well, I don’t have a PhD, but as you can see I am an accomplished scientist. Would you consider hiring such an accomplished scientist who has just a master’s degree? If they say yes, and make you a JOB OFFER, firmly and in writing, then take it and say “hey boss, are you going to let me graduate, or should I take this job as it stands?” If you are as far along in your PhD as I think you are, the school should let you quit with a master’s, and you can ride off into the sunset. You might have your heart set on an academic career, and unfortunately this sort of action might wall off that possibility. But this will enable you to get away from a bad situation that’s unfortunately all too common. Good luck.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Can you call your professor by their first name if you have a PhD?
Answer: This very much depends on your adviser and on your institution. I went to graduate school in California, and once you were in the professor’s research group, you were calling him/her by their first name. People would address *Nobel Laureates* by their first name. It took me a long time to get used to this, and I informally only started doing it once I passed candidacy, but everybody else in the institution called their adviser by their first name almost right away. I don’t think it’s just a West Coast thing either: I noticed that at my undergraduate institution (Pittsburgh), grad students appeared to address their advisers by first name. I wouldn’t do this in Europe, however (I spent a year in Poland before starting graduate school). They appear to be a lot more formal, to the point where I wouldn’t *ever* call my adviser by her first name. So the answer, as with so much else in the PhD sphere, is “it depends.”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How many PhD students can a professor have in the United States?
Answer: Speaking from a perspective of the hard sciences: that depends on funding, space, type of research, and the university. Some schools might have a limit, formal or informal, as to how many a professor can have. I’ve seen a wide range of group sizes, from one (!) to about sixty graduate students and post-docs combined. It also varies from school to school: at Caltech a group of 15 people was “big”, but at Northwestern, a group of 30 was not uncommon. That might also be because Caltech’s student population is actually quite small (about 1200 grad students, and about 900 undergraduate). The two big limitations are going to be laboratory space, and funding. If you have an army of graduate students, presumably you want them to actually be doing something in lab. For that you need space and equipment, to the point where a large group could be taking up an entire floor or an entire wing of a building. I think the University usually allocates space, and likely does so based on how successful the professor is in research. So if you have space for 5 students, why would you hire more? Second factor is money: the expectation is that PhD students are getting paid. They aren’t getting paid much, but there are overhead costs which go on top of salary. That can add up to about $50–100k per student per year, and more for post-docs. So if you have a large group, your salary line-item in the budget can get into the millions of dollars, for which you need to pull in the grants. That’s not even counting the supplies required for these people to actually be doing something, that’s just the cost of getting them in the door. Finally, there is the “span of control” problem. Humans are only able to adequately manage a certain number of people, which is why we have chains of command: a general is not telling each and every member of his 15,000-man division where to go, he’s doing a lot of delegating. In a research group, if a professor is trying to manage each graduate student, well, there are only so many graduate students he or she can manage. Larger groups will sometimes have “research assistant professors” who do a lot of the day-to-day management, or the professor can deputize his or her post-docs to serve as middle management. But this is a stopgap solution, and post-docs are usually only around for a few years. So in short, I don’t know if there are formal limits on the number of PhD students a professor can have, but there are definitely going to be financial and other practical limits that cap the size of a group.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do Poles know a lot about each other?
Answer: Back in the Bad Old Days, i.e. Communism, some Poles knew everything there was to know about other Poles! Pictured: crest of the Polish People’s Republic (PRL), which was used by the Security Service (Służba Bezpieczeństwa, or SB), the Polish equivalent of the KGB. All joking aside, this was a nasty, nasty secret police, and may it never return in any form.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is the US really a terrible place to live, or are the people exaggerating?
Answer: I forget where I read this, might have been Quora, it isn’t original to me but I think it’s highly accurate: The people who keep talking about how terrible America is, either have never lived here, or have never lived anywhere else. You always have to ask, “terrible compared to what?” Many countries overseas have problems that you never hear about, because those problems aren’t in the tourist brochures, action movies, or romantic comedies. You also need to ask, “terrible under which circumstances?” If you’re viewing America from the cardboard box you live in at Central and 6th in Los Angeles, yes, it’s awful. If you’re viewing America from your mansion in about 30 miles away in Malibu or Bel Air, it’s amazing. I will say a lot of what you hear is exaggerated, especially when it comes to safety on the street, and violence in general. A lot of the violence is concentrated in specific neighborhoods in specific cities. You don’t see car chases and shootouts like in the movies.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it true that teachers/professors don’t care if you come to class in college?
Answer: It depends. Some teachers and professors take attendance, others don’t. In some cases, the class sizes are so large (200+) that the professor probably doesn’t even notice if you aren’t there. Personally, I didn’t really care if my students didn’t show up. But if they flunked their exams because they weren’t showing up, that was their decision, and their problem. These are adults, and they can face the consequences of their own decisions. I was a TA for one of those large (250-person) classes. It was a pass-fail class, and at the end of the quarter all the TAs met with the professor to decide who passed and who failed. Most of the decisions were easy, but there were a few students who were on the bubble, a few percentage points below the cutoff. The decision was, pass them, require them to do remedial work before they would pass, or flunk them outright, and the professor asked the TA of each student what they thought. I think four of those students on the bubble were in my section. One of them was always in class, always paid attention, and his grades got steadily better as the quarter went on, and that’s what I told the professor. He got passed outright. Second student was fifty-fifty participation and attendance-wise, and got a provisional pass. The other two students I’d never seen all quarter, and their grades were on the lower end of the bubble. I said “I don’t know these people”, they flunked, and had to repeat the course. So I would say, attendance helps give a student the benefit of the doubt. If I see a student who is showing up, who is putting in a lot of effort, and they are right on the margin of a C+ to a B-, or a B- to a B, I’m inclined to say “well, we all have different gifts, and maybe this student’s gifts are in some other topic, but they really seem to care about this, work ethic is to be encouraged, so, eh, give them the higher grade.” But if someone’s on that bubble, and they don’t seem to give a crap, why should I give a crap about them?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the most ostentatious and grandiose graduation ceremony in the world?
Answer: It wasn’t a graduation ceremony, but I went to the 100th birthday party for Prof. Adam Bielanski of the Jagellonian University, which was quite a big do. It was in the Aula of the Jagellonian U., which is a room that gets opened only for special occasions. What was hilarious is that a number of Rectors (what we would call a university President or Chancellor) were in attendance, and were introduced not only by name, but by full academic title, for instance: “His Magnificence Mister Professor Doctor Habilitated Engineer Architect Jan Kowalski” They did this for about 15 guys. Maybe not ostentatious, but definitely pompous! Yes, the rectors of many universities are referred to as “Jego/Jej Magnificencja” (His/Her Magnificence). “Habilitation” is like a super-PhD that is done in German-influenced university systems. Engineer is kind of like a master’s degree in engineering, and “architect” is kind of the same. Professor actually means a little bit more in Poland, as it’s a title given by the President of the Republic (well, sort of: there are two kinds of professors. A “professor extraordinary” is a professor who gets that title from a university. A “professor ordinary” gets this title from the President).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should be included in the acknowledgements section of a PhD thesis?
Answer: A guy I work with has the mantra that “ink is cheap, and electrons are even cheaper.” Basically, it costs you nothing to include someone in the acknowledgements, but you create goodwill by being generous. So basically, if you *think* someone should go in the acknowledgements, they should go in.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What does it mean when a referee holds up a yellow card?
Answer: In soccer, this is known as a “caution.” It means that a player or coach has been formally warned for a semi-serious offense. I write down the player’s number, the time of the infraction, and the reason. If the same player or coach commits another yellow card offense in the same game, they get kicked out (red card, or “sending-off”). Unlike in many other sports, being sent off means your team is playing short-handed….for the rest of the game. So, if you get a red card in the 5th minute, your team is playing with 10 men against the other teams’ 11 for the next 85 minutes. For hockey fans, that’s a permanent power-play. What are the reasons for getting a yellow card? Here they are: Of course, discretion applies. If I think a player really didn’t hear the whistle stopping play, and cleared the ball, I’m not going to caution for delaying restart of play. In youth games I rarely caution for failure to respect the distance, I’ll just tell the kid to back off and he usually does. On the other end of the spectrum, when do you give a yellow as opposed to a red, which is an ejection? Well, red is for violent conduct or serious foul play. What’s the line between “reckless” and “serious foul play?” Up to the referee. Or, is it stopping a promising attack (yellow), or is it denial of a goal-scoring opportunity (red)? Every situation is different, and that’s why you have a referee. There’s a whole little ceremony that’s supposed to accompany a yellow card. The referee is supposed to modulate his or her whistle to match the severity of the foul: a small foul, I’ll give a quick “chirp” on the whistle. But if something’s serious, it should be a long “TWEEEEET!” Ideally, the players should know from the whistle that a card is coming out. Then, giving the card itself: First, the referee should run over to where the foul is, then separate and isolate the player being cautioned/carded, so everybody knows who it is. I’ll usually go “red #17, step this way please” while taking the card out. Then, the referee holds the card over his or her head, then the referee writes down the player’s information. I usually talk to the player as well, saying something like “red #17, you are cautioned for a reckless challenge” before holding up the card. If it is a SECOND yellow card, the referee first holds up the yellow card, then holds up the red card, then points to the bench with a dramatic flourish, then writes everything down. The player has been sent off. The rules of competition sometimes also specify that the player who gets the yellow card has to go sit on the bench. They can be replaced on the field, and come back on at the next opportunity to substitute. That’s called a “hot-head” rule, and not all leagues have it: high school has it, a lot of recreational leagues have it, USSF and FIFA do not. You can be carded twice on the same play, and thrown out! This is usually funny to watch on YouTube: usually a player commits a reckless tackle at one end of the field. The referee signals “advantage”, meaning that he saw the foul but is letting play continue because it is to the advantage of the team that was fouled. That doesn’t erase the yellow card, however! The referee makes a mental note to issue the card at the next stoppage of play. So, play continues, and the fouling player runs down the field, and takes the guy with the ball out (stopping a promising attack). The referee will pull out the yellow, point to the spot of the first foul, show the yellow, then point to the spot of the second foul, then show the yellow followed by the red.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it okay for professors to express their political views in class, and how should students respond when they do so?
Answer: I would say it depends on the subject being taught. If I’m in a science class, or a math class, the focus should be on science or math. I’d say that science, not being a “settled” subject, would allow for more opinion to creep in, but it should be an opinion about the topic at hand. I don’t think you can really have an opinion about calculus. If it’s an economics or political science class, then I would expect the professor to have a point of view, but also to share and be ready to discuss other points of view in that particular field. For instance, I once had a course on the economies of East Asia in about 2010. I dropped it, because there was a LOT of reading, but on that reading list was the Communist Manifesto, something of Mao’s and Deng Xiaoping’s, as well as some Milton Friedman. The professor struck me as a crusty conservative type who probably didn’t love Karl Marx, BUT, when you are discussing the economic development of China and Vietnam, Communism is/was a thing, and you have to understand it if you’re going to understand those countries.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How should one compliment their university professors in order for them to take it seriously and not just brush it off as flattery?
Answer: What I found to be a good formula (and this works if you’re also cold-calling someone) is to say something along the lines of “I read your papers on X, Y, and Z and thought that this specific thing was really interesting. Have you thought about doing A, B, or C?” I’m writing from a perspective in the hard sciences, but it’s probably applicable to the liberal arts as well. It shows you put in the effort to find out something about this person, and that you appreciate their hard work (those papers usually take at least a year, frequently two or more….and few people actually read them). And it also gives the professor an excuse to talk about themselves, and who doesn’t like talking about themselves?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is your opinion on telling your husband "I love you so much?"
Answer: If it is heartfelt (and I thank my lucky stars that from my wife, it is), I really like to hear that. It’s a reminder that our relationship is really special.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are the attacks against Crimea intended to terrorize the civilian population and summer visitors to the Russian territory? Will they be effective in doing that?
Answer: I am amused that the Russians are reacting with outrage, and calling it barbarous and perfidious to attack air bases, ammo depots, and the military headquarters of the Black Sea Fleet. If those aren’t legitimate military targets, what even IS a legitimate military target? The Russians have been caterwauling about the insult to their sovereignty when 1) they are actively violating the sovereignty of another nation and 2) Crimea isn’t even Russian sovereign territory. If you don’t want people to blow up your stuff, don’t start wars. It’s that simple.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do you not notice the existence of a fierce campaign against masculinity? Who is behind it and why?
Answer: I think there’s a campaign against masculinity. It is being conducted by those who claim they are its fiercest defenders. Masculinity, properly understood, means protecting the vulnerable and not taking advantage of them. It means having strength, both physical and mental, but also the self-control to know when and how to use it. It means treating women with respect. It means recovering from setbacks and forging onwards with all the effort you can muster. Men are supposed to build things, even when it’s hard. I think the best summation of masculinity is embodied by the poem “If” by Rudyard Kipling, who was writing in an era that made a big deal about manly men: Another example of masculinity was defined by Theodore Roosevelt in his famous “Man in the Arena” speech, particularly the passage that starts “it is not the critic who counts.” However, what do I hear from the supposed champions of men and masculinity today? That women are whores and sluts, while these selfsame champions whine that these supposed whores and sluts are having sex with everybody except them. That it isn’t their fault that they aren’t successful, but rather it’s the feminists, the immigrants, the Chinese, the liberals, etc. That the way to be a man is not to control yourself, but to be a bully, and demonstrate your superiority by flexing over anybody who’s weaker than you. That an ability to hurl insults is the mark of a man. And you can do all of this on the internet, where the risks are very low. This is not being a man, this is being an uncontrolled, noisy little boy. Any boy with a pack of matches can burn down a house. It takes a man to build one.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: At what time does it become unsafe to be out in Poland?
Answer: Here’s my two cents: on at least two occasions I walked home underneath a bridge over the Vistula River near the castle after 1:30AM. I thought nothing of it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do I survive in the streets of Poland?
Answer: Do you mean, how do you survive as a homeless person in Poland? I have frankly no idea. But if your question is more along the lines of “how do I survive just walking around in Poland on the streets”, that’s a little silly. I walked under a bridge by the river in Krakow at 1:30AM on at least two occasions, and really thought nothing of it. Basically, stay away from the drunks and the soccer hooligans, and you’ll be fine. The only time I really felt unsafe in Poland was, I was wearing a scarf which from a distance must have looked vaguely like a Cracovia scarf (one of the two soccer teams in town: the hooligans of one team hate the hooligans of the other, and vice-versa). I had two guys approach me and try to unzip my jacket: apparently stealing the “enemy’s” scarf is a thing. I slapped the guy’s hand away and started hollering at him IN ENGLISH. Basically, I was sending the message that they were jumping a tourist. So they wandered off without incident. I reasoned that, if its soccer hooligans fighting, the cops don’t really care. But, soccer hooligans jump a tourist….the police care about that, because that’s embarrassing. The hooligans knew this.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is "Richard II" by William Shakespeare worth the read?
Answer: Other commentators on Quora point out, rightly I think, that Shakespeare is meant to be seen. So it’s probably best to see the play first, done by a good ensemble, then read it. I recommend the BBC’s “Hollow Crown”, starring Ben Whishaw in the title role, Rory Kinnear as Bolingbroke, Patrick Stewart as John of Gaunt, and David Suchet as the Duke of York. There’s also a hilarious Shakespeare webcomic called Good Tickle Brain that presents Richard II in stick figures. It’s an accurate summary, and I love this site for all things Shakespeare: That being said, yes, Richard II is absolutely worth the read. It is an often-overlooked, and in my opinion very underrated play. The central question faced by the protagonists is, what do you do when you have a legitimate ruler who sucks, and there’s a challenge to him from some guy who is a better ruler, but his claim to power sucks? Richard II isn’t exactly a tyrant, he’s just bad at his job and strongly implied to be gay. Does that mean you can get rid of him? And if you do get rid of him, where’s the line between doing what you’re doing because you care about your country, and doing it because you are an opportunist? These are some serious philosophical questions which are carried through to the other plays of the “Henriad”, namely 1 Henry IV, 2 Henry IV, and Henry V. 1 Henry IV is just about my favorite Shakespeare play, I think you can skip 2 Henry IV, and Henry V is pretty good. But back to Richard II: The language is magnificent. It’s some really, really good writing, and it also differentiates its characters very well: Richard is dramatic, Bolingbroke is very businesslike. Now, I’d say this shouldn’t be the very first Shakespeare play you read, because the language is very stylized and almost all of the play is in verse. But if you’re already familiar with how Shakespeare writes, then this is well worth the read. I mean, just look at this! For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed; Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd; All murder'd: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp, Allowing him a breath, a little scene, To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks, Infusing him with self and vain conceit, As if this flesh which walls about our life, Were brass impregnable, and humour'd thus Comes at the last and with a little pin Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king! Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood With solemn reverence: throw away respect, Tradition, form and ceremonious duty, For you have but mistook me all this while: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is Othello a racist play?
Answer: You first have to ask, what makes a play racist? I would argue that it has to show racism as a positive thing, or to make us believe that racism is good or right or proper. Alternatively, it has to argue that people of a certain race are inherently inferior because they are members of that race. Based on those standards, I would say that Othello is not a racist play. There are definitely racist characters in Othello, but they are the villains (Rodrigo, Iago, Brabantio), and in fact their racism motivates their villainy. One of my pet peeve interpretations of this play is “Iago has no motive! He’s just evil because he’s evil!” NONSENSE! Iago *tells* you what his motives are, and some of them are racist. Iago also manages to use people’s racism to his advantage. Does Othello do bad things? Yes. But I don’t think the argument of the play is “you see, they’re all like that!” In fact, what makes the play powerful is that we are invited to imagine ourselves in Othello’s position. One of the saddest parts of this play is that Othello has actually internalized the racism of the culture that surrounds him: when asked “so if you aren’t using magic, why would Desdemona want you?” he answers frankly that he doesn’t know. Part of his insecurity with Desdemona stems from his sense that her love for him is somehow unnatural because she’s white and he isn’t, and therefore her love can’t be real. You could make the argument that Shakespeare is in fact showing how destructive racism can be. Now, is it possible to *perform* this play in a racist way? Absolutely. It’s also embarrassing that Othello was performed in blackface….into the 1970s! But I think that the fact that white audiences refused to accept that someone who was an actual black person could play the role is a weird testament to how well that role is written, and how desirable a part it is: Othello is a noble man, a loyal servant of the Venetian state, who is undone by his flaws and by someone he thought was his friend.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why doesn't the football referee carry a smartphone for viewing replays to make decisions?
Answer: I’m assuming by “football” you mean “soccer” (American here). In high levels of competition, the referee has a microphone and an earpiece, and on his “circuit” he’s able to talk to, and listen to, the VARs up in the booth, who have the bazillion angles you see on TV, and a bunch of other angles you don’t get to see. The VARs can look at a play from several angles simultaneously, and tell the center referee their opinion, which has a much better appearance than a referee whipping out a smartphone and having to call up the right angle. At lower levels, as the referee, you simply don’t have the cameras.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do Millennials blame the baby boomer generation?
Answer: One thing that I think everybody forgets is that 1950–1970 was a huge anomaly in American and world history: the other industrialized countries of the world were flat on their backs, having been thoroughly smashed by World War II. China, India, and other developing countries were impoverished and not industrial at all. What that meant was…..we’re number one, baby! There was no foreign competition, the world is rebuilding, the US was the only nation really able to do it, and so anybody with a pulse could find a job. A lot of open land was being turned into suburbs, so you could afford a house and it was expected that you wouldn’t live with your parents anymore. There wasn’t really pressure to cut costs or be super-efficient, because who’s going to do better than the USA? Sure, there was political and military competition from the Soviet Union, but who was lining up to buy Ladas, Kvass, and Bulgarian shoes? (well, a lot of people were lining up in the Soviet Union to buy damn near everything, but I digress). The problem is, this era of relative peace, prosperity, and lack of foreign competition was seen as normal. And when the world regressed to the mean, so to speak, and the rest of the world started to industrialize, well, all of a sudden the high labor costs of the US start to bite, and you can’t get a job unless you have some skills or serious advantages over someone working for cheap overseas. Millennials got the short end of that particular stick. But it’s easier to blame a generation (like your uncool parents!) than it is to recognize that your parents were lucky, you aren’t, and that’s how the ball has bounced. Of course, the Boomers don’t do themselves any favors in the popularity department. They have a tendency to fall into the very human idea that MY success is never due to luck, it’s due to hard work, clean living, the American Way, etc. etc. etc. And if YOU aren’t successful, well, that can’t come down to luck, you entitled brats. Now, I think there are some specific policy decisions for which the Boomers CAN be blamed. First and foremost, NIMBY-ism and opposition to new development. The reason Millennials can’t afford a starter house is that building them is expensive and tangled in lots of red tape (especially in places like California). The reason that’s the case is, if you already own a house, you don’t want to have new ones built. I bought a house for $320k. Part of the reason that was the case was that there was a brand new development going up across the street, with pretty similar houses that were selling for $350k. The value of my house is not going to exceed that of a brand-new one. But if there are no new houses, and people keep wanting to move into the neighborhood, then my house value goes up and I make money. Sure, it’s bad for people who are trying to buy a house, but as long as they can afford to buy my place someday, I don’t really care. I’ll also blame the Boomers for pushing college, college, college, while also greatly expanding the market for student loans AND coming up with things like the FAFSA, which enables colleges to effectively price-discriminate. The problem with a student loan, especially when everybody can get one, is that it effectively masks the true price of college, and ultimately makes college more expensive for everybody. Imagine you had to cough up $40,000, cash, every year for college. You couldn’t do it, and odds are, nobody else could either. Colleges would go out of business very fast. BUT, if instead college is about coughing up $160,000 over 30 years plus interest, a lot more people are willing and able to do that, especially as a college education is the one product you “have to have.” And if you can cough up $160,000 over 30 years, why not $180,000 or $200,000 or $250,000, or even $300,000 over 40 years? Especially when the interest rates are low, and you’re able to easily qualify for a loan, all in the name of making college “more affordable.” I was also shocked to learn that in the FAFSA process, you pretty much give the colleges a complete picture of your family’s financial status. That lets the college charge you *exactly* the highest price that you are willing and able to pay (price discrimination) under the guise of “financial aid.”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What’s in it for a PhD advisor to advise someone?
Answer: If you’re in a “publish or perish” position, the only way you’re going to publish is if you’re advising PhD students and/or postdocs. And until you’ve made a name for yourself, you might not even have first pick of the students in a given class. In the sciences at least, you cannot succeed as a professor unless you have PhD students and are publishing with them on a regular basis.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I’m about to publish my first paper as a graduate student, and my supervisor is afraid I might not include his name as co-author since he contributed little. Ever since, he has been giving me the cold shoulder. What do I do?
Answer: I think this may very much depend on what field you work in. In my field (biology/chemistry/materials science) it is extremely unusual to have a single-author paper, almost to the point where I’d say it’s unheard of. It’s broadly understood that the last author of the paper is the PhD adviser of the first author. While your adviser might not have contributed much to the paper itself, he provided the funding (not trivial: the average paper in biology probably cost something like $200k to produce), he usually pointed you on a specific direction, he gave you feedback on your experiments, and he helped write the paper, or at least edit it. Not to mention, peer review may be a lot easier if your adviser’s name is on it. Advisers are also typically overseeing groups of 5–30 grad students and post-docs: their participation with each student is likely to be minimal on a day-by-day basis. But of course their name is going to be included. This may vary a lot from field to field, and I think in something like particle physics, where there are occasionally hundreds or thousands of authors, leaving out an adviser’s name looks even sillier. But at least in my field, you’d look petty and stupid to try to do something like this. Now, I *don’t* like the idea of including your adviser’s friends/the department chair/some big cheese the adviser is trying to impress if he or she didn’t contribute to the paper. That’s a different matter. But at least in my field, the assumption is that your adviser’s name goes on the paper.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How is the rivalry between MIT and Caltech?
Answer: I once wore my “Caltech Beavers” T-shirt across the MIT campus with pride, and wasn’t even met with side-eye. A few people thought it was kind of funny. A lot of MIT alumns end up working at JPL, or at Caltech, and they fit right in (heck, the current Provost of Caltech went to MIT for undergrad). We’ll occasionally make jokes at MIT’s expense, but it’s all in good fun. That’s kind of the only “rival” that Caltech has: we aren’t a football school, and I don’t know how many people actually attend the basketball games.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are countries like Czechia, Poland, the Baltic states, and Romania jealous of the close relationship Serbia has with Russia?
Answer: In Poland, no. I strongly suspect that Czechia, the Baltic States, and Romania also say no. And I’m puzzled that many Russians see the world as being composed of two kinds of people: those who are Russian, and those who wish they were Russian. There’s an awful lot of Eastern and Central Europe that is perfectly happy being Ukrainian, Czech, Polish, Lithuanian, etc. One very important factor in the historically close relations between Serbia and Russia is TURKEY. We forget now that the Ottoman Empire was the 800-pound gorilla in the room (or depending on your perspective, just outside the room) in Europe between about 1400 and about 1750-ish, and the Turks menaced/conquered/generally made themselves unpleasant across Serbia for longer than that, about 1350ish all the way up to World War I. There’s a religious aspect to this as well, as both Russia and Serbia are Eastern Orthodox. Russia was Serbia’s champion against the Turks, Serbia made a handy cats-paw for the Russians, and that’s why relations are cozy. Ironically, you could say that historically Turkey is to Serbia what Russia is to Poland: the big, menacing imperial neighbor that you really wished would go away. Polish relations with Turkey were, if not exactly friendly, at least those of “worthy opponents.” The Ottoman Empire actually continued recognizing Poland as a county well into the 19th century: there was a Polish ambassador to the Sublime Porte when there wasn’t any Poland to represent, and this in part was probably because the Sultan recognized that the Great Powers were very much interested in partitioning Turkey the same way they had just partitioned Poland.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If Crimea historically belongs to Russia, why doesn't it give back Kalingrad to the Germans?
Answer: I’m waiting for the day the President of Mongolia says that the existence of Russia is an accident of history, and that the Russians should return to the control of their rightful overlords, the Mongols. Or, for the King of Norway and the King of Sweden issue a joint statement pointing out that both Varangian AND Kievan Rus were founded by Vikings who had wandered south, and therefore Russia should return to its historical roots as a protectorate of Norway and Sweden. Or for the Turkish government to point out that Crimea was under the control of the Crimean Khanate, which was an Ottoman protectorate, and therefore Crimea should return to Turkish control. Or for Japan to press its claims to Sakhalin Island. The problem with historically-based arguments for Irredentism (the belief that long-lost lands must be returned to their “rightful” owners, usually the people making the argument), is that you can always pick your favorite time in history to make whatever point you want to make.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How can anyone learn to be literate and write at Caltech?
Answer: If they’ve learned to be literate, that implies they know how to write. If they learn how to write, that implies they are literate. If they write semi-illiterate questions on Quora, perhaps they didn’t go to Caltech.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which university do you consider to be generally the more liberal, MIT or Caltech?
Answer: I’m assuming you mean “liberal” in terms of campus politics, i.e. on the spectrum between Berkley on the left and Hillsdale/Liberty on the right, where do Caltech and MIT fall. I can’t answer for MIT, but Caltech was an oddly apolitical place when I was there. You didn’t see a lot of protests on campus. In my six years there I remember exactly THREE protests. The first one had to do with a change to the Institute’s housing policy, where they were moving away from the traditional Harry Potter-esque houses to something more like dormitories. Some of the undergraduates didn’t like this, so there was a protest in the center of campus. The second protest was directed against a professor on campus who had developed a crush on his PhD student. His way of coping with this was to make her life difficult and eventually firing her. He was busy discussing all of this with *another* female student in his group, who also ended up leaving. It was a big scandal, and pretty much everyone on campus didn’t like this guy, and there was a sit-in protest in the physics building over it. My adviser actually polled our group, which had a diversity of political opinions ranging from slightly to the left of Joseph Stalin to slightly to the right of Genghis Khan, and everyone said “throw the bum out.” The third protest was some kind of labor action on behalf of the campus food service workers, but as I recall it consisted of about two guys (who weren’t students) standing on the street on the edge of campus with a sign. Historically, the only protests that happened in the sixties by Caltech students, at least that people will acknowledge, was when Star Trek (The Original Series) was cancelled. I’m not even sure if there’s a Republican Club or a Democrat Club on campus. There was a Socialist club set up while I was attending, but I’m not sure how many members they actually had. Basically, everybody is too darn busy to really get involved in politics, left or right, at Caltech.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: As a PhD, are you infuriated when someone leaves out your "Dr." prefix before your name?
Answer: About the only time anybody addresses me as “Dr.”, or refers to me as “Dr.”, is on my annual performance reviews, or in a very formal communication. Many of the people I interact with on a day-to-day basis are PhDs, or if they aren’t, are kind of assumed to have one by courtesy. In an academic setting (I was an adjunct for a few months), I encouraged my students to call me “Dr. K”, but I didn’t get miffed if one of them addressed me by first name. And because I’m relatively young, and our society is generally pretty informal (doubly so in California, where I did my doctoral work!), it’s still surprising to even get called “mister” anything. Also, I referee soccer on the weekends, and some of my fellow referees are high school aged kids (there are usually three officials to a game). Maybe if I was their teacher, in class I’d like them to call me “Mr.” or “Dr.”, but when we are on the field, if we are to work effectively together as a team, we must be equal, and therefore we must be on a first-name basis. Your fellow officials are your friends, and between the lines, during that game, they are the only friends you’ve got. When I started my degree, titles were important to me. Now that I have the title, I find I really don’t care. I’ve met some real idiots who have PhDs, and some very smart and capable people who only have a high school diploma, but keep learning. Or who are very capable in their fields: that electrician may not have a college degree, but he can work magic with a piece of equipment. One exception to my lack of irritation at being addressed informally: I don’t like being called by my first name by total strangers, because that usually means they are trying to get all “buddy-buddy” in order to sell me something.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Has Putin outsmarted the West?
Answer: Uh, no. Let’s leave aside any questions of morality or right and wrong, and just talk about Russian national interest. What was the situation Russia faced on February 20, 2022? What’s the situation Russia faces right now (late July 2022)? Bottom line, Putin probably could have got more of what he wanted had he played it cool, and gradually tried to influence politics in Ukraine. But he got impatient.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do colleges even exist for anything unrelated to becoming a doctor?
Answer: Ah, I sense a pre-med student asked this question. I remember being a semi-celebrity and/or first class weirdo in my Organic Chemistry laboratory classes because I was pretty much the only person there who was majoring in Chemistry, and who had no intention of applying to medical school. The other students, who were all pre-med, couldn’t comprehend why I was there. They also couldn’t comprehend that I actually liked organic chemistry. No, seriously. It’s beautiful. The concepts aren’t that hard, there are just a billion of them you need to know. Believe it or not, there are other skills and skillsets unrelated to the practice of medicine that are necessary to modern life. Like accountants. Because doctors like to get paid, and somebody’s got to keep the books. Like civil engineers. Because it’s much better to do surgery in a hospital than under a tree. Many of the designers even of medical devices are not actually medical doctors: there are many mechanical engineers, bio-medical engineers, chemists, and chemical engineers who make these things possible. All of them have to train somewhere. Oh yes, a lot of pharmaceutical discovery is done by chemists who don’t necessarily know what effects a particular molecule will have. But they have the skills needed to actually make that molecule. All those reactions you learn in organic chemistry? They are actually used to make stuff. And that’s just discussing things related to medicine that require non-medical specialization! Here’s my question to you, question-writer: what are you going to do if you don’t get in to medical school? While your question has a somewhat sneering tone, I ask this of you seriously, and in good faith. You not getting in is a very real possibility: depending on who you ask, only somewhere between 17–40% of pre-med students actually get admitted to medical school and become doctors: There are many, many, many worthwhile things you can do other than become a medical doctor.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does your PhD supervisor matter?
Answer: I would argue that your PhD supervisor is the most important factor in how your PhD goes. Consider: At the end of the day, you need to ask yourself, what matters to you? I feel like my PhD was sort of mediocre in terms of impact, and I’m not well-positioned for an academic career. Now, that happened in large part because of who I was as a student, and who I am as a person, but my advisor’s style contributed to it as well. On the other hand, my advisor’s style made it possible for me to enjoy graduate school. I had fun. I had hobbies, a life outside the lab, and that’s how I met my wife. I’ve seen a lot of people age 10–15 years during a 5-year program, leaving with a large number of gray hairs short of their 30th birthday. I know of at least one student who was starting to get health problems because of overwork. In my case maybe I got a little fatter, and while I had less hair at graduation than when I started, none of it was gray yet. I feel like I’m lucky: there are very few PhDs who can honestly say they miss graduate school, and I’m one of them. I ended up not caring about an academic career anyway, and the whole experience positioned me to make a good living doing something else. I think I learned the lessons I needed to learn to be successful in my chosen career. And I’m not really broken up about the fact that my PhD work didn’t get published in Science or Nature. So I think I got lucky when choosing an advisor. But that’s me. Other people in my shoes would see my PhD as a failure, or at least as a disappointment, and other advisors would probably have disowned me.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do most fathers detest female children?
Answer: Do they? The stereotype I’ve always heard is that fathers tend to favor and spoil girls, and/or fathers tend to think their girls are the sweetest beings in the universe who can do no wrong. This is why it’s not good to think in stereotypes.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do Philadelphia and Pittsburgh feel like they are in two different states?
Answer: Not really. There are some differences. I’m from the Midwest, and Pittsburgh feels like a Midwestern city, whereas Philadelphia feels more like an East Coast city. The accents are different, the histories are slightly different, but they don’t feel like the differences between, say, Pittsburgh and LA. They are different flavors of Pennsylvania. There were a lot of Philadelphians at Pitt when I was there, and they didn’t seem puzzled by this strange new world of Pittsburgh. I’d agree with another observation made here, that class differences don’t seem as pronounced in Pittsburgh as in Philadelphia: in certain parts of Philadelphia you will hear people affecting a Cary Grant accent while talking about going antiquing, or summering on the cape or whatever the hell rich people do. Pittsburgh definitely has some nice areas and nice suburbs, but the denizens of them tend to affect Mike Ditka, beer n’ bratwursts, and the city’s blue collar heritage more than Cary Grant and high society (it’s always funny to hear a couple of doctors in scrubs in a bar saying things like “I gotta get Dahntahn so I can go to that Stillers game after rotations n’at tomorrow.”) Golf is probably the most “high class” thing even a well-off Pittsburgher would do, or maybe skiing in the hills nearby, and they will try to make high-powered lawyering sound like working in a steel mill. I’ve also lived in a few other places, and I’d say the differences between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh are smaller than the differences between, say, San Diego and San Francisco.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is it that majority of PhD holders are giving scary testimonies about their experience, so making prospective PhD students even more scared about going for PhD? What exactly is the most scary part of PhD?
Answer: The scariest part of your PhD is the sense that your entire career path and fate rests on the whims of a small group of people (your boss most of all, and your thesis committee to a certain extent). If your boss tells you to go jump in a lake, the expectation is that you will do it. You can come up with an elegant Grand Unified Theory of Everything which turns out to be right, and if your thesis committee gets a bee in its bonnet, it can prevent you from graduating. (Dan Shechtman proposed the idea of a quasi-crystal, and was asked to leave his research group for coming up with a concept that was considered so incredibly idiotic, it was an embarrassment to have him in the group. Shechtman got the last laugh, though, winning the Nobel Prize in 2011. Had he had this idea as a graduate student, he would never have been able to publish it). Emotional abuse by advisers towards their students is so commonplace, it’s considered part of the experience. In our institution, there was a case of a professor sexually harassing one of his students, and behaving in an unprofessional manner with another one of them. Both of those students did end up getting a settlement, I think, but their careers were ruined, and they had to finish their PhDs at another institution. Now, you can get lucky and have a boss who is compassionate, patient, and wise (I was lucky in this way), but if you’re working for a jerk, your choices are to either tough it out, transfer, or drop out. The other thing that’s scary about a PhD is that there is no definite end date, and no really good way of measuring your progress. If you are in high school or college, you know you have to pass X classes in order to graduate. Not so with graduate school, and your boss is very much setting the standard for what it takes to graduate. That standard is opaque, and can shift. Worse, there is nothing that says you can’t be in a program for 3 years, start making some decent progress…..and then your adviser pulls the plug, and you have to hope that somebody else will hire/mentor you. There’s this constant nagging sense of “am I really good enough?”, which a sociopathic mentor will exploit. As to the other part of the question, why do people give scary testimonies: in large part, because they are true. There are people who have had good experiences working towards a PhD (I’m one of them, even though I had some rough patches). But also a lot of bad stories out there. One thing a PhD *should* instill is a sense of rigor and intellectual honesty. If I’m being rigorous and intellectually honest, I shouldn’t sugar-coat things.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Today I learned that my sister's Spanish class (middle school) is making each student change their name to a ‘Hispanic’ one if they have an “American” name (example Mark to Jose). Does anyone else find this alarming and very odd?
Answer: I went by “Manuel” in my middle school Spanish class 20 years ago, even though that’s not the equivalent of “Mark.” It was kind of a role-playing exercise, part of an attempt to immerse oneself in the culture of the language you were learning, and a lot of kids chose names that were different from their English ones. I understand that’s been standard practice in language instruction for a long time. Growing up, when someone was speaking to me in Polish they’d address me as “Marek”, and that’s how I preferred to be addressed when I lived in Poland. Consider that many Chinese or other Asian students coming to the US take on an “American” name that’s different from their given ones. Pop culture is full of examples of Americanizing names, hence viz. Israel Beilin becoming known as Irving Berlin, Ramon Estevez being known as Martin Sheen, or even Marion Morrison being known as John Wayne. Those who went to Catholic school may have an add-on saint’s name: my father-in-law went to Catholic school in Malaysia growing up, and was known as “Leon.” He hates it nowadays, but at the time, who knows. So no, it’s not odd or alarming.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do I know if a professor is tenured?
Answer: In the American system at least, those with the title “Associate Professor” or “Professor” or “Joe Bixfizz Distinguished and Endowed Professor” are tenured. Those who are “Assistant Professors” are not. A “lecturer” or an “adjunct” is likely not even on the tenure track or tenure totem pole. In the UK I think a “professor” is a rank that is equivalent to the American “full” professor, and I’d assume they were tenured.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: California's population has dropped for the 1st time in the state’s history. What are your thoughts on why this is happening?
Answer: I recently visited Pasadena again after having moved away a few years ago. I had a conversation with an engineer at JPL (Jet Propulsion Laboratory. You know, the guys who put the rovers on Mars). She has a PhD in physics, and is engaged to a guy who also has a PhD in physics, and also works at JPL. So we’re talking about a couple that has pretty darn solid earning potential. They are likely going to leave LA soon because they can’t afford a house. California used to be a place where you could start a computer company, or a band, in your garage, and maybe someday it could be something. But how are you going to do that now, when a garage costs a million dollars? You can still dream the big dreams in California, but there is a very high cost of admission. You’ve already got to be rich. Another day I was taking a stroll, and saw a homeless guy walking around holding a folding chair, muttering to himself, and periodically swinging that chair into thin air. So I give him a wide berth, but he spots me anyway and starts swearing at me, saying he’s going to f*** me up. I walk away gingerly, saying absolutely nothing, and he’s hollering at me up to about a half a block away. It occurred to me that had I still lived there, this would not have been a remarkable occurrence, and I might not have even noticed. I also wondered, in a situation like that, at what point does one call the police? Maybe if I lay bleeding on the sidewalk, but for anything short of that they probably would have said to quit wasting their time. Even years ago, before the current inflationary pinch, gas was about a dollar a gallon more expensive in California than it was on the East Coast. And you’re going to need a lot of gas when you’re driving from the town you can actually afford to the place you actually work. That trip is also frequently made on bad freeways: the 210 in particular in LA is in really bad shape. Other parts of California’s infrastructure are creaking, especially electricity and water.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is Krakow similar to Warsaw?
Answer: I lived in Krakow, and visited Warsaw a few times, and they are very different places. In Krakow the pace is a little slower, the city feels somewhat compact, the streets are narrower, and it feels unlike anything in America except for maybe Boston. There’s also not much sprawl to Krakow: you can take a bicycle ride from the city center out to the countryside, and it makes a nice day-trip. Warsaw feels a lot like Chicago or Berlin: the streets are broader and busier. People are hustling. And there is definitely sprawl. From what I saw, there are three basic layouts to a city in Poland: you’ve got one type where the city is centered on a square, and radiates out from that center (Wroclaw, Krakow, Poznan, Torun). You’ve got a second type where there is one “main drag”- one big street away from a central point, and the city is built around this main axis (Lodz, Czestochowa, Radom, and if memory serves, Katowice). Warsaw is in a class all by itself: there are *three* “downtown” areas or centers. There’s the business district where all the skyscrapers are. It’s actually centered on the intersection of Jerozolimskie and Marszalkowska, in front of the Palace of Culture. The northern “downtown” is the Old City, which is built on the central hub-and-spoke model. And in the south….I’m not sure, I didn’t spend much time down there. Anyway, Warsaw is a unique city in Poland, and very unlike Krakow.
