Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do I address a professor with a PhD?
Answer: It depends. “Dr. X” or “Professor X” is always a safe bet to start with. But in California at least, it’s frequently on a first-name basis, particularly if that professor is your adviser. One of the things that makes Caltech great is how casual it is!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: As a nation, is America really in as much trouble as people tend to act?
Answer: Dallas McKay’s answer is really good, and I want to expand on it a little bit (linked here). In particular, I like his point about how there are two kinds of people who say America is doomed, those who don’t live here, and those who have never been anywhere else. It’s a little funny to me when people who have never lived abroad say “Americans are greedy” or “Americans are stupid” or “Americans have no culture” or “America is horribly politically divided.” No. People are stupid, greedy, uncultured, and politically divided (at least some of them), and you don’t really see that unless you’ve spent some time abroad. Every country has problems, some of them quite serious. You don’t see those problems when you’re on vacation, because part of what you’re doing as a tourist is paying to see the best of a country, not the worst. There are slums in Paris too. When I lived in Poland, some people stated, flat out, that America doesn’t have any problems. Their point of reference were the problems that Poland has: an increasing wealth gap, a paranoid, populist right-wing government that propagates conspiracy theories, fraught and complex relations between Church and State, emigration of some of the best and brightest, a strange inability for society to change, and now an unprecedented (for Poland) refugee crisis, coupled with a very real fear that the war in Ukraine will spill over the borders of Poland. When I visited Bosnia, we spoke to a Serbian post-doc at a university there. He said all this talk of American decline seems faintly ridiculous in the Balkans. After all, everyone in the Balkans has hated each other’s guts for at least 600 years, and they kept killing each other over it. But then in the mid-1990s, the US said “that’s enough!”, deployed military and other assets…..and all that crap stopped within a year or two. From the Balkans, America looks like the most amazing country on earth. OK, so maybe you assume Eastern Europe is not a fair comparison. In Western Europe, people live in smaller houses and apartments, generally keep them colder than we do in the states, and pay $7–8 a gallon for gas. Sales tax is something like 20% in many countries. They are having serious problems integrating large and growing immigrant populations, and in France I was shocked to see troops, in full combat gear, walking the streets because of concerns about terrorism. Yes, America has problems. We can’t pretend it’s a perfect country. But neither is any other country that ever has, or ever will, exist.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How many PhD students felt like quitting part way through but carried on against the odds?
Answer: Damn near all of them. The PhD is frequently a taxing, strenuous experience, and you can spend months working on something for absolutely none of it to work. Or, you made some error somewhere, and the last six months of your life didn’t really accomplish very much. And it’s not unusual for a PhD student to not collect any data that actually goes into the thesis until their third or fourth year. There’s a lot of wheel-spinning that happens. One of my grandfather’s favorite poems was “If” by Rudyard Kipling. I put it on the last page of my PhD thesis, both as a tribute to him and because it’s actually great advice for getting a PhD:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I plagiarized only part of an assignment and the professor gave me a zero and would not let me redo it. How can I change his mind? I really need a good grade in the course.
Answer: There are a lot of good answers here saying that plagiarizing “just a little bit” isn’t really a thing: you either plagiarized, or you didn’t. If you did, that is a serious academic offense that can get you expelled in many places. A professor of mine put it this way: academics work in the marketplace of ideas. Therefore, professors think of plagiarism the way a shopkeeper thinks of shoplifters. What I will add is my perspective as an adjunct who busted four students for copying off each other on three separate take-home tests at the start of COVID: looking the other way on cheating is not fair to the students who came by their Bs and Cs honestly. In the course I was teaching, there were students who struggled mightily to get a B. There was one student who got a C whose wrong answers were so strange that it was clear he came up with them by himself. These students needed a good grade just as much as the ones who copied off of each other, or just as much as you do. If I, the teacher, let the cheating go, what message does that send? That the students who came by their grades honestly are suckers, because they could have cheated, done less work, and done better in the class. That’s not a worldview I’m ever going to endorse.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which historical events do you feel are underrated/overrated in our present history textbooks, and why?
Answer: I can only speak to American history textbooks, as I’m an American. Broadly, I wish we learned more history in school, and that it was better taught, as there are some shocking blind spots in many people’s historical knowledge as a result. Underrated World history in general. There are so many parts of the world that we just don’t learn very much about, like Eastern Europe or India or South America or even China. But the two biggest things we didn’t learn about at all were The Partition of India, and the Taiping Rebellion. I was shocked to find out that over a million people died during the Partition, and millions more were involuntarily displaced or deported. That’s part of the reason why the Indian Subcontinent features two nuclear-armed powers that are constantly glowering at each other, and sometimes doing more than that. The Taiping Rebellion in China went on for 14 years, killed something like 20–30 million people….and we never heard anything about it in school. Similarly, World War II as it was fought in China/the Asian mainland is something that is almost completely overlooked in school. In a sense, World War II began in 1931 in Manchuria. Specific to American History, we don’t really learn about Reconstruction. We learn that it was a thing, and that the South was being exploited, and that there were these guys called Carpetbaggers, and US Grant was a disaster, and then we move straight into Jim Crow. Now, I’m not saying we shouldn’t learn about Jim Crow. What I’m saying is we should learn more about what proceeded it. Reconstruction was a missed opportunity, a golden opportunity, to push for racial equality and civil rights. The Federal Government had the resources, and the ability to do so: the first Ku Klux Klan was destroyed by the Justice Department, it didn’t go away of its own volition. There were Black members of congress, senators, state legislators, etc. Had civil rights for freedmen been established and protected after the Civil War, it would have saved us a lot of trouble, shame, and embarrassment later. Unfortunately, that opportunity was lost. Overrated The Battle of Iwo Jima. Understand, I’m not knocking the courage of the men who fought there, much as I wouldn’t knock the courage of the men who fought at Tarawa, the Kokoda Track, Eniwetok, Bougainville, Manila, Guam, Guadalcanal and Okinawa, all of which rate only passing mentions in most history textbooks. I can also understand why Iwo Jima is a central part of the mythos of the United States Marine Corps, and it would have outsize importance to a Marine. But why should it have outsize importance to an ordinary American? Guadalcanal was more important strategically. Okinawa was bloodier, and led to the decision to drop the atomic bomb. After Iwo Jima was taken, not much was done with the island, and one could reasonably ask if the invasion was necessary in the first place. Basically, it’s well-known because of an iconic photo.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Poland seems desirable to Putin due its mountainous defense regions and would provide a secure border for Russia. Do you think that once Ukraine becomes consolidated under Russia, Putin will invade Poland and capture its major cities?
Answer: “Mountainous defense regions of Poland?” Yes, Poland does have mountains in the South, but central Poland, from East to West, is flat as a billiards table. The mountains will help you if you want to defend against an invasion from Slovakia, but won’t help you with much other than that. A Russian invasion of Poland would be extremely stupid for all kinds of reasons. First and foremost, Poland is a fully-fledged member of NATO, covered by Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, saying that an attack on one member is an attack on all. So, war with Poland means war with NATO, which Russia would lose. Badly. OK, let’s say for some reason NATO doesn’t keep its promises. Second, the Polish military is not incompetent or inconsiderable in size: about 114,000 men, equipped to NATO standards, and they have contingents with recent combat experience in Iraq and Afghanistan. Third, Russia had serious logistical problems invading the country next door. Add more distance to that. It’s not going to be logistically easier. Last, historically, Russia is The Enemy to the Poles. The Russians would have a very nasty insurgency to deal with, even if they managed to invade.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How do you deal with your professor when a page is missing from your midterm?
Answer: You go and ask him or her. Say, very politely, “Excuse me, I am missing page X”, at which point your professor should apologize and provide you with page X. If your professor for some inexplicable reason says “tough titties, that’s your problem”, you go to the dean, and the local psychiatrist, because this person is not in their right mind. What other way would you deal with this?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What rude awakening are graduate and PhD students in for?
Answer: The rudest awakening is, you aren’t as special as you thought you were, and are no longer the smartest person in the room. I see this in particular where some professors get a reputation for being hard to work for/slave drivers, and yet people join their group every year. Why? I think part of it is “well, I’m so brilliant, and the current grad students are just dumb, and I’ll get through it no problem.” Remember, those grad students were once YOU! All of your peers will have had good grades since they could talk. Many of them will have internships or research experiences under their belt already, and quite a few of them will already have publications. I went from being a promising young mind in my undergraduate class…..to average or below average at graduate school. Now, this revelation really bothers some people. But it shouldn’t. If you are the smartest person in the room…..you are in the wrong room! You have a chance to learn. It’s called graduate SCHOOL for a reason. Don’t be so fixated on trying to impress people that you lose what the point of the exercise is, which is to become a good scientist.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does England have an East Coast?
Answer: No. England is remarkable in that it is on an island, and occupies the entire southern part of that island, and yet somehow has no East Coast.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does completing a PhD feel like a monumental personal achievement?
Answer: Honestly, it felt like a bit of an anticlimax. I worked for years and years, wrote the thesis, handed it in, and the lady in the office said “thank you. Good luck with your defense.” And I was like, “that’s it?” Then I defended successfully, but had to revise the written part of the thesis. So I did, and handed that in. And that was that. “It’s over?” was what went through my head. And I got on with it. Graduation was pretty cool, though. I’m glad I went, and it felt pretty good to get the hood.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why does Ross kill Banquo but spare Fleance?
Answer: In the text of the play, it’s not Ross that kills Banquo: the murderers are identified only as “First Murderer”, “Second Murderer” and “Third Murderer.” In some adaptations, Ross is one of the murderers. And in the text, Fleance isn’t “spared”: Banquo tells him to run like hell, and presumably Banquo fights with the three guys who jumped him. There’s a light that goes out, and Fleance is able to flee in the confusion and darkness. Plot-wise, this fits right in with the prophecy of the witches that Banquo will never be king, but his descendants will be. Which is why Macbeth is not happy that the murderers missed what’s actually the most important target: Banquo’s only son.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What do teachers think when they hear someone say that society has changed a lot in the past 100 years, but education hasn't or that the education system is an outdated model to produce factory workers?
Answer: WHAT we are teaching students has changed considerably in the last 100 years. Most people are taught less religion, no Greek or Latin, and not really taught rhetoric. On the other hand, calculus is routinely taught to high school students, science instruction is much different (and probably improved, partly because the knowledge base has improved), and 30 years ago, nobody was learning computer science, or how to code, even though computers were gradually starting to become more commonplace. So, what constitutes “educated” and “a good education” is very different than it used to be. HOW things are taught, well…I think there’s too much emphasis on technology and bells and whistles. You can have a very engaging, very informative lecture given by a good teacher armed with a piece of chalk and a blackboard. You can have a crappy lecture given by someone using a bad PowerPoint slide deck. In fact, I think I teach better when armed with only a piece of chalk, because I have to think carefully about what I need to write down, and what I need to draw, to get the class from point A to point B efficiently. And some of the best tech demos are very old-school. With technology, there is the temptation to cram too much information onto slides, or into a video, and the message is lost. There are some excellent YouTube videos out there. There are also some very bad ones. Technology by itself does not solve everything. There is good and bad homework, and in some subjects (math and physics especially), it is essential: the only way to really understand something is to do a lot of problems, where you apply what you learn. It’s also useful feedback for the instructor: huh, everybody is messing up problem 4 in the same exact way. Guess that’s what I need to review. Similarly, the only way you can get better at writing essays…..is to go write essays. You can do that in a word processor, you can do that with voice-to-text, you can do that with papyrus and a reed dipped in ink, but the only way to get better is to do a lot of it. The next time somebody tells you this, ask them, what do they mean by outdated? What reforms do they have in mind? How would they make teaching better and more modern? What’s the alternative?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Have you experienced love at first sight?
Answer: Oh yes. When I first saw the woman who would become my wife, I thought “that’s the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen.” We were working on a stage play together: she was the lead makeup artist, and I was in the cast. I really liked it when she came over to smooth my hair, I’ll tell you. That’s one of the only times I’ve ever felt that strong a feeling about someone. And when we started dating, I found out she had a lovely personality as well. She’s still the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I had a “date” [we went to the rollercade] with this guy today who goes to my school but it didn’t feel right. He told me he had fun and when I think about it, I feel off. Why do I feel like this?
Answer: You might never know why you feel off about someone, but trust your gut. You are under no obligation to date anybody, and you don’t need a reason to not date them. If something seems wrong, don’t talk yourself out of that feeling, or rationalize it. Just trust it, and move on. On the flip side, when I started dating my wife, it felt right, and I couldn’t tell you exactly why. It still feels right 7 years later. If you are looking for a long-term partner, I would recommend prioritizing feeling comfortable, and feeling right, as opposed to feeling passionate.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Has Putin made the biggest mistake of his life by invading Ukraine?
Answer: Yes. Remember, “war is the continuation of politics by other means.” What was Putin’s political objective? Integrating Ukraine firmly under Russian control, and preventing it from joining the West. Had Putin been patient, or as clever as he’s claimed to be, he might have achieved what he wanted (or a large part of what he wanted), at lower cost than what he’s paying now. However, with the war turning out the way it is, he might lose his chance to ever achieve those objectives. Consider where things stood at the beginning of 2022: Consider where things stand now: So, Putin has lost almost all the advantages he possessed at the start of the year. While Russia might still beat Ukraine by shear weight of numbers, and by attrition, the eventual political settlement is extremely unlikely to favor Russia.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are some common myths about PhD students and PhDs?
Answer: I’d argue that the PhD is not a credential that shows intelligence. It’s a credential that shows stubbornness! Sticking with something for 5–8 years, you must be either insane or really stubborn, or both. And maybe I’m both. Another myth is that PhDs are horribly specialized, and can never find work, or be useful in work outside of that field. What a PhD really teaches you is *how* to learn, and to figure out what you need to learn in order to reach your objectives. That’s the difference between a PhD and a Master’s: the PhD has floundered around for a few years trying to figure out what he or she needs to know, and figured it out, at least somewhat.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I have two employees who usually leave work at 6pm each day. They are good employees, but I do not like that their commitment lasts only for working hours. What should I do as the boss?
Answer: You should hire more employees. If your staff is doing everything they are supposed to do, but there’s still a lot of work that is left undone at the end of the day, it means you do not have enough people to do what needs doing. Also, why should their commitment last more than working hours? Are you paying them for doing work outside of work, or are you willing to give them overtime? And if they called you when you were on vacation, or “off”, would you drop everything and hurry to the business? EDIT: I thought of another thing: does your commitment to your employees last only during working hours, or are you committed to them 24/7? Would you drive over to their house at 3AM to take their kids to the hospital? Probably not. Why would you expect them to have more commitment to you than you have to them? One of the most important things I’ve learned in my limited managerial experience is, nobody is going to care as much about YOUR project, and YOUR problems, as you are. Sure, they’ll help if they have to. If you’re lucky, they will even care more about your problems than you are paying them to. But you can’t expect them to be as committed as you are.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is the term “toxic masculinity” just used to put down men or is it really a big problem?
Answer: As usual, there’s no subtlety in discussions of politically-charged concepts. Toxic masculinity is a thing, but not all masculinity is toxic. Properly defined, I think toxic masculinity the idea that to be a manly-man’s-man, you have to be loud, boastful, abusive, looking to pick fights and win them, and when it doubt, take the stupid-aggressive option. Toxic masculinity glorifies aggression, violence, and domination for its own sake. There are definitely men out there who are like that, and if you’re being honest, you’ll realize you’ve met some of them. However, I think the term “toxic masculinity” is abused when it’s defined SO broadly as to encompass all masculinity, or to say that there’s something wrong with men because of how they are built. Men are not defective women. Men tend to be more direct, more physically-oriented, more interested in building stuff and knocking it apart, and not as socially adept as women (and perhaps more literal-minded). Yes, this is a stereotype, and we should accept that there are many different ways of being a man or being a woman. But if you look at the average man, and the average women, you’ll notice that their priorities, world-views, and approaches are different. There wouldn’t be so much comedy about men and women not understanding, or misunderstanding, each other, if this weren’t the case. Basically, we shouldn’t talk about the “toxic masculinity” of a guy who likes cars or motorcycles, unless what he really likes to do is de-tune the car so it rattles all the windows on the street as he drives by. Consider, also, the difference between a sports fan, and a hooligan. As I see it, becoming a man, as opposed to remaining a boy, is about learning to control your natural urges, and channel them into something productive. A boy with matches can burn down a house. A man builds one instead. Boys talk. Men do.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the greatest scientific paradigm shifts of the last 30 years?
Answer: I can answer most readily from the biology/synthetic biology side of things: Before the Human Genome Project was completed in 2003, the thinking was that once we had decoded an organism’s genome, that would be that. We would understand what made an organism a specific organism. We would unlock the “code of life.” What we found out is, genetics and how it connects to phenotype (how an organism looks, behaves, etc.) is WAY more complicated than that. We know that certain genes are associated with certain conditions, but we are very far from being able to say “well, just from his genome, we know that Otzi the Iceman had high cholesterol, and was left-handed.” We have also started to focus more on trying to understand how genes are regulated and expressed, which isn’t easy. Related to this, the idea of Lamarckian Evolution was a joke until relatively recently. Lamarck had argued that the environment could change an organism in a way that was heritable, i.e. the “giraffe has a desire to stretch its neck to reach high branches, and this desire to stretch passes on to its offspring, so that’s why giraffes have long necks.” More recently, however, the concept of epigenetics states that environmental factors can actually change how genes express, and therefore change the phenotype of offspring, in a way that is heritable. Now, this doesn’t “invalidate” Darwinian evolution, and it does have a tendency to be oversold (that is, epigenetics doesn’t explain everything, and there are limits as to what it can explain), but the idea that environment can affect phenotype in a way that is heritable would have been an eccentric view 30 years ago, but is widely accepted today. The idea of prions as agents of infectious disease is also a change we’ve seen in the last 30 years or so. Essentially, you have these bits of rogue protein that are mis-folded, and can cause other proteins to mis-fold.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is academic integrity important? What are some examples?
Answer: From an instructor’s perspective, it has to do with fairness. I taught a class at a community college where I ended up busting 4 students for copying off each other (we had gone remote at the start of COVID. I didn’t have any special proctoring software, so I explicitly told the students, in writing, that I was trusting them to be honest on the by-definition take-home exams we were doing). This wasn’t an unfounded suspicion: because the turn-ins were electronic, I had copies of four tests at my fingertips, and on three of them, including the final, there was at least one question where the copying was so obvious, it was almost as though the answers had been traced from one paper to the other. The evidence was pretty good. All 4 of them ended up getting an “F”, and a note in their student file, in accordance with course policy established at the start of the semester, and the policies of the school. If the students got caught like that again, they would be expelled. Seems a little harsh and unfair, doesn’t it? But consider: in that same class, there was one student who busted their butt to get a low B. They were at every office hour, did every assignment, asked me to give some additional problems (i.e. they asked for extra homework for no credit), they worked really, really hard to get that B. There was another student who really wanted an A for scholarship reasons, but simply didn’t make the cut, and it wasn’t close enough where I felt like I could fudge it. There was another student who ended up with a C, whose answers were sometimes so creative, and so bizarre, that it was obvious that the student was working alone and not copying off of anybody. And last, there was one student who turned in tests that were half-blank, and ended up either getting an F, or dropping out of the class because that’s what was going to happen. I had no doubts about the academic integrity of any of these kids. Now, let’s say I let the cheaters slide. What that would mean is, all those honest kids who got Bs, Cs, and Fs were suckers for not cheating. They were committed to doing it the right way, and for that, they deserve to get punished with a worse result than those who took the easy way out. How is that fair, or right? The other part of this was, of those 4, I think what happened is that one of the students did the work (as this student’s work was consistently the best of the lot), then let the other 3 copy the answers. That’s not really fair either: one person does the work, four people get the credit. Aside from fairness considerations, showing that the students had cheated was a big fat waste of my time that could have been spent doing other things. I was putting together a “gag reel”, basically a lecture to entertain the class, and was also thinking of recording some additional lectures to perhaps help the students taking the course in the next semester (I was leaving that school because I got another job). But I didn’t do any of these things, because I was spending time painstakingly compiling and comparing multiple tests, to confirm that what I really, *really* didn’t want to have happen, had happened.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are people looking for when they ask "What does academic integrity mean to you"?
Answer: I think they’re asking, broadly, what actions do you consider to be cheating, and which you wouldn’t do? What’s your line between “collaboration” and “copying”? Are you offended by academic dishonesty and if so, why? How do you practice academic integrity/show you care about this sort of thing?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How remarkable would it be that someone educated in the Dominican Republic (a country with almost no mathematical tradition) is generalizing theorems of Newton and other German astronomers and mathematicians of the nineteenth century?
Answer: Why not? Brilliance can come from anywhere. Perhaps the greatest mathematician of all time was Srinivasa Ramanujan, and while India does have a long mathematical tradition, there was nothing in the circumstances of his birth and early life that suggested he was destined for great things:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the benefits of completing a Ph.D.?
Answer: The PhD is not a degree that displays your brilliance, or even a reasonable intelligence: the PhD is a stubbornness degree. I don’t think I’m especially bright, but I ground it out for 6 years. The biggest benefit is knowing that I can buckle down and deal with years of discouraging results if I have to. Completing a PhD also makes you a little more modest. I got roughed up by my thesis committee during candidacy. When I finished my thesis, I thought, “wow, I thought this was going to be longer/more important/cooler.” I definitely saw other people in my program produce better work. So, the process got me off my high horse. When you’re working at the leading edge, you get to see new discoveries every day by following the literature. And the requirement for getting a PhD is that you discovered something new. There’s a very real satisfaction in being able to say “I’m the first person ever to do X.” That’s really cool. The training provided by a PhD is, or should be, an antidote to the types of non-thinking that are common in our age of misinformation, bluster, and overall baloney. During a PhD you have to ask yourself, what do we know, and how do we know it? What is the mechanism for something to be working in a particular way? And, do I have enough information and evidence to conclude what I’m about to conclude? This runs contrary to the trends of today, where people frequently say, “I know X to be true because my favorite politician/pundit/random guy on Facebook said it. I’m not going to worry about how X could possibly be true, or look for evidence running in the other direction.” This sort of trained skepticism is especially important during COVID, when a lot of discussion is on scientific topics. At least in chemistry, your career is limited if you have just a BS. To get a position with more responsibility and better pay, you kind of need an MS or a PhD.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What do you call someone from Pittsburgh?
Answer: The other answers have got it, either “Pittsburgher” or “Yinzer”, but what I would add is that “Yinzer” tends to be used to describe someone who is working-class, and who speaks with the particular dialect of Pittsburgh. “Pittsburgher” is the more general term.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If you got rejected from your dream school(s), what would you do?
Answer: Funny story: my dream school was MIT. I got rejected by: MIT, Caltech, Princeton, and Yale. I was accepted by: Johns Hopkins, Michigan State, and University of Pittsburgh. I got a scholarship at Pitt, so Pitt is where I went. I had never heard of Pitt (it’s not well known in the Midwest), I had never visited Pitt (I did visit Carnegie Mellon, which is literally shouting distance), and the only reason I applied was that Pitt sent me a free application and I said, why not, it’s practice. So I went to my safety school, and had a fabulous time. My education was great, I got to experience a new city, I wrote for the paper, coached speech and debate, sang in the Glee Club, got involved in undergraduate research and got to be a co-author on two different papers, ended up getting a Fulbright Fellowship, and for all that I steered clear of the sourpusses who spent a lot of their time bemoaning the fact that they didn’t get into the Ivies. Four years later, I was deciding on a graduate school, having been accepted to 7 of them, including MIT and Caltech. At MIT, the graduate students didn’t seem very happy, I wasn’t all that interested in the research the groups were doing……and I had to sit down for a minute because I knew I didn’t want to go there. Nearly 10 years of trying, I’d finally made it…..and I didn’t want it. I ended up going to Caltech where I found out that I probably would have been miserable there as an undergraduate, but grad school was, on balance, kind of fun. I’m one of the few PhDs that would say that. So my point is, I WAS rejected from my dream school, and years later, I found out that was probably for the best. College is what YOU make of it. Hail to Pitt!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is the USA getting a supposed reputation of a country in decline when it still seems such a vibrant diverse country with an immense breadth of creativity and innovation?
Answer: One thing that really helps my mental health is the realization that every day, around 150 million Americans wake up, go to work, do whatever it is they do, then they go home, spend time with their families, watch TV, whatever. For all the noise we’re hearing, most people are living their lives. The other funny thing is, you frequently see these surveys asking Americans what they think about the country, and what they think about their own lives. The majority opinion is “The country’s going down the crapper! Well, I’m doing somewhere between OK and great, but the country’s doomed……” Here’s what I blame, in no particular order:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What should I bring to meet a professor who’s invited me to coffee to discuss my future plans and graduate school?
Answer: Depends on the context. Is this a professor who is at your current institution, or one at a completely different institution whom you met at a conference or something? If at your home institution, I would say bring a notepad, and an idea of what you want to do next. Be organized, have some specific questions, and you can probably just tell the professor which courses you took because they all know what that means, at least vaguely: “I took CHEM 175 with Prof. Smith” “Oh, yeah. How did you like Bob as a lecturer?” If it’s a professor at an outside institution, maybe have a CV and a transcript with you just in case, and be ready to explain the transcript a little bit more, as “CHEM 175” doesn’t mean anything to someone outside your institution.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What do you respond if your ex texts you to say they found someone better?
Answer: “How nice for you.” And leave it at that. You aren’t going to “win” anything by being witty or mean. Cut the cord, and don’t look back.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which people living today will be remembered 1,000 years from now?
Answer: It’s difficult, if not impossible to say, and the question is also “remembered by whom?” Very few Americans know who the heck Aurangzeb was, for instance, and that’s only 300 years ago. There are also always going to be specialists and history nerds who remember more obscure figures like Sallust or Jugurtha or John of Gaunt. What a person needs in order for their reputations to survive is art, by or dedicated to them. Julius Caesar was a highly successful Roman general who became dictator….just like Cornelius Sulla. But Sulla died in bed, and Caesar was assassinated. “I am as constant as the Northern…..oops.” So why do we remember Caesar and not Sulla? Well, Caesar wrote memoirs and had great publicity. The early Emperors found it politically savvy to equate themselves with this legendary figure. Similarly, King Tut was a not-very-successful, not very long-ruling Pharaoh who died when still a teenager. His father, Akhenaten, is a more interesting figure whose attempts to introduce a new religion made him of more consequence to Egyptian history. Sure, some people remember Akhenaten, but everyone remembers Tut because we found his face mask of bling. And he got an SNL skit. Skipping forward a few thousand years, probably nobody called John of Gaunt by that name during his lifetime. And how many third sons of Kings of England do we even remember after 100 years? [Note to history buffs reading this: yes, yes I know he was a wealthy and powerful magnate, and that’s where the Lancastrian claim on the throne came from, which was a major factor in the Wars of the Roses. How many of your non-history-buff friends know that?] However, when Shakespeare makes Gaunt a pivotal character in one of his plays, and gives him a really cool speech schoolkids have to memorize (“This royal throne of kings, this sceptred isle…..”), he’s cemented this man’s place in memory. Last, coming back to Aurangzeb, most Westerners will be more familiar with his predecessor, Shah Jahan, because he’s the guy who built the Taj Mahal. Finally, Lisa Gherardini was a semi-obscure 16th century Italian noblewoman. But she’s famous, because she’s the subject of this painting: Aside from art, how do you become famous in a way that lasts a thousand years? By being an a##hole of epic proportions. Ivan IV of Russia was mixed news as Tsar, and by killing his heir ended up causing very serious problems for Russia, like invasions by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in support of a couple of guys claiming to be Ivan’s son, Dimitry. Cześć! But we know Ivan IV as Ivan the Terrible, because he was, well, an exceptionally not nice guy. Similarly, to consider Aurangzeb again, he’s likely going to be remembered for a long time in the Sikh community, as Aurangzeb ordered the execution/martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur. For that matter, Pontius Pilate was an obscure governor of an obscure province in the backwaters of the Roman Empire, and Roman records about his rule are scarce. But boy oh boy, are Christians going to remember him: Though I can’t think why. So, if the people most likely to be remembered are people who have made epic art, or people who have been epic jerks, who’s likely to be remembered in 1000 years? If Xi Jinping or Vladimir Putin manage to start World War III, they will probably be remembered. The art route is going to be tough, because a lot of our art is now made in forms that are volatile/easily deleted. Many films are lost, some even starring some well-known actors: If there’s ever a serious crash over at YouTube, a tremendous amount of art will be lost. Perplexingly, future historians might have a hard time reconstructing history after about 1990, because very little of what’s happening is recorded on paper anymore. My short answer to the question is: Aurangzeb

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: In the United States, is it wrong to address a full professor as "doctor"?
Answer: At some institutions, people are flattered if you call them something other than “hey, you!” At least in my lab, we were on a first-name basis with the boss, though it took me a really long time to get comfortable with that. Might be a California/Caltech thing, where *maybe* you address a Nobel Laureate as “Professor”, but sometimes not. In general, I don’t know too many people who would get insulted if you called them “doctor” rather than “professor”, and frankly, if they did get offended, they need to get over themselves. The only time I see “Dr. Kozlowski” is on a formal performance review, or formal correspondence from people I don’t know.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is a superior university bigger?
Answer: A few others have mentioned that Caltech is a very small school, and it’s true: there are about 800 undergraduates and 1200 graduates on-campus (though that’s probably closer to 1000 undergraduates and 1300 grad students by now). It’s frequently in the top 10 worldwide. Caltech is excellent because of its small size. Pretty much everybody knows everybody, or knows somebody who knows somebody, so collaboration and cross-pollination is easy and relaxed: I hung out with some pretty good astronomers, for instance, because we had the same extracurricular interests. Because it’s so small, and so informal, if you have a question you’re dying to ask a Nobel laureate, you can go ahead and ask it: I had some random chats with professors not in my field just by sending them an e-mail, and asking to see them (“oh, and your student Steve is a buddy of mine and says you’d be a good person to talk to about this.”) A lot of things at Caltech are done by the seat of the pants with very little bureaucracy: it was nerve-wracking when I started there to throw things together in about 2 days, but you could do it, because you could just waltz right up to the senior administrator in charge of X and ask a question….because they were the only administrator in charge of X. Getting permission to do things is pretty easy as well. If Caltech were to get large, it would get bureaucratic and sclerotic, and it wouldn’t be as good a school.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What's the biggest no-no when you are a PhD student?
Answer: I like to talk about the dreaded “Three Nos” when giving a group meeting: no results, no plan, no clue. Generally, if you can answer “yes” to one of those (you have results, or a plan, or a clue), you will generally be OK. I’ve seen some very good presentations that go like this: “so, here was my hypothesis. After testing it 3 different ways, very rigorously, I can tell you that this system does not work this way, and we can’t build the thing I want to build. I’ll try this idea next.” If your adviser is sane, they will actually pat you on the back for this: that’s good science. Science frequently doesn’t work. OR, if your talk is “so, I’ve got these really weird results. I think they mean X, but I’m not sure. What do you guys think?” That’s also good: why do you have group meeting if not to share ideas? But what you don’t want to do is stand up there and say “yeah, I didn’t really do anything, and I’m not sure what I’m doing, and I don’t really know anything about anything,” because that shows a lack of effort and engagement. You’ve also letting yourself drift aimlessly, and that’s not the point of a PhD. I gave a related answer here:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the dark side of PhD?
Answer: There are a lot of good answers below. Here’s my take: Suddenly, you aren’t the smartest person in the room anymore The people who go on to try and get a PhD are usually academic high-fliers, and have probably been academic high-fliers since grade school. They’ve gotten used to thinking of themselves as special….and now all of a sudden they might be stunningly average in their PhD cohort. You can either react to this with a good dose of humility and good humor, or you can let it eat you up. Students don’t want to admit they have a problem because they think that will make them look weak This is especially pronounced in the early years of a PhD when students feel insecure and want to impress each other/do some macho posturing. What do I mean by “have a problem?” That can range from “I just spent 4 months getting this thing to…..not work” all the way to “I’m horribly depressed and coping with it by substance abuse.” You feel like the only people who can really understand you is your fellow classmates….but you don’t want to tell them because you think you’ll look weak or stupid. Part of the reason the PhD gets easier in the 4th year is not only are you getting results at that point, but your classmates start to open up a little bit more, and you realize you aren’t alone. There is a constant desire to compare yourself to others Much as they say the problem with social media these days is that everyone presents their life as perfect, so it seems like everyone’s life is perfect except ours, that’s how it goes in research. Somebody gets a grant, or a fellowship, or a flashy new paper. Meanwhile….what have you got. This is not a good way to think about it. The PhD is ultimately a competition with yourself, and you have no idea what other people are going through. One of my colleagues did an extremely impressive PhD. She was an absolute wizard at it, very smart, very dedicated. But she worked SO many hours that it ended up negatively affecting her health. Academia is probably not going to happen So, your adviser, over his or her career, may churn out something like 70 graduates. You are all competing, basically, for your adviser’s job if you decide to go into academia, as the number of positions has remained pretty much static, and most tenured faculty stay in their positions for 40 years. Most people come into the PhD program with the desire to become professors, but most will not make it. I know I won’t. Now, this wouldn’t be a bad thing in and of itself….if we were getting good advice about what to do instead. In terms of getting a non-academic job, we sort of have to figure it out on our own. And in some cases, you end up “defaulting” into a job. I think I applied to something like 75 jobs, got 2 interviews, and 1 offer. I got lucky, because I really like my current job, but I could see how numbers like this, and a bad initial placement, could breed a certain resentment.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are the students at MIT and Cal Tech somewhat the same level? Are their students also the same among their peers?
Answer: I did theater and music as extracurriculars at Caltech, and a number of people working at NASA-JPL (Jet Propulsion Laboratory) were involved in those activities as well. Quite a few of those JPL folks were MIT alumni, and they fit right in at Caltech. Heck, the provost of Caltech is an MIT alum. I suspect it’s the same with Caltech alumni who end up in Cambridge. I *suspect* you run into a broader range of people at MIT than at Caltech simply because there are more people to run into. Caltech is tiny (about 800 undergraduates and 1200 graduate students, around 2000 students total), and doesn’t really have humanities majors. I think MIT is closer to about 12,000 students total, and some students do major in, say, English. I do notice that MIT alumni tend to be very proud of their class ring, “The Brass Rat.” I don’t know if Caltech even has a class ring, and the culture is such that people would probably laugh at you for wearing it. Now, what DOES irritate people at Caltech is when it gets spelled as two words, “Cal Tech” or “CalTech.” Nope! One word. Caltech. For graduate school, I was admitted to both, and visited both. Caltech seemed a bit more laid-back and informal, which is what you’d expect. It is California after all. But both schools seem to be populated with very bright people doing very good work, and I’d say they are comparable institutions. Go Beavers!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are all graduate-level jobs brain dead? I mean you can train a high school student to do most of the jobs that grad students do
Answer: Can you train a high-school student to handle a pipette, run a piece of equipment, and do a bunch of assays? Yes. Can you teach a high school student to think independently, come up with a good research question, design the experiments needed to answer that question, analyze the data, present the data, come up with follow-up experiments, and defend it from potentially withering attack from a panel of people who have been doing all of this for 40 years? Given 8–10 years of training, yes. Also known as college and graduate school. I also knew a guy who had 2 years of college, but had spent 20 years working as a bench scientist. He was as capable as any PhD, because he had basically earned a PhD on the job. High school teaches you how to memorize the facts you need to pass a test on those facts (i.e. “what is the IUPAC name of this organic compound?”) College teaches you how to not just memorize the facts, but to extrapolate from them (i.e. “using compounds containing no more than 3 carbons, make this organic compound.”) Graduate school teaches you how to ask the question, write the test, and take the test (i.e. “what compound do you want to make to dock to this protein, and how are you going to make it? Find an answer and convince me that it’s right, because I don’t know.”) Now, do all jobs that “require a PhD” really require a PhD? Of course not. But there is a big difference in the training and mentality of a high school graduate, and a PhD.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why doesn't Pennsylvania have any large cities besides Philadelphia and Pittsburgh?
Answer: Most states don’t have more than one or two large cities in them. Consider Illinois: there’s Chicago, the Chicago suburbs, and…..the St. Louis suburbs. New York State has New York City and….everything else. Michigan has Detroit, which isn’t even that big a city anymore. Speaking specifically about Pennsylvania, a lot of the state is pretty darn inaccessible because of all the hills. Driving the Pennsylvania Turnpike between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, you get a sense of this: they had to blast the hell out of those mountains to put the road through. Pittsburgh is where it is because of the rivers, and because it is at the headwaters of the Ohio river: when the Northwest Territories opened up, Pittsburgh was the Gateway to the West, and when steel came around, Pittsburgh was perfectly positioned to receive iron from the upper Midwest, and coal from the hills of Pennsylvania. There are some sizeable towns in Pennsylvania like Allentown, Redding, Scranton, and Erie:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Pennsylvania (state): What are the differences between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia?
Answer: Went to school in Pittsburgh, and a fair number of Philadelphians come to Pitt for college. “On” is pronounced “Ouwn” in Philly, but “Ahn” in Pittsburgh. “Yinz” or “yunz” is a Pittsburghism for “you guys.” I don’t know what Philadelphians use. “Coffee” is pronounced “Cauwfee” in Philly, and “water” is pronounced “wooter.” Philadelphians think that Wawa is the best gas station in the world. Pittsburghers say Sheetz is far and away superior. There were many arguments about this at college. Pittsburgh feels a lot like a Midwestern city in outlook, pace, general friendliness, etc. I’m originally from around Chicago, and Pittsburgh felt a lot like home. Philadelphia is more like New York Jr. Pittsburgh is also a smaller city, and feels like it. Topographically, Pittsburgh is VERY hilly, but Philadelphia is pretty flat. Pittsburgh is very proud of its industrial history as the Steel City, Philadelphia is proud of its intellectual history.

Answer: James Madison. Dolley Madison famously saved a portrait of George Washington when the British approached. It was a copy of Gilbert Stuart’s Lansdowne portrait: The man who actually took the portrait down, and removed it for safekeeping, was a 15 year-old slave named Paul Jennings:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is Pittsburgh really gray and depressing?
Answer: It can be gray, and it can be rainy, but I wouldn’t call it depressing. I think there was one January or February when I was in college where there were two days that were “mostly cloudy”, and every other day was solid overcast. And it’s not unusual for it to drizzle for 2 or 3 days straight. Pittsburgh is at its least charming in late January/early February when it’s about 35F and raining. It doesn’t get as cold or as snowy as Chicago, however. That being said, Pittsburgh can actually be quite beautiful, especially in the spring when everything gets so green that your eyes hurt, and fall, when you get some lovely colors. The people are friendly, and you have the amenities of a big city while having the feel of a smaller town. There’s also a lot of civic pride in Pittsburgh that I really haven’t seen anywhere else. So, weather-wise, yes it can be gray. But not depressing.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How can I stop feeling like an impostor in Graduate School? I was admitted to Duke Divinity despite a poor undergraduate GPA (made up for it with my GPA in my terminal Master's Program) and often compare myself to lifelong high achievers.
Answer: In my graduate program (and there were only about 50 of us in my year), there was a very intense young man who seemed to have it all together. He was knowledgeable, had a thorough grasp of our field of study, came out of an elite school, and I was intimidated by him. He sailed through a class I barely passed, and it looked like he had a promising future ahead of him. He committed suicide midway through our second year. This is not a joke, nor something I would ever joke about. My point in sharing this story is, you never know what people in your program are really going through. On the surface, they might seem to have it all together, but sometimes that’s a front, or facade, and underneath is a world of hurt. Our department chair called the whole department into a lecture hall to make the announcement, and the reactions were telling. About a quarter of those in the room sort of shrugged, another quarter didn’t quite know how to feel, and the remaining half looked like they had been hit with a sledgehammer, even those who never knew this young man. I talked to my adviser about this later, and he reacted in a way that suggested to me that the topic of suicide had affected him personally in some way in the past. To anyone reading this, if you are thinking of killing yourself, or harming yourself, please seek help: there is no shame in that. As hard as it is to believe, you matter, and if you harm yourself, it will affect more people than you’ll ever know.

Question: What is the big controversy in the United States?
Answer: Here are the biggest “umbrella” controversies in my opinion, and a lot of controversies can basically be put into one of these buckets:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Should a graduate (PhD) student act professional/dress professionally when at university?
Answer: You should always act professionally. You never know when unprofessional behavior will come back to haunt you. Dress, that depends on your university and what field you are in. If you are in a laboratory all day, you wear things that you don’t mind getting messy, or sweaty, and that’s normal. Nobody’s really looking at you anyway when you’re at your bench. At a place like Caltech, the dress code is casual: the only guy I ever saw wearing a suit and tie on campus was the president right after he got hired, and he even gave that up after a year. What is more important is that you are dressed SAFELY for a laboratory setting. That means long pants, closed-toed shoes, hair tied back, safety glasses at all times, a shirt, and lab coat when required. When it’s hot, grad students will frequently come in wearing shorts, but have a pair of long pants at their desk for this reason. Now that I think about it, you absolutely should NOT wear high heels or a skirt in a laboratory setting. At a conference, or when presenting publicly, you should be dressed professionally, as you are representing yourself, and your institution.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why would someone who does 3 varsity sports, has a 4.5 GPA, got a 1600 SAT score, took a total of 14 APs and got 3+ on the exams, not get into an Ivy League college?
Answer: Here’s the perspective I like to give anyone applying to college or upset at where they got in/didn’t get in: In high school, I was hot stuff academically. Solid GPA, test scores, APs, leadership roles in organizations (but no sports). I got rejected by MIT, Caltech, Princeton, and Yale, and thought I had a reasonable shot at getting into at least one of those (I did get waitlisted at Caltech, and admitted to Johns Hopkins, just to give you an idea that my applications to those other schools weren’t ridiculous). And what happened? I went to my safety school (Pitt) because that’s where I had a scholarship. I had never even heard of Pitt before I applied, and the only reason I applied was they sent me an application, which was free if I returned it by such and such a date. Well, I think I’ve had a pretty happy and successful life since then: I studied abroad, I did end up going to Caltech for graduate school, and I currently have a satisfying job that pays enough that I can pretty much live the life I want. Would my life have been different had I gone to an Ivy League school? Probably. But I’m not sure it would have been better. And guess what? Many, if not most, of my co-workers went to state schools, but they seem happy. The only time where I went to school comes up is when I make good-natured fun of alumni of Penn State (and they make good-natured fun of me). There is a *lot* of weight put on getting into the “right” college, or the most prestigious college, but I think that’s a bunch of hooey. College is very much what you make of it. There are opportunities out there, if you’re willing to go out and grab them. And frankly, while a diploma from an Ivy might open some doors that a diploma from Big Land Grant U will not, in the working world, if you have an intelligent boss, he or she will be more interested in your work ethic and proven abilities than where you went to college. YOU are still YOU, no matter where you went to school.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If you met someone who had six PhDs from Ivy League schools, would you admire the person or ridicule them?
Answer: I would ridicule this person, because for one thing a typical PhD in the natural sciences takes 5–7 years. So you’re dealing with someone who has been doing graduate-level research for 35 years…..meaning that they are at least 55 and have never held a “real” job, being content to make about $30k a year for all that time. Hell, even your workaday postdoc makes more than that, and with an Ivy League PhD, you can probably find a job that pays much better. What would puzzle me is *why* someone would spend that much time in grad school.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is the human body more limited compared to animals?
Answer: Every animal is specialized differently, for a specific niche. We can’t see UV light, or sense infrared, unlike bees or pit vipers, but we don’t really need to in order to survive. We can’t dive as deep as a whale, or hold our breath that long, but we don’t rely on eating giant squid to survive. Compared to dogs, our noses are awful. But some breeds of dogs would find it really cool that we have full-color vision. I can’t climb a tree like a squirrel, but the squirrel would love to have opposable thumbs. An individual ant is pretty stupid and weak compared to a human, but an anthill is smart, and can kill things several times their size. The great strength of humans is our ability to talk to each other, and coordinate plans (shared intentionality). In the wild, you’ll never see two chimpanzees carrying a log. Humans, on the other hand, are able to coordinate tens of thousands of people, over a span of years, in order to put two guys on the moon.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth and Ted Williams played baseball in this era, who do you think would be the most effective and least effective player and why?
Answer: Ty Cobb would probably be in prison, or in and out of prison, which would rather hamper his playing career. Ted Williams would be at the top or near the top of the league, as he would absolutely love all the analytics available to him, and take full advantage. And he was hitting against defensive shifts before defensive shifts were cool: Babe Ruth would also probably be near the top of the league. He probably would have been kept as a pitcher (we forget that he was actually excellent in that role: 94–46 lifetime record, with a 2.28 ERA), and would DH on his days off. The question I would have is: could he stay healthy? The Babe loved to party, and there’s all kinds of ways to wreck your health these days that weren’t as common back when.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why hasn’t Babe Ruth’s status as GOAT in baseball been deteriorated by time, like Pele in football (soccer)?
Answer: I think it has to do with the evolution of soccer and baseball. Soccer is a very different game today than it was in the 1960’s, with better equipment, fitter players, and different defensive and offensive schemes. Baseball, at least superficially, is the same game it has always been: you have a pitcher throwing to a batter 60 feet 6 inches away, and the batter trying to hit the ball with a stick. While there have been some changes that have favored the pitcher in that fundamental duel (Ruth probably never saw a slider, a split-fingered fastball, or a 100-mph fastball, for instance. He also wasn’t seeing statistically-informed defensive shifts, or relief pitching as we currently understand it today), there have also been some changes since Ruth’s time that have favored the batter (after his time the ball got livelier, the pitcher’s mound was lowered, and the seasons got longer). Basically, you could argue that the changes in his favor, and against him, would mostly cancel out, and Ruth would put up similar numbers today as he did in the 1920’s. It’s not as clear if Pele could do the same. This being said (and I’m surprised it doesn’t enter the debate), Major League Baseball in the 1920’s would not have the same caliber of players in it as it does today, for the simple reason that Black, Hispanic, and Asian players were not allowed in. There may well have been a Shohei Ohtani, or a CC Sabathia, or a Bob Gibson alive at that time, but Ruth would never have faced them because of the color barrier.

Answer: Yes, though it’s hard to cover absolutely everything. It also depends on grade level, and whether or not there’s a years-long curriculum designed to take students through history little-by-little (for instance, say 6th grade is Jamestown to the War of Independence, 7th grade is the Constitution to the Civil War, 8th grade is Reconstruction to World War II: in a case like that, it makes no sense for a textbook written for the 6th grade to include stuff on Vietnam). Here are some big events that sometimes get glossed over: I’m sure I am missing others.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are anti-Semitic incidents frequent in Poland?
Answer: As you can tell by the answers, you’ve stepped into a minefield. Here’s my brief answer: If by “anti-Semitic incident” you mean somebody gets beaten up or spit upon for walking down the street dressed like an Orthodox Jewish person, those incidents are rare, or at least, probably no more frequent than in the US or Western Europe. If it makes the news, public opinion is one of outrage. The police would face a lot of pressure to arrest those responsible. However, if by “anti-Semitic incident” you mean somebody tells an anti-Semitic joke, or a merchant has a statue or painting of a “lucky Jew” behind the counter to bring in the money, that’s relatively commonplace. There is a fair amount of low-level antisemitism, but not rising to the level of violence. I think a lot of it comes from ignorance, because there really aren’t that many Jewish people in Poland. The analogy I draw to the United States is this: imagine if we had had a Holocaust targeted at Black people in the US in the 1930s and 1940s. What would the white American perception of Blacks be today? It wouldn’t be so enlightened, as it would likely be informed by the stereotypes of the 30s and 40s and stories your grandfather told you, rather than a perception shaped by the Civil Rights Movement and everything that came after.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: In which part of the United States are there these beautiful red and gold autumns? I think I saw it for example in "The firm" (1993).
Answer: The Northeast in general is where people go to gaze at leaves during the fall. You even see “peak color” maps around this time of year, though some cover the entire country: However, the entire Appalachian range has some nice fall foliage, just at different times. I went to school in Pennsylvania, and went on a retreat in the fall near Somerset, in central PA. It was quite lovely. You won’t see as much color the further west you go, especially west of the “Line of Aridity” at 100 W longitude, as that part of the country tends to be pretty dry.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Has England had any civil wars called something else that weren't the two involving Charles I?
Answer: Shakespeare probably would have referred to the Wars of the Roses as “The Civil War”, or that’s what his reaction would have been if you’d said that term. Speaking of Shakespeare, he wrote a great tetralogy, the plays Richard II, 1 Henry IV, 2 Henry IV, and Henry V, about a period of civil war that is sort of a prequel to the Wars of the Roses (the period from about 1381 to about 1410). It all started when King Richard II was somewhat less than an ideal King, and an ambitious magnate, Henry Bolingbroke, son of John of Gaunt, decided to press his claim to the throne. Bolingbroke won, was crowned as Henry IV, but had to deal with rebellions throughout his reign, such as the one led by the Earl of Northumberland in England, and by Owain Glyndŵr (also called Owen Glendower in English) in Wales. Things were pretty touch-and-go for a while there, and things didn’t really calm down until Henry V came to the throne. I’m a little surprised that nobody has mentioned the Jacobite Wars. After the Glorious Revolution, James II still had supporters in Scotland and Ireland, particularly among Catholics. They continued to support him, and after he died they supported his son’s claim to the throne (James Francis Edward Stuart, “the Old Pretender”), then his grandson’s claim to the throne (Charles Edward Stuart, “the Young Pretender” or “Bonnie Prince Charlie”). There were two major Jacobite uprisings in Scotland, in 1715 and 1745, and the ’45 rising saw London lose control over most of Scotland, and actually saw a large Scottish army invade England. They withdrew among internal arguments, and were decisively defeated at the Battle of Culloden in 1746. There was a neat BBC series some years ago called Battlefield Britain, which discusses some interesting parts of military history. You can find it on YouTube.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Can one still be conservative these days without supporting Trump?
Answer: I talked a bit about this in one of my other answers: The thing to remember is, the idea that everything that comes out of Trump’s mouth is conservative is actually very strange. The man speaks “Republican” as a second language, and when he first started running for President, he sounded like an SNL parody of a Republican. I do not see how you can call yourself a conservative, and ignore, minimize, or justify raising a mob to try and overturn an election.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the difference between conservatives who support Trump and those conservatives who don't?
Answer: I have long thought that Trump speaks “Republican” as a second language, and covered up his inability to speak it fluently by speaking it loudly: when he started running for President in 2015, he sounded almost like an SNL parody of a Republican. For whatever reason, sometime in 2016 it was decided that whatever Trump said was by definition conservative, and anything said against him was by definition liberal. It was an amazing transformation, and both the Democrats and Republicans accepted it as gospel truth. The end result was that eventually, the entire Republican Party started sounding like….well…..an SNL parody of how Republicans talk. I don’t understand how spending lots of money on pet projects, raising tariffs, using the government to try and regulate speech, and oh yes, *forming a mob to try and overturn an election*, is conservatism as anyone would have understood it prior to 2015. Tangentially, why do you think the Trumpists keep pounding on the culture wars? It’s because that’s just about the only thing that unites the Republican Party. Economics? You’ve got old-school union Democrat types, “common-good conservatives” who advocate Socialism with Republican Characteristics, and some businessmen-types that are still Republicans of the old school, i.e., government should leave me alone. These people hate each other. Foreign Policy? The isolationists are in the driver’s seat, but there’s still some national-defense neocon types in the background. You’re about to see some interesting mental gymnastics over the withdrawal from Afghanistan. These people hate each other. Trump manages to draw support from Hasidim….and neo-Nazis. What holds them all together? Fear of The Left, that They are going to change our country beyond recognition. Stoke that fear, and all the other contradictions of the Trump coalition fade into the background.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why would my ex of 20 years, who I believe is a narcissist, sleep with an enemy who lives around the corner from me?
Answer: This is in the category of things that will only bother you….if you let them bother you. You have no control over what your ex does. All you can control is your own reaction. And sometimes the best victory is, to not react the way someone expects you to react.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: My ex tries to win me back every time we meet and apologizes. Then when he was in a relationship, he said that we might not go back together because of our completely different lifestyles. What should I do?
Answer: After he says “we might not go back together because different lifestyles etc….”, what is his reaction if you say “OK” and leave it at that? If he then says “well, I didn’t really mean it, or maybe we could make it work or….”, then he’s jerking you around. In any relationship, romantic, business, personal, and so forth, if the other person really wants to make it work, they will find a way to make it work. That’s the difference between “I’m busy Saturday and can’t do coffee” and “I’m busy Saturday. How about Tuesday?” If they aren’t putting in effort, they just aren’t that into you. Basically, you should find someone else, and not let yourself be kept on a string. Unfortunately, sometimes the only way to get someone to respect you is to walk away, and stay away.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I have never visited New York City but a regular visitor told me it is very similar to London. How true is this?
Answer: My quip is that the difference between London and New York is the difference between David Niven and Donald Trump. Both are large and important cities, but London wears it more lightly than does New York. London is also more of a low-rise city: in The City, sure, there are skyscrapers, but it looks very different from Midtown Manhattan.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do scientists wear white lab coats?
Answer: Not all lab-coats are white. A very common flame-retardant lab coat is the “Bulwark” type, which is actually blue, in order to distinguish it from the non-flame-retardant ones. I’ve also worked in a biology lab that did work with fungus , and bacteria, in separate labs. The fungal labs had black lab coats, and the bacterial labs had blue lab coats, to keep them separate. The advantage of white is that dirt shows up easily, and you know when you need to wash it or throw it away. In a biology setting, you frequently have to use bleach to disinfect things, and if bleach gets on something white, well……all the better. Now, in many labs, people don’t actually wear lab coats on a regular basis. It varies from institution to institution, and depends on what you’re working with. If you’re sitting at a microscope, you’re probably not wearing a lab coat. If you’re doing a chemical reaction, it’s probably best to wear one.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do some Americans think the imperial system is better and easier to use than the metric system?
Answer: One thing I read years ago which stuck with me is, the English/imperial system is based on either base-8 (the mile is actually 8 furlongs), base-12 (length) or base-16 (weight). Now, what is that good for? It’s good for when you have to double or halve things quickly, because 8, 12 and 16 have a lot of factors of 2. This is actually good if you are on the frontier, surveying something, and you need to divide, say, a plot of land into two equal pieces. Or you need to quickly double or halve a recipe. So if you have to, say, divide Ohio into square land parcels you can see from the air, quickly, without a calculator, it’s actually not a bad system. The metric system is much more useful if you are trying to divide something by, say, seven and a half. Which you need to do in a laboratory or scientific setting. Fahrenheit is, I would argue, more useful in a daily setting (the weather), because it rounds more usefully. If I tell you “it’s going to be in the 70s tomorrow”, you’ll expect it to be pretty pleasant. But if I tell you it’s going to be in the 20’s (C), that can range from pretty nice, to actually kind of hot.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which metric unit do you think would be easiest for Americans to adapt to for everyday use?
Answer: Well, we already use 1 liter and 2 liter bottles for soft-drinks, and what used to be known as a “fifth” of whiskey is now 750mL, standard. If we started selling milk in 4-liter and 2-liter bottles, we’d probably start using metric units as a volume standard. It’s also important to note that in industries that have a lot of contact with the outside world (automotive, or the sciences), we pretty much already use metric.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If you were able to live for a thousand years, how would you hide it to not being suspicious?
Answer: That’s an interesting question. I’ll assume you mean a person grew to some adult-looking age, and just stopped growing, and/or you’ve got a “Baby Yoda” thing going on, where it takes 500 years to reach maturity. Because otherwise, a 1000-year old person who just doesn’t die……is definitely going to have Alzheimers or some kind of brain damage, bad knees/back/etc. and will have trouble concealing anything from anybody. The key is going to be moving around every 5–10 years or so. Your neighbors won’t really notice that you don’t look any older in that span of time. The world is a big place. Even a large city can be a big place: how many times do you figure you run across the same (nondescript, random) person in New York City, enough so that you notice? Or, if you spend 10 years in Staten Island, 10 years in the Bronx, 10 years in Manhattan…..nobody from your old neighborhood will see you. You would have to make an effort to stay current with language, accent, and usage. After all, you can usually notice that someone who is 70 talks differently than someone who is 25, so just imagine the difference between someone who is 200 and someone who is 25! Over long periods of time, language will shift, and over the span of 1000 years, it will shift beyond recognition: you probably would think Lincoln’s language was weird, Shakespeare’s tricky to comprehend, and Harold II would be incomprehensible. And vice-versa, actually. One way you could get around this would be to move countries from time to time, and learn the local language. People will expect you to sound funny, because you’re a foreigner. You’d probably have to change countries anyway, for reasons I’ll get into below. Where you are going to have a problem is with anything having to do with the government, or where your date-of-birth is important in identifying documents. After all, you’re not going to be able to collect Social Security for 150 years without somebody noticing. What you would probably have to do every 50 years or so would be to fake your death, and fake your birth, to make it more current. You would still have a problem, though, in that our entire existences after birth leave fingerprints and traces: vaccination records, school records, tax records, census records, and now even something as trivial as baby photos on Facebook. That stuff is very hard to fake. So what you probably need to do, again every 50 years or so, is come up with a new background that means you’re from a place where record-keeping is not very good, or where records have a tendency to go missing for various reasons (war, carelessness, etc.) Moving countries by itself might be helpful, because the people in your new country are not necessarily going to know all of the details of how things are done in the previous country. However, with the internet, even that advantage might be disappearing. Oh yes. You should also be careful not to get in trouble with the law, because your DNA and fingerprints are going to be the same. If you get arrested for one crime now and another in 150 years, that will throw a red flag.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is grass typically always wet in the morning even on days when it hasn't rained?
Answer: What you are experiencing is something called dew. Air can contain a lot of moisture, even when it hasn’t rained, as you might notice on a hot summer day. The amount of moisture the air is able to contain depends on its temperature: the higher the temperature, the more moisture the air is able to contain. So let’s say the temperature is high during the day, and the air contains about as much moisture as it can. What happens when the temperature drops, during the night? The air is what we call “super-saturated”, meaning there’s more moisture present than it can hold in solution. That extra water has to go someplace, and it settles out, or “condenses” onto grass or other surfaces. A useful measure of the moisture in the air, or the humidity, is a temperature called the Dew Point. Simply put, the dew point is the temperature at which water will begin to condense out of the air and onto surfaces. A high Dew Point means that it’s very humid, and that can even be used to tell you when it’s dangerously hot and humid!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I'm about to live in the US, but I'm not used to the US customary units. Am I going to struggle? How long would it take to learn the system if I put a lot of effort?
Answer: I’m an American, and when living in Europe I was a little nervous about living in the metric system (and I’m even a scientist by trade: I use metric at work, but that’s different from using it outside in the world every day). It took some adjustment, but what was really helpful was having a few handy rules of thumb, because most of the time you don’t have to be really precise anyway. If you say it’s “about a mile away”, that can mean anything from 0.8 miles to 1.3 miles or whatever. The other thing to remember is, for most everyday usage, you don’t have to worry about less-common measurements (I’m not sure I have a good idea of what exactly an “acre” looks like, and you probably don’t have a good idea of what a “hectare” looks like), and you don’t have to worry about unusual sizes (when was the last time you ordered 138 grams of something?) The key is, be approximate! Here’s the rough equivalent I had in my head: Distances and areas: A meter is roughly equal to a yard, or three feet. The meter is about 10% bigger, but it’s a rough rule of thumb. A mile is roughly 2 kilometers. Again, it’s more like 0.6 miles = 1km, but 1 to 2 is a good rule of thumb. An inch is 2.5 cm. What might be more useful to remember is, 1 foot = 30 cm. Square feet to square meters: I didn’t have a great system for this one, but the only time this was important was in renting an apartment, when I found out that 20 m^2 is really small, and 60 m^2 is pretty big. Basically, just visit some apartments so you get a feel for what, say, 700 square feet looks like as opposed to 1000 square feet. Volumes: A gallon is roughly 4 liters, and a quart is roughly 1 liter. A pint is a little less than 500mL. So if you’re ordering beer, you’ll usually get about a pint, which is a little less than the standard half-liter of Europe. It’s more fun going the other way, though (expecting a US pint, but getting a half-liter is more fun than the opposite, that is). Yes, 1 gallon = 3.8L, but 1 gallon = 4 liters is easier to remember. A 2-liter bottle of soda is 2 liters. For some very strange reason, we sell “party-size” soft drinks in 2-liter sizes, and that’s about all that is sold in a standard metric size.
