You don’t usually deal in ounces unless you’re ordering shots. And in fairness, when was the last time you were concerned with 237mL of something? For small volumes, you are more likely to see cups, fractions of cups, tablespoons and teaspoons used. Here I’d advise you to just buy some measuring spoons/implements, so you see what they look like and so you can follow recipes directly (more on that below). Weights: A pound is roughly 500g, and a kilogram is roughly 2 pounds. We don’t ordinarily deal in ounces here, either: it’s more common to talk about fractions of a pound, OR, and this is a big one, the place where you’d see small volumes is in cookbook recipes. Our recipes are usually written for VOLUMES of dry ingredients, not weights. So you probably wouldn’t see, say, 1/4 ounce salt. You’d see something like 1/2 teaspoon. In fact, you’d see a volume of butter as well (2 tablespoons of butter, for instance). What’s really great here is, our sticks of butter are usually 8 tablespoons, and have a little ruler printed on the stick, so you can cut out how much you need. Temperature: This one is tricky. But what I think you should do is, rather than try to do the conversion in your head, get a sense of what a temperature “feels” like. Humidity is also going to make a difference, and there’s a very wide range of that across the country: 90F in Phoenix will feel much more comfortable than 90F in New Orleans. And the Fahrenheit units round more meaningfully (and on weather forecasts you’ll sometimes hear things like “highs in the lower 60’s” for that reason) So for instance: Below 0F: Bits of you might start falling off if you aren’t bundled properly. Dangerously cold. 0F-20F: Very cold. Bundle up. Roughly -10C. 20F-30F: Still pretty cold, roughly around 0C. Depends on other weather conditions, though: if there’s wind, this can be quite unpleasant. If it’s still, and you’re moving a lot, it can be a little better. If there’s going to be heavy snow, it’s roughly this temperature outside. 30–40F: Cold, but not too bad, especially towards the end of winter when you’ve acclimatized to lower temperatures. 40–50F: A little chilly, but this is the temperature at which you can start, say, exercising without wearing too much. 50–60F: Springlike temperatures. Wear a jacket, you can probably run around in shorts. Good soccer weather. 60F-70F: Usually pretty pleasant. The lower range of “room” temperature. Still good soccer weather. 70F-80F: Comfortable “shirtsleeves” weather, or a warm “room” temperature. Can start to feel hot closer to 80 degrees, depending on how humid it is. (80F at midnight, with high humidity, is no fun at all and does happen in parts of the country. 80F in the afternoon with low humidity is great weather for barbecue or baseball, or both). 80–90F: This is starting to get hot, and how unpleasant it is depends very much on the humidity. 90–100: Very hot. If the humidity is high, dangerously hot. 100+: Dangerously hot. Temperatures above 100 you’re only really going to see in the Southwest (California, Arizona, New Mexico etc.). It does happen in places like Chicago, but it’s newsworthy. My advice is, rather than try to convert everything in your head, try to live in the US system as best you can. It’s like speaking a foreign language: I find that if I try to formulate a sentence in English, then translate it to Polish, the result is halting and not very good. The key breakthrough was starting to think in Polish. Once you start thinking in Imperial units, it does get easier.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What difficulties would arise due to lack of uniformity in measurement in various countries?
Answer: The idea of having a uniform system of weights and measures is actually more recent than you might think: the Metric System dates to the 1790’s, and the English Imperial System had a standard yard….but not much of a standard anything else until the 19th century. In fact, part of the reason there’s a difference between the American gallon, and the “Imperial” gallon is that the Americans standardized on the “wine gallon”, which was smaller than the “beer gallon” that the British standardized on. In the Middle Ages, the units of measure, and the size of those units of measure, varied from country to country, and even from town to town. For instance, a “lieue” was 3.3 km in Beauce, but 5.8 km in Provence. In Germany, a “mile” was anything from 4119 meters in the Rheinland to 9206 meters in Hesse-Kassel (in contrast, the English mile is 1609 meters). There were similar differences in weights and volumes. What that did was effectively make globalization very difficult to impossible. To agree on a price for something, we have to first agree on how much is being offered for sale, and we can’t do that if your pound is different from my pound. One important function of something like the Hanseatic League was to ensure that everyone was on the same page as to how much was being sold.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the weirdest things that scientists in the past believed?
Answer: As Norman Simenson says in his answer below, phlogiston is a good one. I’ll add a couple of details. When oxygen was initially discovered, it was referred to as “de-phlogistated air”: the idea was that the reason things burn more vigorously in oxygen was that oxygen was simply better at absorbing the phlogiston given off by the burning object. Second, when it was discovered that the ash of something that has burned is lighter than the starting material, the explanation was simply that phlogiston must have a negative weight. But here’s the thing: are you talking about things that were weird…..and false? Or just weird? Because a lot of scientific theories that are currently accepted are pretty darn weird. For instance, it is currently accepted that all of space and time, indeed all of creation, was all compressed into a single point, which underwent a sudden inflation to create the whole universe about 17 billion years ago. That’s a pretty weird theory. Quantum mechanics, in general, is really weird, so weird that Niels Bohr said that if you weren’t outraged by what you were seeing, it means you didn’t understand it. For example, all particles are waves, and vice versa. So a baseball moving through the air is also a wave. And when waves meet an energy barrier, they are able to do something called “quantum tunneling”, which means that waves can penetrate the barrier. Now, this is something which happens with electrons (the Scanning Tunneling Microscope, or STM, depends on it), but which in theory can happen to all matter. Meaning if you throw a baseball at a wall, there is an incomprehensibly small chance that the ball will disappear from one side of the wall, and reappear on the other. Now, the odds of that happening are so very small that you would probably never observe it in the lifetime of the universe, but that probability is not zero. Other weird theories: enormous lizards dominated the planet in the mesosoic era, and were all wiped out by an asteroid impact 65 million years ago. Given 600 million years, random changes and natural selection led from single-celled organisms to humans, and you share a common ancestor, many many many years ago, with a chicken, or anything else on earth. There are some adaptations that organisms make in response to their environment which appear to be heritable (epigenetics). Matter and energy are the same thing, and can be converted from one to the other. The continent you are standing on is actually moving very slowly, and when it bumps into other continents, it causes earthquakes. The universe is a strange and wonderful place!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are Polish people, in general, religious?
Answer: Yes and no. Most Poles would at least nominally say they are Catholic, because Catholicism is part of the national identity and character. Between 1795 and 1918, the Church helped maintain Polish identity. During the Communist era, the Church was pretty much the main focus, and leader of, the opposition to the government, so a lot of older Poles identified as Catholic, and even went to church, mostly as an f—- you to the government. In modern Poland, I was struck by the fact that the national holidays (like May 3rd) have a religious character, whereas some church holidays (like Corpus Christi) have a lot of nationalist or patriotic character (there was a military honor guard at a parade, for instance). The crucifix is found in places it wouldn’t be in the US, like assembly halls of public universities. Politically, the government has wrapped itself in the altar cloth, so to speak, doing things like mandating businesses close on Sunday, and a friend of mine said that during the most recent elections, the homilies from the pulpit were divided this way: about 1/3rd were apolitical, 1/3rd were “well, vote your conscious, but Law and Justice is the correct choice at the ballot box”, and 1/3rd were “both you, and the country, are going straight to hell if you vote for any party except Law and Justice.” However, in terms of actual observance, Poland is less religious than you might think. A considerable proportion of the population now views the Church as just another arm of Law and Justice, rather than the conscious of the nation. My neighbors grumbled about rich prelates not following Christ’s example of modesty and humility. Observance also depends on where you are in Poland. Generally, Western Poland is more liberal, and church attendance is lower, whereas Southern and Eastern Poland tends to be more conservative, with higher attendance. I heard an interesting contrast between a homily at a Good Friday service in Poznan (West-Central Poland), which could be summarized as “isn’t this nice? I wish I saw you more often”, and a Corpus Christi service in Krakow (Southern Poland), which could be summarized as “we must fight to preserve our heritage from the Godless heathens that would destroy the nation!” Granted, these rhetorical choices could have come down to the individual priests, but it was interesting to note that the tone was less belligerent in a region which is usually seen as less religious. Last interesting anecdote. I went to a wedding in rural Poland, and was astonished when, out of about 150 guests, 3 of them took communion. I was further astonished when, after the priest said “make the sign of peace to those around you”, nobody did. That’s a standard part of a Catholic service, and the fact that nobody did it suggests to me that they don’t actually go to church that often. So on balance, I’d say that Poles are mostly nominally Catholic, but in terms of actual religiosity are on par with Americans.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is a depressing fact you've realized after/during your PhD?
Answer: A lot of people in the academic world crave fame, or being associated with it. You’ll see these clouds of people clustered around particular scientists. However, this fame is actually very limited: you can be “world-famous” to about 1000 people. I went to one plenary session for a scientist very famous in her field, but across town, at the same conference but a different venue and session, nobody had ever heard of her. And vice-versa: the scientists who were very famous at that other venue and session would be completely obscure to those at the first session. It struck me as funny that the thing people were chasing is actually very fleeting, and limited.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it shady that my professor asked me to meet for a coffee?
Answer: It definitely depends. How large is the class, and how well do you know this professor? And, where is the coffee place? A lot of campuses have known “grab-a-coffee” spots, and if that’s the invitation I would be inclined to say it’s probably alright. Ditto if this is a professor you have a relationship with: I had a few professors in undergraduate who were my mentors, who I’d known for years, and I wouldn’t have been creeped out if they said “hey, want coffee?” But there were other professors who didn’t even know my name. Had they asked me to coffee, that would have been weird. I’ll try to repeat saying what’s already been said on the thread, but maybe consider doing this: do you have a friend in this professor’s class? Suggest perhaps a three-or-four-person coffee meet-up. You can even frame it as “hey, my friend really likes this class, and has some questions, can he/she come too?” If the professor is really just asking you in order to talk about things in more detail, he (I assume it’s a he) will be thrilled at the opportunity to have a larger audience. If it is shady, watch him start backtracking/insisting that it be only you, at which point you can politely say you’d rather keep it to office hours.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do professors mind if a student drops by during office hours to ask questions about a lecture and go deeper into the material? Is once a week too often?
Answer: It depends. Are you really going deeper into the material and asking questions, or are you asking me to raise your grade for no good reason? If you are really there to discuss the lecture, and the material, then that’s why I have office hours! It doesn’t matter what I feel about it, being there to answer questions is part of my job. I had one student who came to every single office hour I held. Was I annoyed? Maybe a little. But I respected this student, because she was taking advantage of resources offered, was focused on the material, and I would much rather have this scenario than one where a student can’t be bothered, gets a “D”, then complains about what a lousy teacher I am to all and sundry.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it physiologically possible for soccer referees to accurately judge if a player is offside at the very same time the ball is footed, each and every time?
Answer: No, not each and every time, as referees are human. Some are very obvious, but in other cases it’s very close, especially as now if the player’s head is offside, then he is offside. If the defending team is not good at setting the line, the person who is second-to-last keeps changing, and that can be hard to keep straight. The other complication is that we are often going by the sound of the ball being kicked, not when we see it being kicked, and the speed of sound is slower than you think. That being said, we’ll get it right more often than a random fan who’s 60 yards away and doesn’t have the correct angle. A difference of a yard or two to the left or right is really all it takes in some cases, to have the wrong angle.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is the most damaging popular pseudoscience?
Answer: Probably a close race between anti-vaccination and homeopathy. I would argue anti-vaccination is more damaging. If I get sick and decide to treat my affliction with prune juice, that’s bad for me but probably won’t matter to you. If I, on the other hand, don’t vaccinate myself or my kids, they can catch something that they can spread to you, or someone who is not able to be vaccinated for legitimate medical reasons. It amazes me that people could see the great progress that has been made in medicine over the last 100 years, which was only made through a lot of effort, trial and error, look at it, and say “nah. I’m going to drink distilled water instead” or “I don’t care what you say about the drastic decline in measles, mumps, rubella, polio, chicken pox, and smallpox after vaccines were introduced for those diseases. Vaccines don’t do anything!” (I’m also a little grumpy at having had the chicken pox…..six months before the vaccine got approved. I might be one of the last people who has to get a shingles vaccine when I get older).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do people in Canada and the US seem to not know much about Europe other than stereotypes like Paris, the Queen, Harry Potter, etc.?
Answer: Well, let’s put the shoe on the other foot. Why do Europeans seem to not know much about the US and Canada other than guns, fast food, and what you see in action and cowboy movies? I had people in Poland semi-seriously ask if America was just like the movies, where there are constantly shootouts and car chases (there aren’t). During the 2012 elections I had someone in Poland mansplain to me that Mitt Romney didn’t believe in technology, because he’s a Mormon. I tried to set him straight (Mitt Romney is Mormon, not Mennonite. He doesn’t use a Mr. Coffee, but other than that he’s OK with technology), but he stuck to that view. And they really don’t understand the precise differences between a Methodist, a Presbyterian, and an Episcopalian. Most people only really know what they grew up with, or what goes on near where they live. Other points on a map exist as a bunch of stereotypes based on what kind of media a person has ingested. If you ask a Californian about Alabama, a Londoner about Belfast, a Milanese about Naples, a Parisian about Marseilles, a Muscovian about Vladivostok, or a Bavarian about Saxony-Anhalt, how accurate a picture do you think they would give you?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it surprising that so many Americans believe conspiracy theories? Why or why not?
Answer: It is not surprising, considering that Americans are humans. There are conspiracy theories all over the world, and they have existed throughout history. Basically, we’re not special, and I’ve heard all kinds of conspiracy theories from around the world (ask a certain type of Polish conservative about the Smolensk Disaster, for instance. Or ask someone in former Yugoslavia about damn near anything). Conspiracy theories are alive and well in Turkey. We tend to fixate on our own country, because it’s what we know. Why are there conspiracy theories? First, humans are experts at looking for explanations, reasons, and order where there might not be any. It’s why we see patterns in the sky, and invoke deities to explain the weather. So when something truly big happens, we assume there must be a big cause behind it, or alternately, we believe that complex events must have complex causes, when that’s not necessarily the truth (you can explain what causes an earthquake in about 5 minutes. The effects of an earthquake, however, are long-lasting). Further, belief in a conspiracy theory is oddly comforting, because it gives the illusion that someone is in control. Belief in a conspiracy theory also makes someone feel smart: they have hidden knowledge that all the “sheeple” don’t. It makes them feel important: they think they are exposing a hidden truth, rather than just ranting on the internet. There is a community aspect of this as well: we, the smart people, are enlightened, unlike they, the dumb, manipulated people. What might explain conspiracy theories specifically in America? Well, a few things:

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why have so many Americans fallen for conspiracy theories about Covid-19 being made in a lab?
Answer: I think an important distinction needs to be made. There are TWO theories out there, only the first of which you could call a conspiracy theory: That said, the reasons people believe COVID conspiracy theories is the same as the reasons they believe in any conspiracy theory. First, humans are experts at looking for explanations, reasons, and order where there might not be any. It’s why we see patterns in the sky, and invoke deities to explain the weather. So when something truly big happens, we assume there must be a big cause behind it, or alternately, we believe that complex events must have complex causes, when that’s not necessarily the truth (you can explain what causes an earthquake in about 5 minutes. The effects of an earthquake, however, are long-lasting). Further, belief in a conspiracy theory is oddly comforting, because it gives the illusion that someone is in control. Belief in a conspiracy theory also makes someone feel smart: they have hidden knowledge that all the “sheeple” don’t. It makes them feel important: they think they are exposing a hidden truth, rather than just ranting on the internet. There is a community aspect of this as well: we, the smart people, are enlightened, unlike they, the dumb, manipulated people. Or maybe people don’t actually believe in conspiracy theories. They just want you to think people believe in conspiracy theories.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the signs that show you will not succeed as a PhD?
Answer: There are a lot of good answers here, but these are my two cents as to what can result in not finishing a PhD program: You don’t have a growth mindset During your PhD, you are going to be criticized. Harshly criticized. By people who will not pass you unless you can answer their criticism. And the criticism will frequently be correct. You can either learn from the experience, or keep insisting that you’re right, and get stuck. You also need to realize that there is a lot that you simply don’t know, and will have to find out. Be willing to learn. It is called graduate SCHOOL for a reason. Similarly, most reasonable people are forgiving of blunders that first and second year students make. But if you’re still making the same mistakes in fourth, fifth, sixth year…..that is what gets you fired. Related to this is: You never ask for help Honestly, my PhD got a lot easier in my third year. Partially that’s because I started to see some results, but partially that’s because I learned how to swallow my pride and risk looking stupid by asking my labmates, my adviser, random people in the department etc. for help. It is easy to spend months spinning your wheels on a problem that has been solved already if you don’t ask someone. You don’t like the subject all that much/you’re just doing this “because I don’t have any better idea what to do.” I think every single person who has gone on to get a PhD has considered quitting at some point. There will be days, weeks, months, maybe even years, where things simply don’t work. You have to keep working anyway, and if you aren’t motivated to keep going, it’s easy not to. Avoid “The Three Nos” Whenever you’re giving a research update, you never want to be in a situation where you have 1) no results, 2) no plan, and 3) no clue. Generally if only two of these things are true, you’ll be OK. For example, “well, here’s what I tried, and I don’t know why it didn’t work, but here’s what I’m going to do next” is totally fine. Ditto “here are my results, but I don’t know what they mean and I’m not sure what to do next.” But if your group meetings and updates start sounding like “yeah, I didn’t really do anything, and I’m not sure what I’m doing, and I don’t really know anything about anything”, you’re in trouble. It’s not just that your adviser will fire you (though I did see that happen!), it’s that you have allowed yourself to get into a mentality where you are content to drift along without direction or purpose, and that’s a bad place to be.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why didn't Lithuania choose prosperous and advanced Prussia to unify with over Poland?
Answer: It may have had something to do with the fact that the (Catholic, and Prussian) Teutonic Knights were at war with the (Pagan) Lithuanians at roughly the same time Lithuania joined a personal union with Poland. The Teutonic Knights had been trying to convert the Baltic peoples for over a hundred years, and had not been doing it peacefully. Also, sure, in 1795 it might not have looked like a good bet to side with Poland over Prussia, but in 1410 that wasn’t so obvious. Poland was a world power in its day. In 1386, The Grand Duke of Lithuania, Ladislas Jogaila, was presented with a golden opportunity: marry Jadwiga, Queen of Poland, and be better known to history as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, King of Poland. Ladislas had to convert to Catholicism to seal the deal, but this had three possible benefits. First, by converting to Catholicism and bringing Lithuania with him, Jagiello eliminated the Teutonic Knights’ stated reason for fighting Lithuania: they were now all nominally the same religion, after all. Second, by becoming the King of Poland, Jagiello was able to bring Polish resources into battle against the Teutonic Knights. Which eventually led to Poland-Lithuania winning the war. Finally, by becoming King of Poland, Jagiello eventually got his picture on the modern 100-zloty bill: We forget that, at least at the start of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Lithuania was actually the senior partner. A considerable number of “Polish” magnates and famous historical people (the Kollataj and Radziwill families, Adam Mickiewicz, Jozef Pilsudski) were ethnically Lithuanian. We also forget that for a period of time, Poland was more than a match for Prussia, and in fact, Prussia was at one time a Polish client state: (The painting is called “The Prussian Homage” for a reason): Poland began its tragicomic collapse at the start of the 17th century. But before then, an alliance with Poland was not such a stupid move.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How is the color of a referee’s uniform defined, in soccer matches, when they aren’t wearing all black?
Answer: I’m not sure how the pros do it, but for your regular youth leagues the center referee (the one who’s on the field) decides what color the team wears. The colors are yellow, green, blue, red, and black. Why five colors? Well, because each team has a color, and each team’s goalkeeper has a color that’s different from their team’s color. So there are potentially 4 colors on the field, so the refs have one which is contrasting. For high school, at least in the US, the visiting team has to wear white, so the refs only really need 4 colors available. In practice, at amateur levels the refs don’t care too much if their jerseys match those of the goalkeepers, they just try to wear one that contrasts with both teams. And at least where I’m working, a surprising number of teams have black uniforms, so it’s rare to see referees wearing black. The US Soccer Federation’s instructions to new referees are to buy the yellow shirt first, then the green one, then add the other colors as it suits us. Which is why, again at amateur levels, you usually see refs in either yellow or green.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What do you think of Meghan and Harry’s Oprah interview?
Answer: Here’s my two cents: in that interview, who was the most important, influential, and relevant person? The one with the greatest clout? The one you would like to be? Oprah, of course. That’s America as it should be, and at its best. It should be (and sometimes it is!) that you can be born into incredible privilege, you can be beautiful, talented, and married to that privileged person, but still be miles below someone who did not have those advantages, but who is canny, hard-working, and gives people what they want.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Who was the most important scientist from Poland?
Answer: Here are some more obscure, but arguably very important, Polish scientists (or scientists born in Poland): Albert A. Michelson- Did some critical experiments determining the speed of light, which was experimentally important for the theories of relativity. He was the first American to win a Nobel Prize in science, but was born in Poland: Albert A. Michelson - Wikipedia Krzysztof Matyjaszewski- currently a professor at Carnegie Mellon, inventor of atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP), which is how the cool kids do polymerization these days: Krzysztof Matyjaszewski - Wikipedia Marian Rejewski- Mathematician and cryptographer who was critical to the cracking of the Enigma codes, and consequently, made a key contribution to Allied victory in World War II: Marian Rejewski - Wikipedia

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why are there so many racial issues in the United States? Are there similar issues in similar countries?
Answer: As I see it, the original sin of the United States was being a country founded on the equality of all men…..while at the same time relying on slave labor for a lot of the economy. Add to that the fact that slavery was racially-based. Now, other countries have had slavery (and it still happens!), but the US was founded on an idea that everybody was born free. Now, when people pointed this out to some of the Founding Fathers, their reaction was to look at their shoes, mutter something about “well, we kinda don’t like it either, and it’s bad, but slavery will die out. Eventually. We hope.” then quickly change the subject. Of course, this is not a great answer if somebody doesn’t let you change the subject. Furthermore, slavery may have been dying a natural death in 1790, but with westward expansion and new technologies like the cotton gin, slavery became *more* important to the economy in the 1820s. And it was at this point that guys like John C. Calhoun started making positive defenses of slavery, even making oxymoronic statements like “our liberty depends on the institution of slavery.” So, how do you justify promoting both human equality, and promoting slavery? Well, you have to see the slaves as subhuman. Confederate Vice-President Alexander Stephens put it very bluntly in his “Cornerstone” speech, that as he saw it, the error of the founding of the United States was that all men are created equal. He argues that this is false: Alexander Stephens on Slavery and the Confederate Constitution, 1861 Late in the Civil War, when the Confederacy was clearly losing, some Confederates said that the Army should enlist slaves as fighting men, with the promise of freedom if they somehow turned the tide. Even at that late date, with defeat staring him in the face, Stephens said if we allow slaves to enlist, we are saying that they are the equals of white men. And if they are the equals of white men, then the entire system of slavery, around which the Confederacy is based, is wrong. While they were promoting the idea that Black people are inherently inferior/subhuman, the Southern aristocracy had another problem: why would poor Southern whites, who couldn’t afford slaves, support slavery? Economically, slavery was bad for poor whites: if you are a farmer, how can you possibly compete in the marketplace with an enormous plantation that doesn’t have to pay people? If you’re looking to work for wages as a farmer on somebody else’s land, you’re out of luck, because you can’t compete with unpaid labor. If you want to move west…..oops, all the best land has already been taken by planters. Want to change things in the state legislature? Well good luck, because the people there are….planters. Why would you support this system? Well, because slavery has given you, a peasant, basically, a status you wouldn’t otherwise have: you may be poor and starving, but at least you’re white and that gives you someone to feel superior to. And those old habits die hard. Now, other ethnic groups were disliked when they first came to America. While “no Irish need apply” appears to be a myth, there was definitely anti-Irish sentiment, or anti-Catholic sentiment that was basically anti-Irish sentiment. Was there antisemitism in this country? You bet, and it has been making an unfortunate return. Italians and Poles were viewed with suspicion, and in 1900, they would not have been seen as “white.” Even as late as the 1950’s, my dad remembers being taunted with “hey you little Communist, go back to Russia where you belong.” I bring this up not to say “oh, poor white people”, but rather, to point out that there were once groups that were disliked, for racial reasons, who are now just lumped in that category of “generic white people.” I think we need to ask ourselves the question, how were we able to integrate these foreign ethnic groups, yet Blacks were still left out in the cold, as a race and people somehow apart? All that being said, I feel like in the US we often act as though our country invented racism, or that racism is a uniquely American problem. It is not. My father-in-law is ethnically Chinese, but grew up in Malaysia in the 1960s, where there is a sizeable Chinese minority. He remembers not being able to go to the beach, because that was “Malay territory”, and if you were on the beach while Chinese, you’d get beaten up. There were race riots in Malaysia at that time, which he doesn’t talk about. Even today, under the guise of “affirmative action”, there is legal discrimination against the Chinese minority by the Malay majority government, such as quotas for university admissions and government jobs. Apartheid South Africa was not a fun place to be if you were anything other than white. From what I know about Apartheid, it sounds like Jim Crow on steroids, and it is frankly amazing (and a testament to the leadership skills of Nelson Mandela, among others) that there was a peaceful transition to majority rule. Racism exists in places where, to our eyes at least, everybody looks the same. Former Yugoslavia is a great example of this: most Americans, I would venture, would have a hard time telling a Serb from a Croatian from a Bosnian from a Kosovar. On top of that, they speak pretty much the same language. Yet they spent the better part of 5 years killing each other over differences in religion, and there was genocide committed against the Bosniaks. This was less than 30 years ago. The Nigerian Civil War (Biafran War) had a distinct racial component, pitting the Igbo ethnic group against the Yoruba and Hausa-Fulani ethnic groups. The war started after a series of race riots: Rwanda in 1994 was another example of genocide brought about by racism. It’s also sometimes hard to separate the difference between racism and tribalism. My friend Robert was a Ugandan who was born in Sudan. He pointed out that he looked a bit like Idi Amin, and there was a reason for that: they both came from the same tribe. When Amin was deposed, there was a backlash against the members of his tribe, so Robert’s parents got the hell out of Uganda and ended up in a refugee camp, where Robert was born. The sanitary conditions in the camp were not good, so Robert contracted hepatitis as a child, and had chronic hepatitis his entire life, which eventually killed him about 30 years later.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is there an opposite to the Eureka moment?
Answer: Oh yes, those happen frequently in the sciences. Sometimes things will fail,and fail pretty spectacularly. You can have “oh crap!” moments, when something breaks. OR, you can have a Eureka moment, and you think you are really on to something…..then you recalculate and find out you were wrong. Or you have a Eureka moment, but then you do another control experiment and…..nope, it wasn’t as exciting as you thought it was. The moral of the story is, always do the right control experiments, and don’t get too discouraged when things don’t work out.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why are Polish women so bad and cold and cannot even talk to them, not approachable women? Why is that?
Answer: I’ll start with the elephant in the room: Polish women tend to get married much earlier than they do in Western Europe or the USA, and before that they are often in committed relationships for some time. I was in Poland when I was in my early 20s, and single, so I was playing the field. It seemed like a lot of my contemporaries, or those just slightly older, were married or engaged already. A number of people were still with their high-school sweethearts. Getting married at 20 is not weird (hell, having a kid at 20 is not that weird), and getting married at 30 is considered “late.” So, someone who would be an eligible bachelorette in the US is already off the market in Poland. Second, Poles in general tend to be more reserved, and will take a while to open up. It’s not like, say, the US, where you can fall into a friendly chat with someone very quickly and easily. That’s true for men as well as women. Third, where are you looking? Are you walking up to random people on the street saying “cześć, laska, masz ochotę mieć stosunki zemno?” (“Hey chicky, do you want to have sexual relations with me?”) Because if you are, yeah, that’s not going to work, and might get you maced. If you’re in a bar, the woman might not actually be there to meet someone: a lot of people just go to bars to hang out with their friends, not to get picked up. My suggestion is to go dancing, or take dance lessons. Fun fact: to make beer a more “girly” drink, you can order a beer with some fruit syrup in it. And a straw. I am not making that up. Finally, there is the language barrier. Are you chatting these people up in Polish, or in English? I’ve noticed that a lot of Poles who can speak English, even those who speak it pretty well, are nervous about doing so because they think you’ll make fun of them if they make a mistake. This is especially true if you are a native speaker of English. I blame English teachers in Poland, who, I’ve heard, make fun of their students for making mistakes in class. That was something I heard anecdotally often enough to make me suspect it’s fairly common. So, one way you might get more traction in Poland is if you speak some Polish, even bad Polish, which some people will see as endearing, especially because few foreigners speak it. Powodzenia!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Who could be the third in this sequence, if alliteration weren't a requirement: Bach, Beethoven,...?
Answer: So the traditional answer here is Brahms, and it’s a perfectly defensible answer, but I think that’s the answer you’re trying to avoid by the way this question is phrased. Other than Brahms, who might we put on the list? It’s very hard to say, because there are many very good composers. Haydn would be a good answer, as his music defines an era (the Classical era), he was very innovative, and his music would influence Beethoven and Mozart, among others (Beethoven was Haydn’s protege). Both the symphony and the string quartet as formats owe a lot to Haydn, and he cranked out many of both of them. He also composed for a long time, and it’s interesting to see how his style changes over time. He did, unfortunately, also compose a lot of dross to pay the bills, but when his aim was to compose masterpieces, he succeeded. Mozart would be a good answer. He wrote very well, for a wide range of instruments and types of compositions (opera, choral, symphonic, solo instruments, etc.) The Russians have the “Mighty Five” (Balakirev, Cui, Mussorgsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, and Borodin). Of those five, I think Mussorgsky might have been the most influential on the music of the rest of the world, though that is, of course, debatable: The Five (composers) - Wikipedia I’m a singer, so I’ll always put a good word in for Claudio Monteverdi, who was extremely innovative, to the point where some of his 17th-century madrigals sound like they could have been written in the 21st century. Some of the things he did became standard compositional techniques, some of them wouldn’t see common use until the 20th century……and there are some things about his music that are unique and were never tried again.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is 25 cl the same as 25 ml?
Answer: No. 25 cl is 25 centiliters, or 250 mL (1cl = 10mL).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If the U.S. became independent in 1676, 1876, or 1976 instead of 1776, how prominently would the prevailing ideologies of the day have influenced the new nation's constitution as compared with the one that was adopted in 1789?
Answer: 1676: you probably would have ended up with a loose federation, or even 10–12 separate countries rather than a single united polity. It’s also important to note that Georgia hadn’t been founded yet, and the colonies in general were still very sparsely populated. What probably would have happened, historically, is that without British backing and military support, the French would have eventually swallowed the new United States. But in terms of ideology, 1676 was right when we were seeing the first glimmerings of the Enlightenment. The Glorious Revolution hadn’t happened yet. You would have probably seen a more religious Constitution, which may or may not have had a Bill of Rights. There probably would have been a monarch, either elected or otherwise. And it is possible that there would not have been a written constitution, because written constitutions only became fashionable after 1787 (the US Constitution is the oldest explicit and written constitution!) 1876: It depends on the scenario that creates a United States in this year. If we were still a British colony, independence probably would have looked something like the independence of Canada or Australia: a slow loosening of control on Britain’s part, and the formation of a federal Dominion, still nominally under the rule of the Queen, but for the most part self-governing under a copy of the Westminster System. The US probably would be a Parliamentary democracy, under a constitution similar to Canada’s. It would be the US of Eh. Canada was organized as a Confederation in 1867, and did not become fully independent until 1931, though the Queen is still officially the Head of State. Slavery would have been outlawed in 1833, along with the rest of the British Empire. That might have triggered a failed War of Independence along the lines of the American Civil War, but on the other hand, Britain didn’t really have a serious problem enforcing anti-slavery legislation…..with the exception of South Africa, where the Boers decided to move inland with their slaves in the Great Trek, and found two independent republics (Transvaal and the Orange Free State). These were a thorn in the side of Britain, but were eventually annexed into the Union of South Africa in 1902. Might something similar have happened in the US, with slave-owners pushing West and establishing separate countries that would eventually be annexed? It’s an interesting question. Now let’s say the scenario is different, and the US had developed as a set of separate states in loose confederation. Well, this was a time of nationalism and unification in Europe, with modern Germany being founded in 1871 and modern Italy being founded around the same time. You might have seen a similar process in the US, with the individual states recognizing that they had a lot in common. The country probably would have organized along German lines, as a federal parliamentary republic. 1976: The Constitution would have been very, very long, like the EU constitution. More recently written constitutions have attempted to deal with a whole bunch of things, from human rights to trade rights to name-of-origin rules to taxation…..they tend to be very cumbersome documents, rather than a rough sketch that is filled in later with legislation.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Without casting blame and purely as an observation, can we agree that something has definitely changed in the US in the last 5 or 10 years? What has changed in your opinion?
Answer: I think the undercurrents of what ail us now have been there for a long time, but what’s changed is how very, very easy it is for every single person to communicate with every single other person, and how very easy it is for us to see the ugly side of people we don’t even know. Nowadays, everybody has a megaphone for whatever ideas pop into their head, and metrics that let everybody know what kind of an audience those ideas gather. 175 years ago, there was an Anti-Masonic party that thought the Masons were going to ruin America. 20 years ago, there probably were people who thought that the Democratic Party had been taken over by Satan-worshipping pedophiles who ran child-trafficking operations out of the basement of a DC-area pizza parlor, but that was the kind of stuff that your crazy Uncle Ned said at Thanksgiving. Uncle Ned didn’t know anybody who thought the way he did, and the more he said it, the less of an audience he had (everybody in the room at Thanksgiving would roll their eyes and change the subject). And your friend’s Uncle Fred may have had the same goofy ideas, but he never met Uncle Ned, and didn’t get one of the 150 copies of Uncle Ned’s newsletter that just about everybody who got it treated as birdcage liner. But now, your Uncle Ned has Facebook. And he links up with your friend’s Uncle Fred, and my Uncle Jed, and now they are able to get in touch with and encourage each other, reinforcing the nutty ideas that they have. And the more outrageous the claims they make, the more of an audience they get, because an outlandish claim will get clicks, shares, angry comments, and so forth. Hell, if the claim is crazy enough, and bought into by enough people, it is no longer your crazy uncle’s political theories you tune out, it becomes a “Movement”, some members of this “Movement” go walking around wearing buffalo horns on their heads, you end up with a riot on Capitol Hill, and it all ends up being covered on TV. But if someone comes up with a relatively reasonable set of posts, well, that’s hardly newsworthy now, is it? So if you want to be famous, be crazy. There is also a need for people to feel a sense of belonging to something larger than themselves. That used to be religion for a lot of people, or some fraternal organization, but now, unfortunately, it is tribal alliance to a political party. People also like to feel intelligent, or wise, and now, with social media, everybody can pretend to be a TV pundit. Unfortunately, this does not mean they actually have anything insightful to say: the way to make up for this is to merely parrot the words of others, without understanding or analyzing them. Finally, every statement now is a public or semi-public statement. And nobody wants to apologize, or admit they were wrong, in public. I don’t think the changes in America in the last 10 years have all been bad. Problems like police brutality certainly occurred before, but we didn’t talk about them, or we would pretend they didn’t exist. It is a lot easier to find things that are very niche or specialized: if you want to learn about lawyers, morticians, classical musicians…..there are YouTube channels for that that produce some good content. We have the potential to understand people, to hear them in their own words, that was simply not possible 50 years ago. What’s unfortunate is that this medium, this possibility, is too often used to publicly accuse people of not seeing what they actually saw, or not feeling what they actually feel.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Do Polish people like to have friends around and have dinner with them or a drink, tea, etc.? Is it possible to be invited home by a Polish citizen or are they cold?
Answer: I certainly spent a lot of time going to bars/restaurants with friends in Poland, usually as an after-work thing. It took a little while, though, because in general people are not as “buddy-buddy” there as in the States. I should also point out that Polish society is more hierarchical, or at least it is in the Universities. I was there after I finished my undergraduate, but did not have a graduate degree. So….did that make me a PhD student? An undergraduate? Something else? People didn’t know, and were reluctant to “hang out” with someone who might be above or below them in the pecking order. I was also in the weird position of being “American enough to not be ‘one of the guys’, but Polish enough to not be exotic.” So it can take a while before people just want to casually hang out, but it does happen. If you are invited into somebody’s home in Poland, this is a big deal and you should see it as an honor. Don’t come empty-handed: bring a bottle of wine or something, and realize that whoever invited you sees you as a special friend.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If sodium and potassium are already Latin names, why does the periodic table use K and Na for their symbols?
Answer: The Latin for sodium is “natrium”, or Na. The Latin for potassium is “kalium”, which is shortened to K.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why do Polish people love their country?
Answer: The most important thing to remember about Poland is that it didn’t exist for over 120 years (between 1795–1918). During that time, Poland only existed as an idea in people’s heads: it was a nation without a country. That led to a stubborn patriotism, and a strong national identity. Poland was also a world power between about 1450 and about 1700, before rapidly declining and being partitioned by its neighbors, so there’s a sense of loss and a desire to, dare I say it, “Make Poland Great Again.” Finally, Poland did accomplish something remarkable in the last 30 years, transitioning away from Communism and becoming a free and raucous democracy. The country has changed beyond recognition in the last 30 years, and the changes in the last 10 years are also obvious and noticeable. It’s actually a rather dynamic place at the moment.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Did democracy succeed in the U.S. as a result of the three English civil wars (including the War of the Roses, the English Civil War, and the Glorious Revolution)?
Answer: Partially, yes, though I would say the most important things were the English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution. The Wars of the Roses were a dynastic struggle, being more about who should be King Of England rather than what the rights and powers of that King were going to be. The Yorkists and Lancastrians probably agreed that the King should be extremely powerful, and that Parliament’s power should be limited to none, they just disagreed about who should wield that power. The English Civil War actually did have an effect on the American Revolution: the Civil Wars were characterized by a lot of different ideas flying around. You had the religious nutjobs on the side of Parliament, and they were pretty much the same sorts of people who settled Massachusetts. You had out-and-out Communists on the side of Parliament (they were called “levellers”, but today we’d call them Communists). On the Royalist side, you had those who still thought the King should be powerful and not have to rely on Parliament. While the Parliamentarians won the first round, eventually the Royalists ended up on top. This meant two things. First, a lot of people had to get out of England in a really big hurry, and one place some of them went was America (at least two of the Regicides of Charles I fled to the American Colonies). When these people fled, they brought their stubborn cussedness with them. Second, when Charles II was restored to the throne in 1660, he did so with the understanding that he had to work with Parliament, otherwise Parliament might cut off his head too. The important precedent was set that the King’s power was limited, and required the consent of the governed. The Glorious Revolution had the most direct impact on the American Independence movement, and on our founding documents. For one thing, William and Mary’s court philosopher was John Locke, whose ideas were thoroughly studied by the Founding Fathers, and adopted pretty much wholesale in our founding documents, almost to the point of plagiarism. Second, William and Mary pretty much had to issue a Bill of Rights as part of the political settlement that placed them on the throne. Tied to this was the idea that certain rights are God-given, and cannot be taken away by any earthly government. And this was different from rights as they had previously been understood: the Magna Carta was presented as “here are the rights the King allows you, because he’s such a nice guy, and because if he doesn’t, the Barons will kill him.” But the idea of rights derived from God, not the King…..that was a new idea that would end up incorporated in the American psyche. The last ingredient for the American Revolution that came out of the Glorious one was the rather dangerous idea that legitimate political power derived from the consent of the governed: basically, the Whigs who supported William and Mary argued that James II deserved to be deposed because he was a jerk (and a Catholic). They did not argue that James II wasn’t the rightful king, or that somebody else had a better claim, just that William and Mary would make better monarchs. Now THAT was a truly revolutionary idea, and would be appealed to in the American Declaration of Independence.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: A pregnant woman with blood type B has a child with a blood type O. What are the genotypes of the mother and child? Which genotype could the father have?
Answer: O is a recessive, so the mother has to have genotype BO. The father could have genotype OO, or really, (anything)O. Neither the mother or father could be AB in this case.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is California a bad state to move to?
Answer: Former Californian here. What I’ll say is, if you have lots of money, California is the best place in the world. You can do anything you want, buy almost anything you want, and at least on the coast (I lived in the LA area), the weather is superb. You don’t even really bother to check the weather on a daily basis, because when rain is in the forecast, everybody in the office is talking about it (“hey, I heard it’s going to rain on Tuesday!”) If you want to surf, or ski, or go hiking, it’s all there. The produce is also VERY good: I don’t think you’ve really had an orange until you’ve had one, in December, in California. But you’re going to need a lot of money to do it. Rent is very expensive, and buying a house is also extremely expensive, particularly in the Bay Area (you can buy a very nice cardboard box for $1 million, and that’s not too much of an exaggeration). Gas is, as other posters have said, around $4 a gallon. A few things are cheaper in California: your heating and cooling needs are less, for example, and wine and produce are both cheaper and of better quality. But the big killer is rent and other housing expenses. The other disadvantage is the potential for long commutes: if you live in a place you can actually afford, you may have to make a long trip to and from work every day, through bad traffic. The state of some of the highways is pretty bad too (the 210 in particular, the Foothill Freeway, is extremely lumpy). After a while, you get used to the street people, and they fade into the background. That’s an extremely depressing sentence to write, but it’s true. I left before they instituted rolling blackouts this last year, but that’s another annoyance. Last, you become a lot more aware of your water usage when there’s a drought on: water-saving shower-heads are mandatory in some cases, and you are not going to have a nice, green lawn without irrigation, and running up quite a water bill: they are trying to encourage people to tear out their lawns. My wife is a native Californian, and was really surprised when we moved to Maryland and she saw no sprinklers or irrigation systems anywhere, because you really don’t need them. Tied to that, at least in LA, everything is kind of brown during the summer. When I came to the East Coast for a job interview, I felt like I had entered a tropical rainforest, because I forgot how green everything is. So the answer to your question is, it depends where in California, and it depends on how much money you have.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are the best states to move to from California? I want to move but am afraid to because I know most other states hold disdain for us.
Answer: I moved into a rather Republican part of Maryland from California, and I suspect a lot of the people around here would say “California, well (scoff scoff).” But I haven’t really run into problems, partly because I don’t go around saying “Hello! I lived in CALIFORNIA!” or even better “don’t you peasants have any decent food in this dump? Why, in CALIFORNIA, everything was so much better.” When it does come around to me saying I moved out of California, the reaction of a number of people has been something along the lines of “well, why did you move here, of all places?” In general, it is harder for people to express disdain for an actual person who is standing in front of them, rather than some theoretical person thousands of miles away. So, just be normal and polite, and don’t make a huge deal about it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: If a book is resting on a table, Earth exerts a force on the book and the book exerts an equal force on Earth. Is this a Newton's third law pair?
Answer: Yes, it is a Third Law pair. Believe it or not, the Earth is getting pulled up just a tiny amount by the book resting on the table! Another third-law pair in this situation would be the force that the book exerts on the table, and the force that the table exerts on the book (the “Normal Force”).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: I’m 26 and never had a girlfriend because I don’t know how to respond to women who play hard to get when I’ve been interested. Do I have to change something?
Answer: My advice is, don’t respond to anyone who is playing hard to get, because it is a waste of time. It’s also hard to tell if it’s an act, or if she’s really not that interested, and it’s a waste of time trying to figure it out. What you should do is, ask people out, and the way you can tell if she’s interested is, she says yes. And you go on a date. It’s as simple as that. After that, see if she wants to go on subsequent dates in a straightforward way. Stick with one who doesn’t play bullshit games with you: the woman I married was ultimately the woman with whom I had a clear and straightforward relationship from day one.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Who in the North during the American Civil War understand what a difference making breech loading rifles standard issue would have made?
Answer: Well, the adoption of breech-loaders and repeating rifles was actually controversial at that time. The old-timers in the Union Army, especially in the Ordnance Department, argued that issuing these types of rifles would make logistics impossibly complicated, because the men would be using up a lot more ammunition, which meant that resupply would have to happen more often. The level of marksmanship by most soldiers in the Civil War was usually appallingly bad, so it’s not even clear how many more casualties would have been caused by broad issuance of breechloaders and repeaters (though there were a few examples, like at Chickamauga, where repeaters were used to good effect, and made a difference in the course of the battle). The other problem was that breechloaders were more expensive, and harder to make in general. So from the perspective of making millions of small arms, it made sense to make the simpler types of weapons.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why does it matter if bacteria is gram-positive or gram-negative?
Answer: Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria respond to different antibiotics, meaning that determining gram-positivity or gram-negativity of the bacteria in an infection lets you know the best course of treatment. Historically, finding out whether a bacterium was gram-positive or gram-negative was an important part of determining what kind of bacterium you actually had, along with what its shape was, how fast it grew, what kinds of medium it could grow on, etc. Nowadays we can do this pretty quickly and easily by DNA sequencing, but that’s only been a plausible option for the last 10–15 years. And in practice in a medical setting, it still might be cheaper to identify bacteria this way (I work in a research lab setting, so I don’t know what current best-practice is in hospitals). From a synthetic biology perspective, if you’re looking to do genetic engineering on a bacterium, the difference between gram-positive and gram-negative is very important. The thick outer peptidoglycan layer of a gram-positive bacterium makes it difficult to insert DNA into the cell, and you usually have to add enzymes or something to shave off some of that peptidoglycan. Gram-negative bacteria, on the other hand, are usually easier to get a plasmid into, and one of the many nice things about E. coli as a synthetic biology workhorse is that it is gram-negative, and easy to transform.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Should I leave my girlfriend after 7 years of living together?
Answer: A friend of mine once said that in any relationship, you should be asking yourself one question, and one question only: “am I getting more *out* of this relationship than what I am putting *in*? And if I am putting more in than I’m getting out, why am I in this relationship?” Relationships take work. You have to put in the effort. But you have to feel like it’s worth it. The only thing I would say beyond that is, realize that any long-term relationship is going to have its bad days, and that in a long-term relationship the picture you’re going to have of the other person is more “honest” than on a first date, both for good and ill, and you should “smooth out” the good and bad parts of your relationship over time. To be crass about it, is the great sex you have on a weekly basis worth having a knock-down, drag-out fight once every six months? You might put up with your partner doing something that, if she had done it on your first date, you would have said “I’ll pass on this one”, but now that you know the person, and her good and bad sides, you may say, “yeah, she does that sometimes, and that’s just the price I have to pay for her otherwise great sense of humor.” You have more information about the work required for the relationship, and the benefits you derive from it. But the calculation, “am I putting more in than I am getting out?” is the same. Knowing nothing whatsoever about this situation, what I would say is, is this pull towards breaking up something that pops up from time to time then goes away, or is it something that’s a constant question for you? If it’s a constant question, I would be inclined to break up. But you should weigh the good and bad parts, and “but we were together for 7 years” should not factor into it.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: A guy told my friend that he likes me but my friend told him that I don’t like him and when I asked him that did you tell my friend that you like me he said I didn’t say that I like you your friend is joking so what does this mean?
Answer: Whenever I have a complicated situation, I like to ask myself simplifying questions. Which in this case are: If you do like the guy, you could just tell him that you like him, and see what happens. If you don’t like the guy, does it really matter what he thinks about you?

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it okay to date a coworker while there was another coworker in the same work place who had a crush on me but I do not like him back?
Answer: Sure, it’s OK, as in, it’s not morally wrong or anything, provided that there isn’t a power imbalance (i.e., you absolutely shouldn’t date your boss, or your reports, because that creates all kinds of trouble and potential for trouble). However, I would very broadly advise you to not date coworkers. Period. In general, it’s best to keep your work life and your personal life separate, because if you do date someone you work with, bad things that happen at work can spill over into your personal life, and bad things that happen at home can’t be as easily escaped by going to the office. You have also created more potential political problems for yourself, in that the office gossip may turn to “well, she did this thing for him because they are dating, and I heard she was even going to……” It’s not fair, it’s not right, but it does happen. Further, if you break up with someone AND you still have to work with them…..yeah, that’s awkward. And this desire to avoid the awkwardness might make you stay in a relationship longer than you should.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What does it mean when your dead ex-husband sees you with your new boyfriend?
Answer: I think it means you’re having a bad dream, a bad acid trip, or you’ve become a character in a Charles Dickens novella.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: How many electrons are in a triple bond?
Answer: 6 electrons, 2 per bond. 2 electrons kind of hang out between the atoms in a sigma bond, 2 electrons hang out above the atoms in a pi bond, and 2 electrons hang out below the atoms in a second pi bond.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why is UC Berkeley not elite like MIT, Stanford, or Caltech?
Answer: I’ve got a slightly different perspective. At least in my experience, Caltech does not encourage people go go around thinking that they are elite, you are not being told that you’re special, and that was one thing I really liked about going there. It’s also a small-enough place (the entire student body, undergraduate AND graduate, is about 2000 students, about equal numbers graduate and undergraduate), that you get to know everybody, or at least see them occasionally, and that makes them less “mystical” in a way. It’s also kind of uncool to go celebrating yourself at Caltech, because odds are, the guy down the hall is smarter than you are. Further, everybody is so damn busy all the time, and they don’t really have time to go celebrating their own eliteness. The undergraduate and graduate curriculum is also very tough, your graduate experiments fail just as hard as they do elsewhere, and that’s a humbling experience for many people. I know it was for me. The bottom line is, when I was at Caltech, I didn’t feel like I was at an “elite” place. It was just, you know, life. Last, a lot of people don’t even know what Caltech is. The equivalent of saying “I went to school in Boston. Well, not IN Boston……” is saying “I went to Caltech. No, not Cal Poly Pomona…..” I was at the Rose Parade one year wearing my Caltech t-shirt, about 3 blocks north of campus. A random guy on the street asked me where my shirt was from, and when I said Caltech he said, I kid you not, “where’s that?”

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which person in history, if they lived 5 years longer, would make the biggest change to history?
Answer: I think Arthur Tudor is definitely up there (see David Paul Evans’ answer below): if he lived 5 years longer, then his brother Henry would have never married Catherine of Aragon, and consequently, would never have divorced Catherine of Aragon. This would have meant no English Reformation, or Church of England, which would have had enormous consequences for the history of England, both internally, and in terms of the foreign policy which it pursued, a lot of which was basically spurred by “we don’t like Catholics, at home or abroad.” Earlier than that, had King Henry V lived longer, he would have become King of France as well as King of England, and a continued English presence in France would have greatly changed how that country was governed. The constant rivalry between England and France would define Western European history for hundreds of years, and without that rivalry, history looks very different. On the other hand, French resistance to Henry would have probably continued, and it is unclear if the Hundred Years’ War would have eventually ended to England’s advantage. After all, giving Henry V five more years means that his successor, Henry VI, would have ascended the throne as a boy rather than as a baby, but Henry VI would still have been the weak-willed and possibly mentally-challenged king of history. So it’s not clear if Henry V living longer would have made that much of a difference. In Eastern Europe, Stefan Batory is considered one of Poland’s most-successful kings, but he only reigned for 10 years. Given another 5 years, he might have been able to make the Ukrainians into more-equal partners in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and also tamp down the power of the Polish nobility. This might have made the Commonwealth a little more stable, and enabled it to endure longer than it did. A possible candidate from earlier in history would be Julian the Apostate, emperor of Rome. He led a number of successful military campaigns, but was killed during one of them. During his reign, the imperial administration of Rome was reformed, and most significantly, he was the last non-Christian emperor of Rome. If he had lived longer, and perhaps had the temple in Jerusalem been rebuilt under his reign, the history of Europe might have turned out very differently: Julian (emperor) - Wikipedia

Question: Can countries like Sweden, Finland, Ireland, Switzerland, etc., be called third world countries?
Answer: As others have pointed out, “Third World Country” is an obsolete term that referred to a country’s political alignment during the Cold War. The “First World” were countries that aligned with NATO and the US, the “Second World” were the countries that aligned with the Warsaw Pact and the Soviet Union, and the “Third World” were those countries that aligned with neither side, and got an unfortunate reputation for being poor and benighted, because it was assumed the reason they weren’t aligned, was that neither side took much interest in them. Funny thing is, by that definition, Pakistan was “First World”, and India was “Third World.” Technically, Sweden, Finland, Ireland, and Switzerland, having not joined either NATO or the Warsaw Pact, would be Third World Countries. The designation is obsolete not only because the Cold War is over (though we are kind of headed towards “Cold War II: Vladimir Strikes Back”), but because a number of countries of the Warsaw Pact are now in NATO, including, well, the country where Warsaw is located.

Question: How do antibiotics create resistant bacteria?
Answer: It isn’t so much that antibiotics *create* resistant bacteria, as that they *select* for resistant bacteria/give bacteria that are already resistant an evolutionary advantage. Bacteria (and everything else, really) are constantly mutating. Most of these mutations don’t do anything at all, some of these mutations are bad, and a very small number of them are beneficial to the bacterium in some way, but usually only in a very specific situation. For example, let’s say a bacterium has a mutation that allows it to survive in the antibiotic chloramphenicol. If there isn’t any chloramphenicol in the environment, this bacterium is not going to survive any longer, or replicate any faster, than its neighbors who don’t have the mutation. The gene exists, but who cares? It’s present in only a small subset of the population. However, when chloramphenicol is present, then suddenly all of the bacteria in the population are dead, *except* the population that has the resistance gene. And now it is surviving longer, and replicating faster, than cells that don’t have the gene, and after a while your population is made up of bacteria that have chloramphenicol resistance. Now, in real life, this would probably proceed incrementally: lets say you have a mutation that allows a bacterium to survive in chloramphenicol…..kind of. Instead of doubling every 20 minutes, the cells double in 2 hours. That’s still a huge advantage over cells that either straight-up die, or double in 4 hours. OK, so you have this population that doubles in 2 hours. Remember, those cells are still mutating! So the cell that is lucky enough to mutate so that it can now double every 90 minutes….has an advantage over the cells that still double in 2 hours. As long as the chloramphenicol is still present, cells that are better at defeating the chloramphenicol have an evolutionary advantage. As I like to say, “evolution is not your friend.”

Question: Are humans just a vessel for atoms to continuously survive?
Answer: Atoms don’t really “die”, they are continuously recycled and recombined. Now, some atoms fall apart because of radioactive decay, losing protons and neutrons as alpha particles, or electrons or positrons in beta decay. When that happens, the identity of the atom changes (i.e., it becomes a different element). But human life doesn’t have anything to do with that, and in fact, any radioactive isotopes in our bodies right now are decaying at the same rate they usually do.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: We know that ideal gas does not exist. Why do scientists mainly focus on ideal gas?
Answer: The ideal gas law works *pretty well* in most situations, because a lot of the most common gases don’t have strong intermolecular interactions (like nitrogen, oxygen, hydrogen, and the noble gases). I remember doing problems with a non-ideal gas in a thermodynamics course, and the difference between treating the gas as ideal, and treating it as non-ideal, was pretty small (maybe 5% or so), except for special cases where the inter-molecular forces were very strong (like water vapor), the temperature was low, or the pressure was high. It is a lot easier to explain the ideal gas law to middle and high-school students than it is to introduce non-ideal gases, what makes them non-ideal, and then go through the derivations of concepts like fugacity, etc. Sometimes, a simple version that gives us a pretty good approximation is better than a complicated version that gives us something more exact.

Question: How do I forgive myself? I blew it with an amazing girl by being a terrible person I didnt know how bad I was. But at this point I just want to apologize to her the best way I possibly can and leave her be. It hurts but I need to grow up.
Answer: I would go ahead and apologize directly, then leave her be. You might get yelled at, she might not forgive you, but at least you can say “well, I did the best I could at this point.” And quite frankly, sometimes people will be pleasantly surprised that you’re owning up to things, because that’s a hard thing to do and a lot of people either don’t do it, or they half-ass it: don’t say “I’m sorry if I made you feel bad” or “well, I was having a rough time, and I was sorta upset…..” No. Just say, “I did X, that was wrong, and I’m sorry.” In terms of forgiving yourself, think of it this way: you could have behaved like a terrible person but not recognized it and kept being that way! So many people either don’t recognize when they were wrong, or they just don’t care. You’ve learned. So the next time around, with somebody else, don’t make the same mistake. When I look back at the mistakes I made, I sometimes think, “if only I knew then what I know now.” But then I remind myself that, had I not made that mistake, I would not know now what I know now.
