Question: Scientists: Why can't Mycobacterium leprae and Treponema pallidum be grown in pure culture medium?
Answer: Bacteria that can be successfully cultured are actually the exception rather than the rule. The dogma is that only about 1% of all known species can be cultured: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1574-6968.2010.02000.x Now, some dispute this and say that 1% is more of an example of “conventional wisdom” rather than a hard and fast number. But the simple fact of the matter is, a lot of bacteria are so well evolved to living in specific conditions, that it can be hard to get it exactly right.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why might fungi be expected as the source of many compounds that are toxic to bacteria?
Answer: Fungi frequently live with and around many types of bacteria in the wild. They consequently are competing with them for resources, food, nutrients, space, etc. Some bacteria are even directly pathogenic to fungi. So, fungi have evolved to compete against bacteria, and that means chemical warfare, which means antibiotics and other compounds which are toxic to bacteria. The reason fungal-derived antibiotics are useful to us is that they primarily operate in one of two ways. First, fungi produce antibiotics that prevent bacteria from forming a cell wall. Our cells don’t have a cell wall, so there’s nothing to inhibit. The most famous example of this kind of antibiotic is penicillin. The second main type is an antibiotic that specifically targets bacterial ribosomes, and prevents them from making proteins. These ribosomes are generally very distinct from ones found in eukaryotes, and so once again, we aren’t affected.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: The “big three” of the classical world is always considered to be Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven. Apart from these, who would your big three be?
Answer: It’s really hard to limit it to just three, because there are a lot of great composers out there, and even more pretty good composers who had great moments. Haydn definitely has to be up there. I think his reputation has suffered from the fact that in addition to his masterpieces, he also wrote a lot of crap: he was writing on command, and a lot of his pieces came about because someone went “oh, court composer, the Prince wants something new to amuse his guests next Thursday. You can do that, can’t you?” But when he was writing to make an impact (like in his Esterhazy Masses, and his late oratorios The Creation and The Seasons), wow. He was also very inventive, could be funny, wrote for a wide range of instruments and forces, and his style evolved over time. Brahms would also be up there, for his technical proficiency if nothing else. He has the reputation for being boring, but that’s a performance challenge. To play Brahms properly, an ensemble has to be very good with phrasing and dynamics, because Brahms has the unusual property of requiring very precise phrasing. And that is really advanced, and perhaps underappreciated, music-making. Stravinsky, I think, also rates a mention for the influence he had on how music developed in the 20th century. From the choral perspective, Claudio Monteverdi, Giovanni da Palestrina, Thomas Tallis, William Byrd, Tomas Luis de Victoria all rate mentions, because I feel like they are kind of obscure outside of choral circles. But they are all great. Monteverdi did things in the 17th century that wouldn’t be done again until the mid-20th century.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Whose music is considered technically more difficult: Bach's, Mozart's or Beethoven's?
Answer: I am a singer, and from a vocal perspective each composer poses different challenges. It also depends on which piece you’re talking about: Bach wrote some very easy chorales, but he also wrote six motets that are definitely on “hard” mode. However, on balance I would say Mozart is the easiest, Bach is the most difficult, BUT I’m going to caveat that because performing Mozart can be scary in a unique way. First, Mozart. He knows and respects the limit of a choir, doesn’t ask his choirs to do crazy things in terms of range or a lot of rapid notes right next to each other, in general his pieces are very logical and pretty straightforward. Sight-reading is pretty easy. In some ways, he writes like the world’s most-brilliant six year old. HOWEVER, what makes Mozart scary to perform is that the music’s relative simplicity, and very logical nature, means it’s extremely “transparent” or “fragile”: if you make a mistake, it’s obvious, there is nowhere to hide, and the audience will hear it (unlike Bach, where you are usually one moving part among a zillion moving parts, or Benjamin Britten, where if you mess up the audience might go “huh, that’s a weird chord/cadence. Britten, eh?”) Next, Beethoven. Who is a pain in the ass to sing. He probably noticed that good choral composers, like Haydn, occasionally asked their singers to sing at the top of their range when there was a dramatic moment in the music. So ol’ Ludwig said, “aha. Drama! I love drama. So, the choir is just going to live up there at the top of their range! That will make it super dramatic.” Like an enema, Beethoven is “high, hot, and hell of a lot.” But what you’re singing is, chord-chord-chord-chord-chord, and you aren’t as exposed. In fairness, I haven’t sung any of his lieder, which might be better in this respect. Finally, Bach. A friend of mine once said that Bach writes for singers who don’t need to breathe, and that’s largely true. Bach also has a tendency to write a lot of really fast notes really close together, which is hard to do for a singer. You also have to be very precise when singing Bach, because his pieces are arranged like clockwork (Mozart actually heard a couple of Bach pieces, demanded to see the score, and spent a few hours lying on the floor studying it. His mind was blown). Another difficulty in singing Bach is that it is easy to do it “bloodlessly.” Some ensembles focus so much on hitting all the right notes that they end up with a performance that takes all the life out of the piece, and ends up being boring. When performed well, some of the works of Bach can (and I would argue, should) be as emotionally intense as Beethoven. On the other hand, Bach is very logical, and range-wise is relatively comfortable to sing, especially if you take it down a half-step. Who do I really like singing? I would say Haydn or Brahms, because they really know how to make a choir sound good without asking too much.

Question: Do bacteria have an exoskeleton?
Answer: Not exactly an “exoskeleton”, but something functionally similar. Bacteria have an outer cell wall, made up of sugars (polysaccharides). It’s basically a tough outer layer that is there to protect the inside part of the bacterium. The cell wall grows with the bacteria, and when the cell divides, a new cell-wall partition is built to split the single cell into two. An exoskeleton is also a polysaccharide, known as chitin. And it serves a similar protective function. So it’s the same idea, but not exactly the same.

Question: If scientists are able to print human organs, then why aren't these human organs given to people who need them?
Answer: This is actually a very interesting question! I’ll start by generally saying that it’s really hard to make an organ, and perhaps the most miraculous thing about our lives is the fact that our heart, brain, kidneys, livers, etc. all end up in the right places. We still don’t know exactly how or why that happens. More specifically, there are a few problems with printed organs, which means they are probably not going to be implanted anytime soon: Bottom line, despite some amazing advances (and I worked in this field: there’s a lot of good work going on), the technology is not quite there yet. But I think within 20 years or so, we will probably be able to implant organs that were grown in a vat.

Question: Why do parents think they know what's best for their kids when they actually barely know us at all most the time? I'm just wondering because my parents always say like, "Oh, because I know what's best for you!" Or something along those lines.
Answer: I’m in my 30s, so I think I’ve got a little of your parent’s perspective, but also remember what it was like to be young, so please hear me out. There are two downsides to having life experience. The first is that you tend to downplay the crises of early adulthood, and the second is, you forget what it was like to not have that experience. Some of the things that were a huge deal for me back in high school (where will I go to college? Does Hannah like me? Does anybody like me?), really don’t matter now: I went to a college that was good-enough, I found a woman who was a better fit for me than Hannah was, and I moved out of state and haven’t been in touch with anyone from High School in years, so now none of that popularity stuff really matters. So it’s easy for me to say “ah, that was just kid’s stuff, I didn’t really have to worry.” But that’s only because I know more of my life’s story. At the time, it was a huge deal, my feelings about them were real, and I didn’t know that everything was going to turn out alright. To put this in perspective, what was something you were really upset about, or really worried about, when you were six years old? Does any of that stuff bother you now? Believe it or not, when you get older, you’ll feel the same about the age you are right now. The other problem, forgetting what it was like to not have that experience, means that it’s hard to logically explain to someone why a certain course of action is a bad idea, because, well, it’s perfectly obvious to you. Think about a baby crawling to the edge of a table or cliff. Can you explain to the baby, rationally and in a way that they will understand, why it’s a bad idea to crawl closer to that edge? Similarly, there are some “cliffs of life” that seem so damn *obvious* after you’ve lived for a while, that it’s hard to explain what they are exactly, or why they are dangerous. You can quote statistics or something, but it’s hard to convince someone using those statistics, because (and adults make this mistake too!), we are all convinced that we will be one of the lucky ones who beats the odds. A challenge for parents is, not all cliffs are equally dangerous. I think about all the mistakes I made, and all the pain I felt as a result, and I want my kid to avoid making the same mistake, and feeling the same pain. I also think about all the mistakes I’m really glad I *didn’t* make, which I know that some of my classmates did make (alcohol, drugs, pregnancy, reckless driving), and I really, really don’t want my kid to fall down that path, because I’ve seen what happens. If I thought my kid were going down that bad path, I would no doubt make myself extremely obnoxious in trying to change their course. But there are two problems here. The first is, some of those very painful mistakes taught me some very valuable lessons, things I would not have learned otherwise. And even if I could go back in time and say “hey, I’m you, from the future. Don’t do X”, I know I wouldn’t have listened. On the other hand, if I had gone back in time and said “be sure not to drink and drive!”, past-me would have said “thank you, Captain Obvious!” Last, you have to remember that your parents grew up in a different world, with different problems and ways of solving them. If you were suddenly transported back to 1990, how do you order a pizza? Find your way to a party? Figure out where the party was happening? Remember, no smartphones or even cell phones unless you were really rich! Bottom line is, your parents would know how to do this, and they might still largely do it this way because it still works. They didn’t have to contend with social media or some of the other dreadful things of our modern era, and so don’t really know how to deal with them exactly. And a funny thing about the internet: I remember, back in the early-to-mid 90’s, that the internet was considered a reputable source of information. It’s true! It used to be a nerdy, academic thing, with most of the content being created and curated by the kinds of people who knew how to code while also having an interest in beekeeping. Boy howdy, are things different now. However….. What your parents are going off of is analogous (perhaps “analogue-ous”) experience. And while it might not be perfectly fitting to what you are experiencing today, it might still be valuable because people, and institutions, by and large, have not changed. The cyberbullies of today are basically the same insecure losers as the face-to-face bullies of yesteryear. Rumors that circulate on Facebook today would have circulated in the hallways at school back in 2001. I’d hear urban legends in the school cafeteria, before it was called “fake news.” The school administration was constantly coming up with stupid “school spirit” events in my day too. I had girls I was interested in not answering my phone messages. So maybe instead of focusing on the letter of your parents’ advice, focus on the spirit of it. Odds are, they know more than you might think.

Question: Whenever my girl calls me she always tells me she will call me later and later, however she takes a long time to call me and makes excuses why she haven't been calling me. I fear that she is betraying me while I'm not expecting it. What do I do?
Answer: Generally, if people want to get in touch with you, or be with you, they will find the time. If she doesn’t find the time, that suggests she’s just not that into you, and you should find somebody else. It sucks, it’s hard to accept that, and it took me a lot of heartache to learn and accept that. Unfortunately when it comes to relationships, oftentimes the truth sucks. Breaking up with someone, or telling them you are not interested, face to face or on the phone, is really hard to do. It’s awkward, and most of the time we don’t want to disappoint people by saying “I’m just not into you” or “I’m just not into you anymore.” We might really like some aspects of a person, but for whatever reason, we don’t want a relationship. That’s something I didn’t understand until I was the one who had to dump somebody, and in one case, I dumped someone by ghosting her. I’m not proud of that, it was wrong, but I understand why some partners ghosted me. On a slightly darker note, some of my friends have told me about their experiences with men who have become verbally abusive, or even violent, after being turned down. Aside from the awkwardness, sometimes people do have concerns for their physical safety when breaking up with someone, and so drift away instead. I’m afraid that the tone of your question, where you are worried about being “betrayed”, and the fact that your girlfriend feels compelled to make excuses, suggests that you might be a somewhat jealous and possessive person. Here’s my question: how many times do you call *her* in a given day, if she hasn’t responded? If the answer is “more than once”, you need to back the hell off. Why are you calling her each day? If your answer is, “because I’m worried she’s sleeping with someone else”, you need to back off. She may very well be afraid of how you will react if she comes out and tells you that she wants to break up. So here’s what I think you should do: you should break up, because she doesn’t seem to be that into you. While you are single, you should honestly reflect on yourself, and how you relate to your romantic partners.

Question: Which actors have not won Oscars despite an Oscar-worthy performance?
Answer: Jackie Gleason was terrific in The Hustler and Requiem for a Heavyweight. He got an Oscar nomination for The Hustler, but no wins (tough competition for Supporting Actor that year: he was competing against George C. Scott for his role in the same movie, among others, and watching The Hustler it’s hard to say whose performance is “better.”) Unfortunately, he was best known for being Ralph Kramden, and being primarily a comedic actor, despite delivering some very solid performances. I am a big fan of Paul Giamatti. He has been nominated a couple of times for Best Supporting Actor, but hasn’t won. His range and his ability to play supporting characters is phenomenal, and I hope he gets the nod. William Powell got nominated three times, with no wins. Which is a shame, because he had a way of playing low-key characters very well. Edward G. Robinson won an honorary award, but had never been nominated for an acting award. Which is a real shame: he got typecast as a gangster (which is something he did very well), but he had a lot more range than he is commonly credited with (he stole a bunch of scenes from Steve McQueen in The Cincinnati Kid, by out-cooling McQueen, if you can believe it.) “I don’t need no little statues to tell me I can act, see? Academy’s gettin’ to be that it can dish it out, but it can’t take it no more.” Fred MacMurray, I was stunned to find, was never even nominated for an Oscar, despite very, very good outings in Double Indemnity and The Caine Mutiny. I have no idea why he wasn’t nominated for either, or both, of those movies. Speaking of Double Indemnity, Barbara Stanwyck was nominated for an Oscar 5 times (including for Double Indemnity), but only won an honorary award. She really should have won one. “We’re going to get a goose egg on this one, baby. Straight down the line.” Amazingly, despite being nominated in all acting categories in 1951, none of the stars of Sunset Boulevard got the nod for the Oscar. Granted, competition was stiff in that year, but come on! Gloria Swanson was terrific, and never won an Oscar despite 3 nominations. “What do you mean? I AM big. It’s the PICTURES that got small!” Agnes Moorehead, I was really surprised to find, also never won an Oscar despite 4 nominations. I mean, for crying out loud, she was the only person who gave a watchable performance in The Conqueror (the infamous movie that starred John Wayne as Genghis Khan). (Yes, this movie does have to be seen to be believed. In this shot, Agnes Moorehead can hardly believe it). There’s a whole list of Academy snubs, and I have to agree that most of the actors and actresses on the list should have won at least once: Academy Awards Mistakes and Omissions

Question: Why can bacteria grow in just water considering there are no nutrients?
Answer: Depends on the bacterium, and depends what you mean by water. You would have a hard time growing any kind of bacteria in distilled water, because they need trace nutrients from the environment in order to survive. In something like ocean water, there are more nutrients present than you might think. Furthermore, cyanobacteria are capable of making their own food given sufficient sunlight, provided that they have the right trace nutrients present in the surrounding water. A lot of bacteria simply will not grow in just water, or buffer. In fact, one trick we used to play in the lab if we wanted to keep E. coli alive, but didn’t want it to divide, was to put the cells in phosphate buffered saline, which is basically water, salt, and phosphate. I should also point out that many bacteria are fussy about what conditions they will grow in. A good 90–99% of bacteria actually cannot be cultured/we don’t know how to culture them, separate from their native conditions.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Who are some of the worst actors to have won acting Oscars? The one that stands out for me is Ernest Borgnine.
Answer: It all depends on what you mean by “worst.” John Wayne won an Oscar for “True Grit,” and as a cowboy/Western hero/John Wayne, he was a very good actor. As Genghis Khan, however….. “My heart lusts for the Tartar woman, Pilgrim.” Sir Ben Kingsley also comes to mind: he’s generally a very good actor, but he’s been in some extremely crappy movies. What we forget is that a movie is a team effort, and to get a truly great performance out of an actor, or to have that great performance remembered as part of a great film, you need a great script, a great director, good lighting, etc. For instance, if you watch Bela Lugosi through most of his career (and especially the stuff he made with Ed Wood), you realize that he’s actually a very good actor. But he’s remembered as a schlock actor, because what he played in was usually low-budget, badly-written schlock. Similarly, especially in the studio era, actors got typecast. So they didn’t get to show their range, or acting chops, because you were expecting Jimmy Cagney to be a ruthless gangster, Edward G. Robinson to also be a ruthless gangster, Henry Fonda to be a heroic man of conscience, Peter Lorre to be the vaguely creepy foreign assistant to the bad guy, and so forth (and each of these actors could and did very successfully play against type, in films like Yankee Doodle Dandy, Double Indemnity, Once Upon a Time in the West, M, etc.) I’d argue that it is hard to judge an actor’s quality, if all he or she ever got to play was one type. Judging actor quality is ultimately all about taste. I personally think Laurence Olivier, Marlon Brando, Richard Burton, and Grace Kelly are overrated (in Brando’s case, WAY overrated), but obviously, there are a lot of people who disagree with me.

Question: Can you connect a Benjamin Franklin invention to a famous composer?
Answer: Of course there’s the invention of the armonium, which Mozart composed for, but why stop there? Benjamin Franklin was famous for his experiments in electricity and magnetism. Which was essential to the eventual invention of the Moog synthesizer, which was famously used for the 1968 album “Switched-on Bach.” Work in electromagnetism was also critical to the invention of the Theremin, which was used by Dimitri Shostakovich in film scores and other works. Benjamin Franklin discovered the Gulf Stream, which makes a key contribution to the climate of Europe, which in turn inspired Franz Joseph Haydn’s oratorio “The Seasons.” Franklin invented bifocals, which Haydn would have definitely appreciated while writing The Seasons, as Haydn was a really old geezer by that time. Franklin may have met, or carried on a correspondence with, William Herschel, who was not just an astronomer, but a composer as well. Most importantly, Benjamin Franklin invented AMERICA, which Aaron Copeland spent so much time trying to capture in music.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it fair to end a conversation with a scientist if he or she says that oxygen is really a kind of poison?
Answer: It is essential to human life, but despite that, oxygen IS a kind of poison: it will kill certain bacteria known as obligate anaerobic bacteria, for instance. Respiration, which uses oxygen and is what keeps our cells going, also leads to the formation of radical species that cause cellular damage. This damage is quickly repaired by cells, and cells are gradually replaced throughout our lives, but eventually as we age, our bodies become less able to repair the damage caused by the processes that keep us alive. In short, we are all slowly rusting. High concentrations of oxygen can be dangerous: when breathing oxygen at high partial pressures, you can get unpleasant effects on the lungs and nervous systems, like convulsions, dizziness, even seizures: Oxygen toxicity - Wikipedia This is also not to mention the fact that high oxygen concentrations will lead to very intense fires, as we saw on Apollo 1: Apollo 1 - Wikipedia Chemists using liquid nitrogen are warned about the dangers posed by liquid oxygen. In some cases when you’re using a vacuum line, you cool part of that vacuum line with liquid nitrogen. It’s called a cold trap, and it lets you get a much higher vacuum. However, we are repeatedly warned to pump the vacuum down to a pretty low level before we apply the liquid nitrogen, and this is because if you apply the liquid nitrogen right away, at atmospheric pressure, you will create liquid oxygen in the trap. It’s a beautiful blue color, but if you see it, you’re supposed to stop what you’re doing, turn off the vacuum, ventilate, and whatever you do, don’t do any chemistry while ventilating. The reason for that is, oxygen reacts with damn near everything. Concentrated oxygen reacts very quickly with damn near everything. There is a risk of explosion if you see liquid oxygen in your cold trap. In conclusion, just because something is vital to life doesn’t mean it isn’t also a poison. That goes for a lot of things that are vital to life: a little phosphorous is essential, but too much phosphorous is deadly, in very nasty ways. You need a tiny amount of selenium, but more than that, and you’re in trouble. As the old adage goes, ’tis the dose that makes the poison.

Question: Which intermolecular forces depend on the polarizability of molecules?
Answer: There are dipole-dipole interactions, which are either the result of permanent dipoles, or induced dipoles. The induced dipole interactions are Van der Waals and dispersion forces. Permanent dipole interactions include hydrogen bonds, and what are simply referred to as “dipole-dipole bonds.”

Question: Would a 'theoretical' metal heated at a temperature of 2000-8000° C be able to kill all* surface microbes (Assuming constant temperature)?
Answer: You don’t really need temperatures that high to kill everything or almost everything on a surface: if you run things through an autoclave at 15 psi of steam at 121C for an hour, that will pretty much take care of it. Dry-heat wise, you only need 160C for a few hours, and that will do the trick. Basically, you don’t need temperatures that high to ensure sterility, or a pretty good level of sterility.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What came first, science or technology?
Answer: I would argue that technology came first, WAY first, because technology is a way of doing either new things, or doing old things better, whereas science is a method of describing the universe, as well as a technique and mode of thinking that allows us to do so rigorously. Spear points, the atlatl, the bow, fire, the wheel, pottery, textiles, animal husbandry, etc., are all examples of technology. But the people making them did not develop (nor were they really all that interested in developing), theories of physics, chemistry, or biology, or genetics. Basically, by tinkering, some really neat things were invented without systematically studying the world around us, and this is technological, rather than scientific, progress. I would argue that actual scientific study is a relatively recent phenomenon, dating to the Early Modern period and really gaining steam in the Industrial Revolution. Experimental physics started with Galileo, chemistry, as distinct from alchemy, has its origins in the 18th century, and the two cornerstones of modern biology, genetics and evolution, didn’t take off until the 19th century.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: As a PhD student, each time I came up with an idea, I found out someone's had/published it before. Can't come up with bright new ideas, what should I do, what's missing in me, what is it that I'm doing wrong?
Answer: Answering this from a scientist’s perspective: the best thing to do is have a lot of ideas. Some of them will be good, some of them will be bad, and some of them will have been done already. Eventually, you’ll find a good, novel idea, and really sink your teeth into it. You should actually feel pleased with yourself that you are coming up with ideas that have already been done: what that means is that your idea is plausible, and can be done! You should also feel pleased with the fact that you found out that your idea has already been done…..because it means your literature search has been focused, relevant, and thorough enough to find out that this is the case. Some of the other posters have pointed out, and they are correct, that even if your idea has already been done, you should still ask yourself, how well has it been done? Is there still something there that has been overlooked, or that is still a problem faced by practitioners in the field? Is there something you can improve? After all, if your idea is “it would be really neat to make carbon-carbon bonds”, well, yes, that has been done. But can you make those bonds with less energy, in a more “green” fashion, with better control of the shape of the molecule after the bond is made (what we call “enantioselectivity”) or with better control of where that bond is being made on a molecule (what we call “regioselectivity”). There are whole careers made out of “doing the same-old, same-old” only slightly better. Last, and here’s something that I haven’t seen in a lot of other responses: don’t expect that your thesis is going to be earth-shattering, and the greatest work ever. A lot of theses are frankly kind of blah (mine included). But consider, depending on your field, 40% (!) of your classmates will not complete one. My thesis is blah, that’s true. But it is infinitely better than all the theses that were never written or defended. So, two wise things I heard were, 1) the greatest virtue of a thesis is completeness, and 2) the thesis is your first major work of original scholarship. It’s not going to be your best, and if you keep working as a scholar, it shouldn’t be your best.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Why did Poland never try claim money from Germany for massive attack & massive damage to the country?
Answer: There are a few things about this question. First, the current Polish government is trying to claim reparations from Germany: Germany owes Poland over $850 billion in WW2 reparations: senior lawmaker Second, Germany did pay reparations to some Polish citizens after the war, such as small pensions paid to former forced laborers: my grandmother was one of them. Third, the biggest reparation that Germany was forced to pay to Poland was the cession of the so-called “reclaimed lands”, which led to a new border between Germany and Poland along the Rivers Oder and Neisse. The cities of Stettin, Posen, and Breslau are now Polish (Szczeczin, Poznań, and Wrocław). At the same time, the Soviets took over part of what was once Eastern Poland (so Lwów and Wilno are now Lviv and Vilnius, part of Ukraine and Lithuania, respectively), meaning that Poland was basically shifted to the West after the war. The territorial changes were probably the biggest single reparation the Germans paid after the war. Oder–Neisse line - Wikipedia Now, the question is, are these reparations sufficient? And that’s a debatable question. Poland waived reparations against East Germany in 1954, under Soviet pressure, but one could argue that Poland at that time was a Soviet satellite state, and not truly independent. Furthermore, Poland never waived its claims against *West* Germany. And technically speaking, the present Federal Republic of Germany *is* West Germany (German unification in 1990 happened on the legal basis of West Germany annexing East Germany). So Poland may still have a case.

Question: What does Shakespeare mean by “fatal loins”?
Answer: “Fatal” in this sense means “fated” or “ill-fated”, and loins would be, well…..where babies come from. So, Montague and Capulet’s children are doomed. In the “Original Pronunciation” of Shakespeare, or our best guess as to how the language sounded to Shakespeare, “loins” is a pun: it is pronounced like “lines”, so “from forth the fatal LINES of these two foes”, meaning “the ill-fated descendants of Montague and Capulet.”

Question: Are viruses gram-positive or negative?
Answer: They would be, I suppose, gram negative: the gram staining only affects a thick peptidoglycan layer, which a virus doesn’t have. Generally, “gram staining” is a way of distinguishing types of bacteria.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does freezing raw milk kill bacteria?
Answer: In general, freezing things doesn’t kill all of the bacteria present in a sample: sure, ice crystals will form in some cell walls, and kill off some of the cells, but other cells will remain behind, in a dormant state. Given the right cryoprotectant (something that is added to prevent ice crystals from forming in the cell walls, and rupturing the cell walls), you can actually store bacterial samples for years as frozen stocks, and revive them later. If you want to kill off bacteria, you should use heat (boiling, or pasteurization). If you want to preserve something, you can freeze it (basically, bacteria won’t grow, or won’t grow very much, when frozen. So when you thaw out whatever it is you have frozen, you don’t have *more* bacteria than when you started/did the initial freezing).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What is a blunt end in biology?
Answer: A blunt end is called a blunt end in contrast with a sticky end. When many restriction enzymes cut a piece of DNA, it leaves behind an overhang, like in the restriction enzyme EcoRI: The green line is where the enzyme actually cuts. So on the top strand, you end up with AATT, unpaired, and on the bottom strand you end up with TTAA, unpaired. What this means is that the AATT is free to pair up with TTAA from a *completely different strand* of DNA, which is called recombination. However, the AATT will pair specifically with TTAA, because that’s how base pairs work. In contrast, some restriction enzymes such as SmaI cut differently: Notice how the cut is straight between the two strands, and there is no “overhang.” This is what is know as a blunt end, because the strands are cut in half and there’s nothing “sticky.” You start with one piece of DNA, and end up with two pieces, with squared-off ends.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Are any plays of the past 70 years, besides Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, worthy of placement alongside Oedipus the King, Hamlet, and King Lear?
Answer: I think the works of August Wilson are definitely up there, but for whatever reason he’s not as well known outside of Pittsburgh. A Raisin in the Sun is also extremely good. Steel Magnolias is a very good play, a better play than the movie adaptation. A Man for All Seasons is almost Neo-Shakespearian in the way that it is written, and in the subject matter that it talks about. It’s also an extremely good play. Arthur Miller writes extremely well, though some of his stuff can come off as over the top after a while. Noises Off is perhaps the funniest play I have ever seen. But you have to see it. On paper, it doesn’t look like much. Ultimately, however, it is impossible to know which plays are “as good”, or as enduring, as Sophocles, or Shakespeare, because not enough time has passed to allow lesser plays to be forgotten. It’s also hard to know which plays will stand the test of time once what they reference has passed from memory, because, well, we still remember what Arthur Miller was talking about. I can’t help but wonder if the entire genre of plays that could be titled “dysfunctional American families yelling at each other” will be quietly forgotten once the United States changes, disappears entirely, or no longer has the idea of the “American Dream” that, in its failure to be realized, hangs over most American plays of the 20th century.

Question: If you could assemble a cabinet from former presidents only, who would you pick and for what job would you pick him?
Answer: This is a very interesting question! Because we have so many cabinet positions, about 1 in 4 presidents would have to get a job. And it’s partially for that reason that I’m going to skip the 7 “cabinet-level positions” like Chief of Staff or Trade Representative, because if they were included, about half of all the presidents would have to get a job in the cabinet. But here are my picks: State- Richard Nixon. While best known for Watergate and generally being a creepy-looking and creepy-sounding guy, he was an excellent poker player, and was widely respected as an expert on foreign affairs, even after his resignation in disgrace. He engineered normalization of relations with China, managed to get the US out of the Vietnam War, and advised his successors (of both parties!) on foreign policy. Treasury- Umm…..I can’t think of many presidents who would be great for this job. Bill Clinton? He was, after all, the last president to balance the budget. Defense- Dwight Eisenhower. As Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force, he knew a thing or two about coordinating the military. Attorney General- John Adams. Absolutely incorruptible, almost annoyingly so. And a talented lawyer. Possible runner-up would be William Howard Taft, who had a fine legal mind that he later applied to being Chief Justice of the United States. Interior- Theodore Roosevelt. Conservationist, major booster of the national parks, spent a lot of time living in the West, which is what the Interior Department manages mostly. I think he could do the job well. Agriculture- Commerce- Labor- Health and Human Services- Housing and Urban Development- Transportation- Energy- Jimmy Carter. What most people don’t realize is that the Department of Energy is responsible for maintaining America’s nuclear arsenal. So who better to run it than a former commander of a nuclear submarine? And we’d get to see his sweaters again, and who wouldn’t love that? Education- Veteran’s Affairs- Homeland Security- George H.W. Bush. After all, he was the only President who also had experience as head of the CIA.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: What are multiple cloning sites and their functions?
Answer: A multiple cloning site is simply a part of a plasmid that is located somewhere convenient, like directly below a promoter or tag, and which contains a lot of restriction sites which are unique to that plasmid (for instance, the plasmid has only 1 SacI site, 1 BamHI site, and 1 HindIII site). The idea is, you can put your gene of interest into the plasmid at the multiple cloning site using a bunch of different restriction enzymes/your choice of restriction enzyme (so for instance, you could use SacI and HindIII to insert your gene of interest in the example I gave). This is useful if you are transferring a gene of interest from one plasmid to another, or if you have designed primers to pull something off by PCR, and added in those particular restriction sites.

Question: Is it possible for us to invent like a bag that contains predigested food and when we need large amounts of energy we hook the bag to our blood stream and therefore we get rapid amounts of energy instantly?
Answer: Interestingly enough, one hypothesis for why obesity has become so prevalent in the developed world is that we tend to eat a lot of processed foods. The processing makes the food softer, and easier to digest, meaning that we get more net calories from the processed foods (which are in a sense, pre-digested), rather than an equivalent amount of food that isn’t as processed (and which we have to invest more energy in actually breaking up).

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Does Andrew Jackson deserve to be on the 20 dollar bill?
Answer: Putting Jackson on the 20 dollar bill was actually an epic act of trolling: Jackson HATED paper currency, and destroyed the Second National Bank of the United States, which was the forerunner of the Federal Reserve. Well, his face is now on paper money, on which is prominently printed “FEDERAL RESERVE NOTE.” Jackson would have been absolutely incensed to find himself on paper money printed by the spiritual successor of the very bank that he was able to destroy.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: In what temperature does bacteria grow the best?
Answer: It depends on the species of bacterium. E. coli are most happy at 37 degrees C. Others prefer 30 degrees, and others prefer higher and more extreme temperatures: Growth conditions There’s a really cool effect you can observe at Yellowstone National Park that comes from the fact that bacteria have different temperature preferences. This is Morning Glory Pool: Note how the center of the pool is bright blue, then moving towards the edge the pool looks more green, then yellow, then red? Well, that’s because the pool is hottest in the center (where there’s a geothermal vent), and cooler further away from the center. Different microorganisms are thriving at those different temperatures: the ones that grow best in the highest temperatures produce blue pigment, and those that grow best at the “lowest” temperatures (in this case, around 50C, so still pretty hot), are colored red, and live best at the edges. Cool, isn’t it?!

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Which one of Shakespeare's works should I read first?
Answer: I would start with the comedies, because they tend to be simpler and sometimes downright silly. I would suggest “Much Ado about Nothing.” The plot is pretty simple and straightforward, it’s funny, and most of it is written in prose rather than in verse, so the characters basically talk like normal people except when they are being melodramatic, and they switch to verse. A Midsummer Night’s Dream is also pretty simple, there’s magic, and love, and mistaken identity, and it ends with a hilarious play-within-a-play, where Shakespeare basically parodies himself, and the actors of his day. Of the tragedies, I think Julius Caesar and Macbeth are the places to start, because the plots are relatively straightforward. I would steer away from the Histories, unless you are a history nerd like I am. Shakespeare basically assumes his audience knows who he is talking about, because he is referring to events that happened 150 years before his time. So basically, if I were to write a play or movie for an American audience today, I wouldn’t have to explain who Abe Lincoln was. But in 400 years, you’d probably have to put in a footnote.

Name: Mark Kozlowski
Question: Is it better to watch a Shakespeare play (say on YouTube) in order to understand it? It seems that that seeing the acting/body language will be much more useful than sitting down and reading from a book.
Answer: I think the very best way to fully experience Shakespeare is to see it live, in front of a full audience. It’s really hard to explain, but there is a kind of magic in being a few feet (OK, a few dozen feet) away from the actors. Also, you can hear, and sometimes even *feel* the audience reacting to things, and that effect is lost behind a computer screen. The other disadvantage of a filmed version of a stage play is that in a film, you’re only focusing on one or two actors at a time. In some scenes, it’s really best to be able to see all the characters on stage at once (one of them might be doing something funny in the background, for instance. This can sometimes be the whole point of some scenes, like in Much Ado about Nothing, where you have two characters “accidentally” overhearing some gossip about them, and of course, reacting when that gossip is unflattering. It’s all a trick, and the people doing the gossiping know that these characters are listening). The other advantage of seeing a performance is that the hard work of “what does all this language mean anyway?” has already been done for you, if the director and the actors are any good. There will sometimes be lines where, as long as the actor knows what he or she is saying, and says it with conviction, you sort of get the gist, even if you don’t understand all the words. If you’d prefer to watch Shakespeare from the comfort of home, I’d recommend watching Shakespeare movies that were made as movies, rather than watching YouTube videos of stage plays. For nerdy Shakespeare-loving reasons, I have complicated feelings about Ken Branagh’s “Much Ado about Nothing” (1993), but it is a very good movie for people trying to get in to Shakespeare: Much Ado About Nothing (1993 film) - Wikipedia. I also really like the BBC’s Hollow Crown series, at least the first one (haven’t seen the second one). That would be Richard II, 1&2 Henry IV, and Henry V. I have heard good things about “Chimes at Midnight” (1966), but have not seen it.
